div.p: K EATING'S COUGH LOZENGES.

EATIN G'S COUGH LOZENGES. 11 "94, Commercial Road, Peckham, July 12, 1889. " Dear Sir,—l am a poor hand at expressing my feelings on paper, but I should like to thank you, for your lozenges have done wonders tor me in relieving my terrible coagh. Since I had the operation of Tracheotomy ' (the same as the late Emperor, of Germany, and unlike him, thank God, I am still alive and getting on well) performed at St. Eartholomew's Hospital for abduct, or paralysis of the vocal chords, no one could possibly have had a more violent cough ; indeed, it was so bad at times that it quite exhausted me. The mucus also, which was very copious and hard, has been softened, and I have been able to get rid of it without difficulty.—l am, sir, yours truly, "Mr. T. Keating." " J. HILL."

div.head: "CAPITAL CHAT."
div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."

The Solicitor-General, Sir Edward Clarke, Q.C., M.P., Las been retained in behalf of Sir William Gordon-Cumming in the forthcoming action which that gentleman is bringing in connection with what is known as the card scandal case. The action, however, is not likely to be reached for some con- siderable time to come.

The Government are particularly anxious to com- bat the impression that their decision to appoint a Royal Commission on the labour question owes any impetus to Lord Randolph Churchill. Mr. Smith last night mentioned that the decision was come to on Saturday, presumably at the Cabinet Council; whereas Lord Randolph's speech was not delivered till some hors after the Cabinet had separated.

An ugly man competition between lady artists was recently held at Edinburgh. The pictures, we are glad to hear, were all drawn from imagination. But amid the diversity of hideousness that reigned throughout the exhibition one uniform characteristic repeated itself in every picture. All the ugly ones were depicted wrth their hair parted in the middle. Henceforth no Adonis when arranging his ambrosial locks will dare to say to tile comb in nwcao tutissimus

One of the batch of newly-created Queen's Counsel, Mr. F. J. Leese, is amongst the ablest of the advanced Liberal candidates fot Parliament. He fought brilliantly for the AccringtonDivision of Lancashire at the last election, being defeated by Hermon Hodge. Historically, the seat is Liberal property, it having formed part of Lord Hartington's old constituency. Mr. Leese is a familiar figure in the Law Courts, the assizes at Slanchester and Liverpool, and on the cricket field, where he has gained distinction.

The " Star " says :—Our statement that Justice Stephen was about to resign, notwithstanding the alleged official contradiction, is again confirmed. Professional opinion is that in the interests of jus- tice the resignation should take effect at once. Justice Stephen's eccentricities on the Bench have been allowed to continue quite long enough. "The truth is," as a legal journal says, "his lordship is not well." It is, therefore, in his lordship's own interest ta retire and receive that special attention which his cb,se requires.

The race of Liberal peers is not to grow extinct. They are about to receive another recruit. It is said that the young Lord Beauchamp is sound at heart, and is developing into a sturdy Radical. It is whispered, too, that a prominent member of the Radical wing in the House, not unconnected with the new peer, has been quietly influencing him for some time past. He has noble examples enough be- fore him—Roseberry, Spencer, and Aberdeen. Every one will look with interest, on the career of the young lord if what is said be true.

The Earl of Albemarle, who died on Saturday, was, except General Whichcote, the last surviving officer xs ho fought at Waterloo. The great biittle will soon pass into ancient history. He wrote his reminiscences of the fight a few years ago and gave a graphic description of the terrible waiting game, while the French cannon played long bowls at the English Infantry lying behind the crest of the hill. Every now and then a shot knocked a soldier over. Asked what was hP thinking of, Earl Albemarle— he was sixteen at the time—said he could not get out of his mind a reply Tom Cribb gave his father. Cribb was training for a prize fight for the cham- pionship, and Albemarle the elder asked him what he thought of the coming mill. "I wish it was fit, sir," replied the pugilist. •

The text of the letter Mr. Parnell wrote to Mr. Rhodes after the Hawarden interview has nevei been publisheq, though \fr. Parnell has read some sentences from it. Private information received from Capetown shows that the letter was under- stood by Mr. Rhodes as an acceptance of the Home Rule scheme sketched by Mr. Gladstone, and this impression was conveyed to persons at Capetown to whom Mr. Rhodes showed the communication. Con- troversy on the matter might be stayed if Mr. Par- nell were to publish the text of the letter,the origi- nal of which he has in his possezesion, it having been returned to him at his request. Failing that, Mr. Rhodes, who has a copy of the letter, might set forth its exact terms. That is a course to which Mr. Parnell naturally could have no objection.

Ministers are greatly annoyed at the smallness of the Ministerial majority (34) On the Welsh dises- tablishment question. The division ,must have been the subject of talk at the Cabinet Council, and it is said that Lord Salisbury anti Mr. Smith had subse- quently a conference on the matter. The Prime Minister is irritated by these small Ministerial majorities, which he regards as weakening to the Government. The fact is that a good many Con- servatives recognise that the Welsh Church is in as hopeless a position as the Irish Ch arch in 1868, and they are not disposed to assist in buttressing it up. Several Tories purposely abstained from the divi- sion on Friday, and others having come down to ,vote against Mr. Morley's resolution, probably thought that they had done enough for the Govern- ment for one week.

A rumour in the House of Commons persistently associates the name of a prominent though not im- portant member with a pending divorce case which is likely to attract a good deal of attention. The house has, however, always been inclined to play practical jokes with the member in question, -though this linking of his name to a pending action is neither friendly nor humorous. About another .case shortly coming on in the Divorce Court, where the respondent is a member of the Upper .House, i there s unfortunately no doubt. The case is actually in preparation. The respondent is one of the youngest members of the House of Peers, bearing an historic name. The case is a very peculiar one, a notable feature in it being that an actual divorce is not asked for, but merely a judicial separation.

A suggestive leaflet has just been issued by the Liberal publication Department. A majority of Liberal Unionists voted, it appears, against every one of the following reforms : Abolition of plural voting for guardians. Reform of the parish vestries. Travelling ( Ic.penses to County Councillors. Control of the London Police by the London County Council.

The division of the rates between owner and occupier. District and parochial councils. The creation of popularly elected allotment authorities. The regulation of railway hours by the Board of Trade. The amendment of the law of conspiracy. • The Religious Disabilities Ilemoval Bill. The Abolition of the Livery Franchise. Welsh Disestablishment, Free Education. Scotch Disestablishm,,, n t Revision of tithes. State assistance to technical t ion. Of course, it goes without sayin,., that the Conserva- tives to a man voted against airthese motions also. Yet these are the persons to whose tender mercies Lord Randolph Churchill calls on the English work- ' ing man Lo aonficle his future hopes.

Members below the gangway on the Opposition 1 side are on the alert to prevent any action on the part of the Government that will lead to another Soudan expedition. In order the better to keep their eye on the course of events in the district q Tokar, the Under Secretary for Foreign Affairs is being pressed to place in the tea-room a map show- ing the frontiers of the newly-annexed territory.

Osman Digna, writes a correspondent who knows him, is not a fighting man, but neither is he a der- vish, nor a saint,nor even a fanatical believer in the Mandi and the righteousness of the cause. he preaches to his followers. He is simply a ruined trader, broken by successful competition on the one hand, and by unfortunate slave ventures on the other, and at the outset his sole object in raising rebellion in the Eastern provinces of the Soudan, and thereby blocking the trade route to Berber, Kordofan,and Darfur,was revenge upon his success- ful rivals at Suakim and Djeddah.

Mr. Ricketts, vicar of Hayfield, Stockport, objects to the description of Sunday schools as" nurseries for Heaven." Of late he assures us our Sunday schools have taken rather to train young people to "tread the stage gracefully and sing bewitch- ingly." Presumptively this means that with their religious training the Sunday school pupils receive some instruction in elocution and music. The sorrowful result, if we may trust this authority, is that they are aspiring not to be a "Joseph," a "Samuel," or a "Timothy," but rather to be an "Irving," a "Sims Reeves," or an " Adelina Patti."

It is now practically settled that the German Emperor is to come to England on a visit to the Queen at the end of June, and he will be present at the wedding of Princess Louise of Schleswig- Holstein and Prince Aribert of Anhalt - Dessau, which is to take place on or about July 1, at Wind- sor, in St. George's Chapel. The Emperor will reside at Buckingham Palace during his stay in London, and he is to be the guest of the Queen at Windsor Castle for a few days during the welding week. The Emperor will stay in England for about ten days, dividing the time between London and Windsor.

The Marquis of Normanby's appointment to the canonry of Windsor closes one of the most extraor- dinary lists of Church patronage that can ever 'nave fallen to the lot of a Prime Minister to fill within the space of twelve months. The list includes an archbishopric, seven bishoprics, five deaneries, and five canonries. The episcopal appointments have been to the sees.of -York, Durham, Winchester, Ban- gor, Peterborough, Rochester, St. Albans, and Wor- cester. The deaneries are those of St. Paul's, Man- chester, Peterborough, Windsor, and Wells, and the canonries of St. Paul's (two),at Windsor (two), and one at Worcester.
WHEN WE THINK OF WIFE AND

div.head: CHILDREN.
div.p: CHILDREN.
We have all read of people on journeys exposed to in-
tense cold:; how they wanted to lie down and go to sleep,
yet if they did so they must surely freeze and perish.
This they knew, and so they fought against the feeling,
and struggled on in hope soon to reach some place where
they should find shelter and warmth.
It is always hard to do anything under compulsion,
but sometimes we ,have no choice.
A miner, Joseph
Bedgwiek by name, who lives at 14, Waterworks-road
Waterhead, Oldham, tells a story of what he had to go
through in this line. He says :—'
"I am fifty-two years
old. Up to about three years ago I never ailed anything.
Then I began to feel queer. At first I didn't know what
to make of it. It came on with a poor appetite and no
relish for my food. I had an awful taste in my mouth
all day long, but worst in the morning, and foul water
and slime rose up all the time and filled my mouth.
Later on my skin was dry and hot, and the secretions
from my kidneys were thick and of a red colour. I had
dizzy pains in my head, and my tongue was coated so thick it was like apiece of brown leather.
"Things went on in this way with me for several
months. I was never well, and never exactly down on
my back. By-and-by, though, I began to have rheuma-

div.head: tisin in my legs and a great deal of pain in the side and
div.p: tisin in my legs and a great deal of pain in the side and
This *axle me so bad I could get no sleep of a night; I would turn over and over in bed, but could get
back.
no rest.
"Then a bad cough commenced to shake me all to
pieces, and I spit up a great deal of thick phlegm. By
this time I was very weak, and it was very hard for me
to drag myself to and from my work; but as I had a
family to support I struvled on. Every- now and then
had to knock off work, and was confined to my bed for
a few days at a time. I took all kinds of medicine I
could hear of, but nothing relieved me f Dr long together,
and at last I went to a doctor, who said it was all from
my stomach. Be gave me medicine and attended me at
my own house for five or six weeks.
"Seeing me get weaker and weaker, one of my neigh-
bours strongly advised me to try Mother Seigel's Cura-
tive Syrup. So I sent to Mrs. Cox, chemist, at Water-
head, and got a bottle. After taking that bottle I felt a
great deal bitter, and by persevering for about two
weeks longer I was able to go back to my work. lam
now quite strong and have never ailed anything since.
"I tell every one that one bottle of Seigel's Syrup did me more good than all the doctors' physic I had taken.
If I had only known of the Syrup sooner it would have
saved me three years' suffering and misery, to say no-
thing of the loss of wages by my being unable to work.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 28, 1891 NOTES FROM MANXLAND. LETTER FROM AN AUSTRABY F. R. R. LIAN COLONIST.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 28, 1891 NOTES FROM MANXLAND. LETTER FROM AN AUSTRA- BY F. R. R. LIAN COLONIST.

Australians pay frequent visits to the Old Country, a proof, as a New. Zealand tradesman, who had made the trip nine times in ten years, observed—that some, at all events, made money in the Colonies. Our passage across the Indian Ocean was very pleasant on the whole, but before it was half over— after travelling for several days as smoothly as on a lake—we encountered the effects of a storm that had been experienced off the Australian coast, and some of the passengers—poor unfortunate me among the number—had a return of sea sickness. But, happily, this was only for a day, and the pitching and tossing which continued for the re- mainder of the voyage was absolutely enjoyable when we had got our sea legs. The Oruba proved a grand boat, but she was not driven at her best, and it became known early on the voyage that she would take two or three days longer in returning to Adelaide than on her maiden trip,which cost £lOOO extra to make her reputation —so it was stated on board. We had two deaths soon after crossing the equator, an old man being found dead on the steerage deck, and a baby dying in the second saloon. The latter was enclosed in a coffin, which, bearing a beautiful wreath, was left floating on the waves. We landed at Adelaide 38 days after leaving Plymouth, and reached Mildura at midnight on Dec. 22nd. But further details I must leave over for a few weeks. Love to all from Mrs. L. as well as myself.—Yours faithfully,
J. J. LEVER.

div.head: 111. A POLITICAL MEETING IN PEEL.
div.p: 111. A POLITICAL MEETING IN PEEL.

All eyes are turned on Peel. The uncertainty which exists as to the date of the forthcoming dis- solution of the House of Keys has prevented the combatants in other towns and in the sheadings from massing themselves in preparation for immed- iate fight, and in some cases there is still a doubt as to who will be the leaders in the fight. But at Peel a ring .has been formed for some time, and the champions have already indulged in a few prelim- inary sparrings. The whole Island is looking on. Our numerous insular newspapers are full of news of the contest, and the air is thick with specual- tions upon the probable issue of it. The political meeting of which I propose to-day to give your readers some account was held about a fortnight ago, but it is by no means to be regarded as a bit of ancient history. A political meeting is about as rare an occurrence here as the appointment of a governor or the capture of a shark. The rule is, I am told, when a representative for any town or sheading is wanted, for a deputation of well- known and respected ratepayers to approach the most likely man—usually the biggest landlord or largest employer of labour, apart from his religious or political views (imperially speaking), and ask his consent to nomination. If he consents, in nine cases out of ten he will be elected without opposi- tion, and if his action in the Keys as it affects local industrial and social interests meet with approval his seat is practically secure for life. On the pre- sent occasion, however, as I have in my previous letters tried to show your readers,a change has come over the spirit of the electors' dreams,and there is to be a fight all along the line. As yet we have had no political meetingsin Douglas and there have been none in Ramsey and Castletown or any of the sheadings. To Peel belongs the honour of opening fire on the enemy in the style so thoroughly ap- proved in England. The mode of calling such a meeting is singular. It is like nothing so much as your method of requesting the Mayor to summon a town's meeting. In my ramble yesterday I noticed on various gate-stumps and farmyard walls a bill signed b 3 some dozen ratepayers of the sheacling of Glenfaba and containing a request addressed to "Philip Killey, Esq., Captain of the parish of. Marown," (the "captains "of parishes are a sort of titular headmen or chief electors) that a public meeting should be called to discuss the political situation in the sheading. The meeting at Peel was summoned in that way, and the Captain was in the chair. The Public Hall was crowded, and was pervaded by a "very ancient and a fish-like smell," for the great majority of those present are engaged "either in fishing or mend- ing their nets." The Chairman demanded fair play for all; if it should be necessary to take extreme measures to preserve order, however distasteful it might be to him, he should not hesitate to take them. Declining in an official and dignified way to give any opinion on the merits of the rival candi- dates, he called upon Mr. Joseph Mylchreest to. ad- dress the meeting. Mr. Mylchreest rose amid a storm of applause. He first vindicated his right as a genuine Manxman to contest his native town against a Yorkshireman. He twitted his hearers with having been too jealous of one another to sup- port one of their own race, and declared that be wanted to fight Peel as a Peel man. With regard to the question of the hour—Church versus Dissent —he said "There is not a man in the Isle of Man who is more liberal-minded than I am, as far as concerns the Church and Nonconform- ists and sectarian business. At that meeting in Michael, the Bishop sat at one end of the table and I at the other." (Laughter). He thought that the vexed question of appointments to .the magistracy would be dealt with by giving the elec- tors the power of choice. He warned them against the attempts being made by the other side to des- troy confidence in the ballot.—" When you come to the poll you will remember that you can vote for either the servant or the master, and what I say is, we are going to stop this kind of serfdom that has lasted so long in the Isle of Man." (Tremendous applause.) Mr. Mylchreest was followed by a local celebrity named Mr. William Moore, better known as "Little Billy "—a tradesman whose shop is the resort of all the "village Hampdens "and budding John Brights of Peel, and whose rising was the signal for much laughter and cheering, and cries of " Hould him." He told the meeting how Mr. Laugh ton had betrayed their interests, and how he was controlled by a small clique of friends end neigliboure. (" done; WU go on Billy.") He went to the House of Keys and voted against what he had promised. But they had not forgotten. (" Hould him :") Mr. Mylchreest had refused "offers to enter the British Parliament (hear, hear) ; he had those virtues which were greatest among the ancients—patriotism and love of country ; patriotism was one of the things which fitted men for heaven." Their candidate might have gone to live at London or Paris,but he preferred his native town. He had a great deal more to say (dis- order, and a voice, "Don't say it !"). "I beg to move," he concluded," that this meeting" (pause, and a voice " Hould him r —laughter) pledges it- self to use every endeavour to secure the return of Joseph Mylchreest, Esq., as a member of the House of Keys for the city of Peel." (Applause.) Mr. W. Quayle,of Ballamoar,said he had for.nerly supported Mr. Laughton, but had found him untrustworthy. If they were going to a meeting together,before they entered the place at which it was held Mr. Laugh ton would ask him what were the views of the people whom they were going to address that night—were they Church people or were they Dissenters? And he spoke accordingly. (Laughter.) Was that the sort of man they wanted for their representa- tive? He should do his utmost to secure Mr. Mylchreest's return. After a few other speakers had delivered themselves in a similar strain the Chair- man, whose official iciness had for some time been giving way, declared himself in favour of Mr. Mylchreest, amid great cheering. The resolution in the latter's favour was carried unanimously. A com- mittee was appointed to help the candidate in his I work and the meeting closed. ' I hear that the Dissolution may be expected next mo. nth. If so the presence of the fishermen of Peel will insure Mr. Mylcheerst's success. Mr. Laugh ton trusted largely in two things, the delay of the i Governor n dissolving until the herring season had begun, and the support of the ladies (We have women's suffrage here.) It must be said, however, that the second leg of support is almost as active as that famous one of Cork which led the poor Dutchman such. a dance. The Peel ladies are inde- fatigable in their efforts to get votes for Mr. Laugh- ton; but if he should be neaten—as he will be— what comforters could he have equal to them?

div.head: JOKE AND NO JOKE.
div.p: A JOKE AND NO JOKE.

A number of little people at a mountain resort gave a play last summer, which was an entire pro- duction of home talent—the play itself, costumes and stage arrangements. All children delight in what is called" dressing up," and this original play grew out of that infantile passion, and the natural taste of a very youthful member of the company for acting. For several weeks the greatest secrecy had prevailed in the little circle, and nothing was known outside save that "a piece had been writ- ten, duly rehearsed, and the day for the first per- formance duly appointed and announced. Parents and friends received complimentary tickets, and, as everybody wished to encourage the children, a large audience gathered to do honour to the event. There were two lovers, and a cross old father, who ob- jected to their marrying" because the young man was unable to support a wife." Love however, stands none of this nonsense, and the youthful twain elope, are married, and return to throw them- selves at the feet .of the cross parent and beg his forgiveness. He is obdurate ; will have nothing to say to the young man except to bid him seek his fortune, and when that is won to return and claim hif bride. The curtain falls on this exciting tableau and ten years elapse before it again rises. In the second act the. husband, having made heaps of money in a far distant land, comes back for the wife who has been so cruelly snatched from him. Their meeting is extremely affecting, and the interest deepens as he throws bags of gold before the now melting parent and his ecstatic spouse. He relates how hard he has laboured to obtain this wealth, what dangers and difficulties have been encoun- tered during this long probation ; yet in all these years his heart has always been true to the beloved ; wife so cruelly torn from him. At this thrilling ' point the wife thFows open a closet door, exclaim- ing with emphatic pride—" Meanwhile I have not been idle !" And then out march ten children, all all dressed alike and graduated in size to a tiny dot only two years old ! The juvenile actors were utterly surprised at the shrieks of laughter that greeted this touching situation, and to this day tney cannot understand what there was so funny about a play that made some of the children almost cry when they read it.

div.head: TEE VOYAGE OUT. The following letter, which has been addressed to the editor of this journal, will doubtless be read
div.p: TEE VOYAGE OUT. The following letter, which has been addressed to the editor of this journal, will doubtless be read
with interest by our readers. It is from the pen of

a pressman, who, as previously stated -in our columns, is giving up the life of a journalist for fruit farming in the irrigation colony of Mildura. The letter to hand, it will be seen, deals with the voyage out.
Ribblesdale, Walnut Avenue, 'Madura, Victoria, January 4th 1891.

Dear Mr. Walker,—Although I shall not be able to finish a letter to-night, as we retire early to rest in our new home, I will make a beginning and fin- ish the epistle on a subsequent night. I am able now to speak about what a hot climate is like, as our thermometer this afternoon indicated 108 de- grees, and even now,after eight o'clock,in the midst of the first downfall of rain we have enjoyed—ex- cept a light shower soon after landing in Adelaide —the temperature is 89 degrees. Seated in shirt, with wristbands and neck unbuttoned, trousers and stockings only,one feels the present temperature is pleasant, but, in the afternoon with a wind that was as hot as if coming from a furnace, the condi- tion was less delightful, though not as oppressive as I have occasionally experienced in night work in a newspaper office in England. But in the latter case, of course, work was in progress, while to-day we all simply reclined as comfortably as we could make ourselves. Before referring to Mildura, however. I must tell

you something of-onr journey hither. As you know the terrible storm on the coasts of England on Nov. 7th delayed our departure horn the Thames until the following morning, and we escaped the full force of the gale. But we felt the result of it in the English Channel, and though our arrival in Ply- mouth Sound, on the Sunday morning, found us little the worse a couple of hours after our depart- ure thence, our time of trial began, and, as I men- tioned in my letter from Naples, we were all pro- strated with the exception of lively little Georgie, and I did not put in an appearance on deck again until the Wednesday morning. It was some conso- lation, however, to know that we had not been dis- turbed by a mere trifle, for the captain at a later stage of our travels said that we had the worse pass- age across the Bay of Biscay he had ever exper- ienced; but as a counterpoise the passage through the Red Sea was the pleasantest in his career. I do not intend to describe our voyage at great length, but I must at least indicate some of its fea- tures. We were greatly pleased with Gibraltar, and I much enjoyed a day on shore at Naples. Mrs. L. remained on board, as we could not both desert the youngsters ; but I joined half-a-dozen others, and placing ourselves in the hands of a guide, with whom a bargain was made before start- ing as to the charge per head for devoting him- self to us for the day and paying all charges, including railway fare to Pompeii, carriage, and luncheon, we saw a great deal of interest. We visited a couple of magnificent churches, but there seemed to be very little reality about the services. Although priests were officiating at small altars at the siaes of the buildings no notice was taken of visitors strolling through and having the chief fea- tures pointed out to them by guides, and to me it had too much the sound of a penny show at a fair to hear a bell at the entrance rung at short intervals for a minute or two to call worshippers from the busy streets. The day was evidently a gala day, for, as we were rowed across the bay to the Oruba in the evening, there was a very effective display of fireworks visible, and one or two streets were illu- minated by means of innumerable small coloured lanterns. by king's palace was charming, and the paintings made up for a sense of disappointment felt on viewing the art collection at a tine museum. But we found that even in king's palaces all "things are not what they seem." A fine pair of" bronze gates" and a "magnificent bronze vase " proved to be of wood, while a beautiful "floor of polished wood" was tile work, the counterfeits being so clever that few other than experts would detect the imposition. Pompeii (pronounced Pompa) was even more interesting than Naples, and on returning to the railway station in the evening we had a capital view of the streams of burning lava flowing down from the summits of Vesuvius. The arrangements at Italian railway stations are singular to 'English folks. Both at Naples and Pompeii we were kept all outer MOm adjoining the platform until the train was almost due to leave, and at the latter place there was no platform, and the passengers entered the carriage from the "six foot."' The metropolitan beggars were not quite so bad as I expected from their evil reputation, but it is necessary to be on the alert to avoid trickery in dealing with the hawkers of fruit, &c. I was so amused by the unblushing way in which I was cheated by a fruit girl that I could not do other than laugh and allow her to defraud me without protest. She sold me a basket of fruit on the landing stage for 6d. The basket is always included in the bargain, but after being paid, she declared the basket was not included and was 2d. extra. I gave her a penny, but she still persisted, and I accord- ingly handed over a 3d. piece. Then she was sharp enough to count the penny I had given her as the change, and this made up 9d. for hr 6d. basket, which I discovered on getting on board,was half full of leaves. But the fruit and basket were worth the money, despite the roguery. Another striking fea- ture of the people who visit the liners for trade it the various ports of call is their system of bartering. As a rule they ask for five times the amount they are content to accept. Almost invariably they demand half-a-crown or time or four shillings for an article that they readily sell at a shilling (a favour-' ite price with them). Sometimes the fall in price was more marked. For instance Mr. lbbutson, of Black- burn, when asked 2s. 6d. for an imitation tortoise shell match box offered 2d. for it, and was told he might take it for 3d. In another place a passenger purchased for 12s. Gd. or 155., I forget which, an ebony inkstand for which .E 2 10s. was at first de- manded, but the purchase was only completed after bartering on and off for more than an hour. The punishment of any hawker discovered cheating on board is prompt, one man being pitched overboard from the deck by the coxswain for attempting to cheat a passenger. Mrs. L. went ashore at Port Said, and much en- joyed the novel sightg. I had a very bad foot for a , fortnight after leaving Naples, and had to move about as little as possible, and I undertook ,00 take charge of the youngsters at Port Said, but the dust from the coal made all who remained on board dur- ing the process of taking coal in,as black as miners. We were a sight to behold when visitors to the shore returned. The rapidity with which the coal porters carried the coal from the barges moved alongside, and to the steamer's bunks, was remark- able, equaling 100 tons per hour. The passage through the Suez Canal we shall long remember. The brilliancy of the electric lights seen at the bows of vessels we passed in the darkness ex- celled everything we had experienced, while camels crossing the desert to Suez and the sight of a rail- way train speeding along the sandy waste from Suez to Cairo were other noteworthy incidents. We only stopped off Suez for an hour and three-quarters, but we were visited by native boats bringing fruit and coal, &c., and on their departure we had a lively fusilade, as some steerage passengers pelted the Arab boatmen, who retaliated, one who had been struck on the face being in such a rage that he used a considerable number.of eggs as missles. Remembering the Port Said experience,we all went ashore at Colombo to avoid the" coaling," but hav- ing the children with us prevented us from driving into the suburbs as other passengers did,and I got so disgusted with the continued pestering of beggars, guides, and hawkers, that I could not stand more than a couple of hours ashore. The heat was great, and, as we had been under an awning in going ashore,we felt as if we were stepping into a furnace on landing. But we walked very slowly, and suffered no harm from exposure to the noonday sun. Soon after landing, a native, who claimed to be a sailor,attached himself to us, and, even, after being driven off by a native policeman,he turned up again as soon as we got round a corner. A soldier, on duty as a military policeman, finally drove him off, and walked some distance with us, chatting about military life, and subsequently the native policeman informed us that the persistent sailor was a very bad character. The view of the town from the Oruba was very pretty. After the start in the evening I was surprised to discover in the saloon Alderman Holden, of Burnley, who had been staying in Ceylon a fortnight as a break in the voyage to Australia. We th Us had an addition to the Lancashire representatives in the second saloon, in which there were passengers hail- ing from Preston, Blackburn, Accringtoti, Burnley. Southport, Bury, Manchester, Barrow-in-Furness, Rochdale, and Liverpool. In fact the County Pala- tinate was better represented than any ether shire. Colonials were numerous, and 1 found that some

div.head: O'SHEA V. WOOD WILL SUIT.
div.p: THE O'SHEA V. WOOD WILL SUIT.

In the Probate Division, on Wednesday, Mr. Justice Jeune further heard the arguments of counsel in support of the application for the discovery of the documents in the pending will suit of O'Shea a. Wood and Another. The suit has reference to the testamentary depositions of the late Mrs. Anna Maria Wood, widow, of the Lodge, Eltham, who died on the 19th May, 1889, possessed of a large amount of property. The plaintiff, Mrs. Catherine O'Shea, respondent in a recent divorce suit and daughter of the late Rev. Sir John Page Wood, of Hatherley Court, Gloticestershire, propounds a will of the 7th of March, 1888, and a will of 1887, as well as a number of codicils, by which she claims to be entitled to a considerable amount of property. The defendants who are brothers of Mrs. O'Shea, namely, General Sir Henry Evelyn Wood and Mr. Charles Wood, dispute the wills in ques- tion, and allege that the deceased was not of sound mind, memory, and understanding, and that she had executed them under undue influence. As reported, on Tuesday, the motion was an appeal against an order of the regis- trar calling upon Mrs. O'Shea to give inspection of cer- tain documents which were alleged to be material to the case.
His Lordship said he would give his :decision on Tues- day next.

div.head: DEATH OF A SOMERSETSHIRE CENTENARIAN.
div.p: DEATH OF A SOMERSETSHIRE CENTENARIAN.

Mr. William Adlam, who died on Sunday evening at Taunton, at the age of 106 years and eleven months, was an excellent:,example of a life passed peacefully in the open air. From boyhood until he reached the prime of manhood he tended sheep on the Wiltshire downs. About seventy years ago he found that his earnings were not sufficient to support his growing family, and he reluct- antly gave up his calm pastoral existence and travelled to Taunton in search of employment. In that town he soon obtained work as a gardener, and remained in one situation until he was over eighty years of age. His re- collections of the Jubilee of King George 111. were very vivid, and he was a prominent figure in the Jubilee festi- vities at Taunton in 1887. His love for open-air exercise was very strong, and it was his custom, up to within a few days of his death, to rise at six or seven o'clock and take a morning walk. The old man was assiduous in the performance of his religious duties, and until recent- ly was a regular attendant at a Bible class for aged peo- ple. Except for a slight deafness, he retained the use of all his faculties to a degree marvellous in one so old. He was always ready to converse about the events of his youth. His wife died at the age of ninety, and out of ten children only two are living.

div.head: LOCAL M.P.'S AND THEIR ATTENDANCES.
div.p: LOCAL M.P.'S AND THEIR ATTENDANCES.

The number of divisions taken during the three weeks ending Saturday, February 21st, was 35, taken on twelve days. We give below the returns published by the House of Commons of the attendances of local mem- bers of Parliament. As several divisions frequently take place upon one day, the number of days' attendance atdivisions is a better test of attention to Parliamentary duties than the actual number of divisions attended. The greater number of these divisions took place on the Tithe Rent-Charge Recovery Bill. The other principal divisions of importance were :—Wednesday, Feb. 4: Mr. Gladstone's Religious Disabilities Relief Bill, for admit- tiug Roman Catholics to the same full rights of citizen- ship as jews and other religious persuasions enjoy. This was defeated by the Government. Wednesday, Feb. 11 : When the Deceased Wife's Sister's Bill was carried by 47 votes. Monday, Feb. 16 : When Mr. John Morley's motion of censure on the Government for its proceedings at Tipperary was defeated. Friday, .Feb. 20 : When Mr. Pritchard Morgan's motion for Welsh Disestablish- meat was only defeated by 235 to 203.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse, on Wednesday morning. Alder- man Harrison presided, and there were also present Messrs. Blackhurst, T. Jones, Davies, Jolley,Heaton, J. Houghton, W. Houghton, Smith, Clarke, Turton, Humphries, Warburton, Ratcliffe, Hood-Wright, Gill, Dignum, Balharry, Aukland ; J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (workhouse master), and 11. M. Mines (superinten- dent of Padgate Schools).

A LIBRARY FOR THE WORKHOUSE. The Matron of the Workhouse reported that she had received a present of sixty handsomely-bound volumes of the "Illustrated London News" for the benefit of the inmates of the Workhouse.—The CLERK said it would be useful if the House Committee would arrange fora small library at the Workhouse.—The CHAIRMAN supported this suggestion.—Mr. HEATON said that although the in- mates did not use the books much they did not destroy them.

THE PRICE OP GAS AT PADGATE SCHOOLS. The Padgate Schools Committee, in their minutes, sug- gested that the Warrington Gas Committee should be approached with a view to getting the price paid for gas at Padgate Industrial Schoots reduced, they being of opinion that 6d.per 1,000 feet above the price paid in the borough would be sufficient,seeing that the consumption was considerable.—lt was resolved by the Board that a deputation should wait upon the Gas Committee.

div.head: SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE
div.p: SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE
This Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 73 cases.
A 4 ' ROMAN CATHOLIC INSTRUCTOR."

The Local Government Board wrote with regard to the proposed payment of £lO a year to Father Feeney for his ministrations to the Roman Catholic inmates of the Workhouse, and suggested that in order to put the matter on a proper footing the Guardians should for- mally appoint Father Feeney as "Roman Catholic reli- gious instructor." The Board agreed to this suggestion, and passed a resolution accordingly.
GUARDIANS AND CONTRACTS.

Mr. DAVIES asked if a member of that Board sent in a tender to supply any article in connection with the Workhouse, what would be the penalty he would render himself liable to.—The CLERK said that while he should always recommend that no tender sent in by a member of the Board should be accepted,yet it was quite a doubt- ful question as to how far a member of the Board was absolutely prohibited under all circumstances from sup- plying goods to the Workhouse. The old statute upon the subject was that no member of a Board of Guardians— and the words had also been held to apply to the Clerk— should be concerned in thesupply of anything for the use of the poor. Points of law had since arisen, and he mentioned one case in which a judgment against a Guardian had been reversed on the ground that the goods supplied were not for the use of the poor, but for the building itself. The position of the Board was this—they accepted tenders believing them to be right tenders, and if a Guardian broke the law he must himself accept the responsibility.—The CLERK said the Board had a right to assume that everybody that tendered had a right to ten- der.—Mr. FLOOD-WRIGHT asked if Mr. Davies in his question was reflecting upon any member of the Board, or was he simply seeking for information.—Mr. DAVIES said he had only been asking for information. The relief cases were then taken.

div.head: GUN-MAKER OF MOSCOW;
div.p: THE GUN-MAKER OF MOSCOW;
OR, VALDIMIR THE MONK.
BY SYLVANIIS COBB, JR.
CHAPTER XIX.
CONCLUSION.

Pale as death sat the fair young countess in her dressing-room. She did not tremble now, for every nerve had become fixed in utter despair. "Will you not change your dress, my mistress ?" asked Zenobie, in a low, tremulous tone. "No, no," the maiden replied; and her voice sounded strangely even in her own ear, it was so low and hollow; " why should I dress for the sacri- fice? The dumb beast may suffer garlands about its neck befoce being led to the heathen altar; but alas! God has not given me a brute's ignorance to help me now. No, no, Zenobie, I will not dress for the bride."
"But the duke expects it." "I care not. Ile can not ask me to do it. He may do all he wills, for I am helpless here, but he dare not ask."
"Oh, my dear mistress!" cried the faithful girl, throwing her arms about the neck of her mistress, and weeping as she did so, "would to God that I could bear this for you." _ _ _
"I thank you all-the same, my best of friends," the countess replied, gazing gratefully up into her attendant's face; but it matters not much now. I

shall not suffer long. My sorrow Will soon cease." Zenobie looked inquiringly up, but she did not speak. "God will soon take me home," the wretched maiden murmured, after a pause. "I feel the chill hand upon my heart even now, and I know that earth cannot bind my spirit long with such a curse upon it ! " Zenobie had no words of consolation more to offer, so she did all she could do. She drew the head of her mistress upon her bosom, and there she held it for a long time. She held it thus until the door of the apartment was opened and a female domestic entered. "Lady," the new-comer said, trembling percep- tibly while she spoke, "the duke bade me tell you he awaited your coming below in the hall." She stopped here, and seemed to wait for an an- swer; but Rosalind did not speak. "What answer shall I give him, lady?" At this the countess started up, but she sank back again without speaking. "Tell him we will come," interposed Zenobie, who saw that the announcement had taken the last power of effort from her mistress. "Yes—yes," whispered the countess, as the mes- senger hesitated and gazed inquisitively into her face.

And with this the woman left the apartment. "My dear mistress," spoke Zenobie, now calling all her power of self-control to her aid, " all means of help and escape we have tried in vain. The time has come—"
"Oh, God have mercy ! " groaned the coun- tess.

—"And we must meet it, since there is no fur- ther hope. It will be better to go down a:-, once than to arouse the bad man's anger by more delay. Were there the least slimmer of hope, we would not go; but there is not. You know what I mean."

A few moments Rosalind sat like one dead. Then she started up with her hands clasped, and raised her eyes toward heaven. She did not speak aloud, but her lips moved, and she surely uttered a prayer to God—and it was none the less eloquent because it was silent. Then she turned to her companion. Her lips were set and colorless, and a deathly look had Gverspread her whole face. "Zenobie," she said, in a tone which bore no feel- ing more than the gliding of cold, icy sound, "I am ready. Once more, before the last joy of earth de- parts from me, let me bless thee, and press thee to my bosom. lam pure now ! " She opened her arms as she spoke, and when she closed them again Zenobie was within their em- brace. "Bless you—bless you ever! God keep and guide you to the end of life, and then receive you home to Himself! Kiss me.—There—l am ready now !" The broken-hearted girl wiped the tear from her eye, and in a moment more she was as cold and passionless as before. "Lead on, Zenobie. help." Without looking around the Moslem maiden led the way to the hall. She walked slowly, and she fancied she couid hear the beating of her mistress's heart. In the hall stood the duke with some half dozen of her old male attendants. He took the hand of the countess as she approached him, and gazed earnestly into her face ; but he did not speak. He led her towards one of the drawing-rooms, and when they entered there they found the hump- backed priest already in waiting. Rosalind came well-nigh fainting when she saw this miserable villain ready for his work. She knew now that the priest was like the master. "You see, my dear Countess," spoke the duke, in a low, hypocritical tone, "that we have all pre- pared. I trust we shall have no trouble before this holy man." This last sentence was spoken in a threatening tone, but it had no effect upon Rosalind. She hardly heard the words he spoke. "Come father," said Olga, turning now to the priest. We are ready." Savotano moved forward, and mumbled a Latin prayer. Then he looked upon the twain before him, and directed them to kneel. "No ! no! no !" gasped the fair countess trem- bling for the first Lime. "I can not do that !" " Kneel !" hissed the duke, between his clenched teeth. And as he spoke he grasped the maiden more firmly by the arm and forced her down. She uttered a quick cry of pain as she felt the unmerci- ful grip, hut she could not resist the strong arm of her persecutor. "bow go on !" the duke cried, as he held the maiden down. "Go on, Savotano, and let the busi- ness be done as soon as possible." "HOLD!" It was a voice of thunder which spoke thus, and it came from the door. The duke started to his feet, and ho beheld Ruric Nevel, the gun-maker, ap- proaching the spot. But the youth came not alone. Behind him came the huge bulk of Valdimir the monk. And more still—back of the monk came the widow, Claudia Nevel, and the boy Paul. And then there was, besides all this, a heavy tramp of feet in the hall, and a clang of steel. " Hold ! Stop this accursed mockery !" Ruric shouted, as he strode up the apartment. "Miserable dog !" grasped the duke, mad and frantic with rage, " how dare you come hither ?" "Look • ye, proud duke," the monk interposed, coming quickly forward, "I am at the bottom of all this. / have come to stop this foul work !" Rosalind had started to her feet when she first heard Ruric's voice ; and now, as the monk spoke, a ray of hope darted to her soul, and with a quick bound she reached her lover's side. " Ruric ! Runic !" It was all she could say; and with a flood of tears she piliowed her head upon his bosom, and his stout arms were wound fondly about her.
I shall walk withow
"Fear not," he whispered, "for, oh, Rosalind, thou art safe now." The mad duke saw the movement, and with a bitter curse he started towards them.

" Now by the livingiOd's-F1;-shOuted, with his fists clenched, and his eves flashing fire, "you have come to your death! What ho, there !—Without ! Slaves, where are ye ?" In a moment more the side door was thrown open and a dozen of the duke's servants came rushing in.

"Ha !" Olga cried," you are in time. Seize these dogs.! Kill them on the spot if they offer one act of resistance. At them now! Down with the dogs!" "HOLD !" It was Valdimir who spoke, and every arm dropped as they heard that voice. It was differ- ent from the voice they had heard the fat monk use before. The duke started as though a thunderbolt had burst at his feet.
"Who art thou ?" he gasped, staggering further back.

"Olga—Duke of Tula—" spoke the monk, in tones which sounded strange for him, because they were so different from those he had been wont to use," I am thy master !" As he spoke he threw open the long black robe which enveloped his person, and cast it upon the floor at his feet, and there it lay, a huge pile of wadding and stuffing! The vast rotundity of per- son was gone, and the strange man now stood in his own fair form. His chin—that prominent chin —was no more hidden, and he was but a small man —not much larger than the boy Paul who stood near him. Next he placed his hand to his head and tore away the tight skull-cap, and the ring of gray hair came away with it,' leaving a cluster of glossy , hair floating down over the neck and shoulders!

"Great God of Mercy !" gasped Savotano, stag- gering back, "it is the EMPEROR !" "Aye !" cried Peter, turning his darkly-flashing eye upon the staggering duke' " I am your Emper- or. Paul, go and call the guard." The boy hastened from the palace, and when he returned he was followdd by a party of the Imperial Guard.
" Mercy ! mercy, sire !" gasped the duke, sinking down on his knees.

But the Emperor answered him not. He only turned to his guard and bade them secure the duke and the foul priest. Rosalind Valdai gazed npon the transformed man until the strange truth worked its way to her strug- gling mind, and then she turned once more to Ruric. She gazed up into his face, and she saw the holy smile which rested there. The joyful truth came to her now, and with one long, low cry of frantic hope and bliss she sank upon her noble lover's bosom. She could not speak—she could only cling closely and more close to her loved protector, and with her head pillowed close by the heart that beat for her, she wept away all the grief of her opened soul. "Olga," spoke the Emperor, after the nobleman!, had been firmly bound, "your race of iniquity is run. " No,no,sire, ' the duke cried,in humble supplicat- ing tones, " say not so. In this single thing i may have been wrong, bnt let my mad, consuming love be some palliation for my offence. Oh, you will not crush me with public shame for this ! You will not cast me from you one who loves you well." "Oh, miserable man! " uttered Peter,with a look of utter contempt upon the base wretch," add not perjury to your already accumulated crimes. Hark ye: Some months since_ I knew there was corr

spiracy in my capital, and I knew there was much ot evil, too, which was never reported to me. I resolved to ferret it out, and to that end I meant tin mingle among ray people without their knowing me. So I had that robe made, and so stuffed and wadded that I could even hide my chin in the seeming fat. I assumed the _garb, and my own master-at-arms did not at first know me. Once in a while I made my page assume the garb and be , seen in it about the city, and thus all thought of suspecting me was cut off. I have been at the work, Olga, and I have found out all I sought. it was mere accident that first threw me in the way of this young gun-maker, and it was by accident too, that I overheard the Count Damonoff and his' companion discussing the subject of their mission, to the gun-maker's shop. Of course I followed that scheme up, and I should have snatched our fair young countess from your grasp ere this had I not - been desirous of arriving at another point first. Per haps you know that the Princess Sophia and the Minister Galitzin have planned a grand overturn of my throne—Ah, you tremble!—And now, my noble Duke." the Emperor continued, in deeper tone,' I have learned of your own guilt in that affair! —you love me, do you? But I know you now. Tv° of your poor tools are in my hands. They sr, named Totma and Viska. They have made a fui;. confession, and I now know all your villainies. know what you have planned against this noble countess, and against her noble lover; I know whit! you planned against the Count Damonoff ; and know, too, what you have planned against your, Emperor—not a word, sir? You are the Duke (-1_1; Tula no more. A more worthy man wears the dues' coronet from this hour. Runic Nevel shall assume, the station you have disgraced, and I know he 'WU' ennoble it once more." As Peter ceased speaking he waved his hand th his officers, and they bore the prisoners from tli room. The priest said not a word; but Olga curse loudly and bitterly. When the dark villains had gone Peter stePPed forward and took Rosalind's hand. There was II tear in his bright eye and his nether lip tremble,d,•, "Fair cousin," be said, in a low soft tone, ;`, could not promise thee that thou should'st not with the Duke of Tula, for I had even then planneu that you should do that thing. But it will not be very hard, will it ? " The countess gazed up, and a murmur of thanlad was upon her lips; but the gushing flood starte , forth anew, and she could only look the joyfti_J blessings she could not speak. Peter imprinted_o kiss upon her pure brow, and then gave her hand riu. Runic, and as he did so he said, with a warm smile,„; " You must be her guardian hereaftet, and shoal': you tire of the duty your Emperor will be evu'' ready to grant her the asylum she needs." * * * * * *

A week had passed away from the time of the strange scene just recorded. The former Daker Olga, had been convicted of treason, and was 110v7 on his way to the eternal wilds of Siberia. But let me say here, he never reached the land of his baw, d ishment. His proud heart broke o the road, SP, he died, unknown, and uncared for, in a peasant!' cot among the rugged mountains of Uralia. lie ht begged of the officer who guided him not to tell 11" station, and the peasants supposed they were burr ina a common traveller when they laid awaY tilde mortal remains of Olga in the cold grave they ha prepared. Savotano, the humpbacked priest, was executed._ as a common murderer, while his companions 1 crime were punished as their various degrees ° guilt demanded. And now comes the closing scene. Within the largest apartment of the ducal palace were assembled a brilliant company, and the 8131- peror himself was master of the ceremonies. Ruric Nevel, the Gun-maker of Moscow, knelt a/ the Emperor's feet ; and Peter drew his sword an laid the glittering blade upon Rune's shoulders. And as he did so he said: "Arise, Sir Ruric, Duko of Tula, and receive tIIY just titles and bonded inEtruments The youth arose, pale and trembling with Oh! strange excitement of the moment, and then t.,1; Emperor handed him a broad parchment roll, wirg its heavy seals and vignette bearing the arms of tm" Dukedom. "Now," cried Peter, whose brow was flushed
st with the joy he himself was making, "let the 11.4 of the work go on. Come, holy father, we nedd help to perform the rest of the ceremony." Rune was pale no longer. As he felt the WO

hand of Rosalind trembling within his own thelle:. blood mounted to his brow and temples, and in 13" dark eyes the strange love-light danced like re. fleeted sunbeams. The word was spoken—the bond of union Wag _

made—and, after all, Rosalind Vald-allti-cr b-ecoulee Duchess of Tula. The widowed mother was tislt. first to bless them—and the Emperor came Ile Then came Paul and Zenobie, hand in hand. ,ht "Aha," spoke the happy Duchess, as she cauk, the new light of Zenobie's eye, and then turn; the glowing face of Paul, "you are playing at ts" game of Love." fait "You will not object," whispered the girl, hiding her face upon the bosom of her tress. "No, "No, no, Zenobie." "And you, my master," spoke Paul, gazi.„l eagerly into Ruric's face,----" you will not not nay." "No, no, my noble Paul. If you can win her VII have my consent. But she was won already. But there was yet one more to come. Cofl Count Damonoff, somewhat pale and weak, but on the sure road to health, moved slowly forvio;;; and took the hand of the joyous bride Theu Pof reached forth the other hand and took the pall° ha Ruric, and as he thus held both their hands said: of "My lord and lady—and, I must say, my best_.4 friends—let this moment atone for all of darlan between us in the past. Be you happy both--41 may God bless you. Let me be accounted ara7s your friends; and let the future prove how grate I can be." head "Aye," cried Ruric, grasping the Count's --, more firmly, "let the future show how gratefilikiie can all be for the blessing of this hour; and Nv",„. we look to God for help we will not fail to renege ber in our prayers the author of our joys—our 110 Emperor—Peter of Russia! " : 000 And so closed the scene as it should—with" - long, loud shout of— " God bless our Emperor !" WiitPeter never forgot that moment. In the s years thereafter, when he sometimes let the el°ll.t of passion settle upon his soul, he remembered toll% scene and that shout. It was one of the br;ler.. spots in the memory of his youth which he c ighed always.

A BOON TO LADIES. A BOO* TO LADIES. A BOON TO LADIES.
IMPERIAL PABLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.—MoNray.

_ The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter past four. INFANTS AND MONEY LENDERS.—A Bill rendering it a misdemeanour for money lenders to send circulars to in- fants at school or college was read a first time. BILLS ADVANCED.—The East Indian Officers Bill, the Elementary Education 'Blind and Deaf) Bill, and the In- termediate Sche',..s and Sites Bill passed through Com- mittee. The Clergy Discipline Bill, introduced by the Archbishop of Canterbury, was read a first time. The House adjourned at twenty-five minutes to six.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-MONDAY.

_ The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. THE OCCUPATION OF TOICAR.--SiTLFERGUSSON told Mr. Morley that the occupation of Tokar and Handoub was rendered necessary by the action of the dervishes, who had constantly harassed the neighbourhood of Suakim. No further advance would be made into the interior.

- TEN-SHILLING NOTTS.—Mr. GrOSCHEN, replying to Mr. Sinclair, said the basis of the ten-shillinc, note would be that it was payable only in silver, and it would be a legal tender only to such amount in silver as the silver coinage itself.

FORTIFICATIONS.—MT. SMITH told Mr. Shaw Lefevre that the estimated expenditure for the year 1891-2 for fortifications under the Imperial Defence Act was 2600,000, and for armaments £210,000. SUPPLY—EGYPT &c.—The House having gone into Committee of Supply, Colonel NoLes resumed the debate on the vote for men of all ranks. In the course of the discussion, Mr. STANHOPE stated that such steps had now been taken with regard to mobilization that all our forces could be mobilized in a very much shorter time than had. ever been the case before. Mr. LABOUCHERE moved the reduction of the 'Vote by 3,320 men, the number of men at present in Egypt. Sir J. FEROUSSON having spoken of the great increase in the improvements of Egypt within recent years owing to British influence, and the intention of the Government to withdraw from that country when their mission had been fulfilled, Mr. MORLEY followed, and accused the Government of slipping into the old position of making moves into the Soudan, with the pro- bability that British troops would have again to be sent to the rescue of the Egyptian troops. The amendment was eventually rejected by a majority of 72.
The Rouse adjourned at 12.15. HOUSE OF LORDS.—ThESDAY.
The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four. The sitting was merely formal. Three private Bill were advanced a stage. The House adjourned at half-past four.
HOUSE OF COMMONS—TUESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock.

THE IMPRISONED IRISH LEADERS. - Mr. BALFOUR assured Mr. Sexton that Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien are in a better state of health than previously, and there was no ground for the suggestion that Mr. O'Brien had broken down. The Chief Secretary presumed that the ordinary course would be followed as regards their bail.

THE ROYAL COMMISSION ON CAPITAL AND LABOUR.— Mr. W. H. Sutra informed Mr. Beckett that the Govern- ment would recommend the appointment of a Royal Commission to inquire into the relations 'Aetween capital and labour.' THE REGULAR ARMY.—Mr. BRODRICK told General Goldsworthy that the regular army was short of 1,857 men, and the militia 23,731 non-commissioned officers and men. The yeomanry was deficient of 94 officers and 2,387 men. THE INCOME TAX.—Mr. BARTLEY moved for the appoint- ment of a Committee to inquire into the working of the income tax, and whether some juster system could not be adopted by different rates being imposed on incomes derived from realized capital and those derived from in- dustry. Out of the payers of income-tax more than half paid on less than £2OO a year, and he gave instances in which improper payments had been enforced. Mr. W. H. SMITH admitted that dissatisfaction existed in many qnarters on some of the points raised, but said it was impossible to conceive a tax of this character that did not cause dissatisfaction. It was an impost, however, on which considerable reliance must be placed in adjust- ing the finances of the country. Upon a division, the motion was rejected by a majority of 55. THE COMMITTEE ON RAILWAY LABOUR.—On the motion to appoint a Select Committee on the hours of railway servants, objection was taken to some of the names sub- mitted, owing to their connection with railways.—Sir M. H. BEACH then said the Government were perfectly will- ing to add two more members to the Committee, one of whom should be a labour member.
LOCAL BANKRUPTCY (IRELAND) BILL.—The Local Bankruptcy Ireland Amendment Bill was read a second time.
'ill-a Hauge adjourned at 12.10. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY.
The Speaker toox the chair at a quarter-past twelve, and a quorum was formed at twenty-five minutes to one. _ _

PAROCHIAL BOARDS.—Dr. CAMERON moved the second reading of the Parochial Boards (Scotland) Bill, whizh was opposed by Mr. MARK STEWART and others and sup- ported by Sir G. TREVELYAN and Dr. CLARK. The second readingwas negatived by a majority of 26. RATING OF MACHINERY.—Mr. H. S. WRIGHT proposed the second reading of the Rating of Machinery (No. 2) Bill, which he stated differed in principle from that of last year. The principle of last year's bill was to define what should be rated, whereas that of the present mea- sure was to except what should not be rated. Mr. W. James who described the bill as essentially a manufac- turer's bill, moved the adjournment of the debate. The motion was seconded by Mr. T. H. BOLTON, and agreed , to without a division. The rating of Machinery Bill, on which thedebate on the second reading was adjourned on the 11th inst., was withdrawn. MISCELLANEOUS.—Thn Local Authorities (Scotland), Loans Bill was read a second time. The Parliamentary Elections Bill, which stood for second reading, was with- drawn. The Museums and Gymnasiums Bill passed through committee, with an amendment introduced by Mr. Sexton extending its provisions to Ireland. The Re- gistration of Electors Acts Amendment Bill also went through committee: The House adjourned at a quarter to six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THIIRSDAV. The Lord Chtncellor took his seat at a quarter-past four o'clock: The Inca' Government Provisional Order (Poor Law) Bill was read a second time. THE TITHE BILL.—The House then went into Com- mittee. Lord BRAMWELL drew attention to clause 1 (sub-section 1.) After a discussion the whole question raised was left to the Grand Committee. Clause 1 and 2 as amended were agreed to. On clause 3, affecting the rating of the owner of tithe rent charge, The Bishop of LormoN movedthe insertion of a new sub-section, pro- viding that no .rate reJoverable, as a tithe rent charge should be recoverable until four months after it had been due. Lord Monk-Bretton, Lord Basing, and the Earl of Kimberley opposed the amendment. The amendment was withdrawn, and clauses 3 and 4 were agreed to. The Bill, as amended, passed the Committee, and the House resumed. The House adjourned at twenty minutes to eight. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. QUF.STIONS.—Mr. MATTHEWS, answering; Mr. LENG, said he had the power to appoint female inspectors of factories and workshops, but there were strong objec- tions to the exercise of that power on grounds of administrative impracticability. Sir JAMES FERGUSSON informed Mr. JOHN AIORLEY that no final determination had been come to in regard to the permanent occupatic of Tokar. Mr. SMITH stated in reply to a question that the interests of Ireland would be duly considered in the constitution of the Royal Commission on Capital and Labour. THE FACTORIES Bit,n.—The second reading of the Factories and Workshops Bill introduced by the Govern- ment was moved by Mr. Matthews, who proposed that the measure should be referred to the Committee on Trade, to which Sir Henry James's Bill had been referred, and said that the questions as to particulars of work and the half hour for cleaning werequestions for Committee. Mr. FIELDEN said that the managers and workers in his district thought that on the whole the bill was a good one. Mr. BUXTON and Earl Crwarrrox pointed out various deficiences in the bill, the latter remark- ing that women were overworked to a ' terrible degree in some of the large towns, and that this state of affairs would not be improved until women inspectors were appointed. Sir HENRY JAMES said that after consultation among those concerned it had been decided that it would be undesirable that there should be two Acts passed in the same sesion dealing to some extent with the same subject matter, and while he . should maintain the position of his bill, yet practically he would attempt in the first instance to , mould the Government bill by introducing into it the clauses of his own. The operatives deemed the Govern- ment measure a very good one, but he should retain his own bill, so that he might go on with it if necessary. Considerable discussion followed on the proposal to abolish the certifying surgeon and the question of child labour. The Bill was then read a second time. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Assessment of Taxes (Regula- tion of Remuneration) Bill was read a second time. The Factories (Certificates of Birth, Fees) Bill was read a second time, the mover, Mr. BANDELL, agreeing not to take it a further stage until the Government Bill dealing with factory legislation had been further considered. The Howie adjourned at ten minutes past twelve.

div.head: MR. PARNELL IN IRELAND.
div.p: MR. PARNELL IN IRELAND.

Speaking at Roscommon on Sunday, Mr. Parnell, M.P., referring to the Boulogne negotiations, said he had done all he could to secure peace, but having failed he was determined to fight the matter out. He referred to the,control of the Irish Constabulary, and said the posi- tion he had taken up with regard to this question was a .simple one, capable of being defended upon grounds of Justice, reason ,and equity. A large.force of police existed to gather rackrents, but he contended that they could be diminished in number, disarmed, and transferred in a civilised condition to the Irish Executive, responsible to the Irish Patliament. No other course was compatible with Irish freedom. Then he dealt with the land ques- tion, saying that the Imperial Parliament would make a pretence of settling it, and would say they had settled it, taking care, however, however, not to allow the Irish people to have much hand in the settlement. The people must preserve their ranks unbroken until they got more satisfactory assurances on these two important points, and also with regard to the future Home Rule Bill. On Tuesday night the Gaelic Athletic Associations, of County Dublin presented an address to Mr. Parnell in the gymnasium of the National Club. Mr. Parnell in acknowledging the presentation, said the movement against himself had been started by some of the lowest of Englishmen, who were ignorant of Irish history. Ireland would not repeat the mistake of Grattan when he sur- rendered the Volunteers.

div.head: COMMISSION ON LABOUR.
div.p: COMMISSION ON LABOUR.
SCOPE OF INQUIRY.

It is announced that the Cabinet have decided upon the appointment of a Royal Commission to inquire into what are termed labour questions. There is a very gen- eral desire among the Labour party that Lord R. Church- ill should be made chairman of the Commission. ___

The" Standard" says :—The scope of the inquiry will include the conditions of agricultural as well of indus- trial employment. The chief subjects of the inquiry will be the hours of labour, along with the question of legis- lative interferences, strikes, and the practicability of es- tablishing boards of conciliation ; but the terms of refer- ence will be suffieiently general to enable the commision to deal with almost every branch of the labour contro- versy. Several names are mentioned in connection with the chairmanship of the Commission, including those of the Prince of Wales, Lord Randolph Churchill, Lord Derby, and Sir John Gorst, but up to the present no- thing has been settled on the point. The Commission will include a prominent member of the front Opposition bench, and we believe Mr. Morley will be asked to serve. We believe that the Opposition leaders claim that if no action had been taken by the Government in the matter of labour, a motion in favour of some form of inquiry would shortly have been made from the front Opposition bench.

div.head: STATEMENT IN PARLIAMENT,
div.p: STATEMENT IN PARLIAMENT,

In the House of Commons, on Tuesday, Mr. Beckett asked whether it was a fact, as stated in the newspapers, that the Government intended to appoint a Royal Com- mission on the relations between capital and labour, and what would be the scope of the reference to that Corn- MiSSiOLI.-Mr. Smith said the object of the Commission would be to make a careful inquiry into the causes of recent disputes, and to ascertain whether it was desir- able to institute legislation. The terms of the reference would be stated in the course of a few days. The Com- mission would not in any way interfere with the inquiry of the Select Committee on the Hours of Railway Labour. Mr. Beckett had a motion standing in his name for the appointment of a Committee to inquire into labour dis- putes, but withdrew it on Mr. Smith's announcement. Mr. Broadhurst has given private notice of his inten- __ _ _ . _ .

tiOn—to ask the First LO-rd of the Treasury for a definite assurance that the Royal Commission to be appointed on the subject of the relations of labour and capital, shall not be authorised to inquire into the rights of the labour- ing classes, established by the legislation of 1875.
THE BATTLE IN THE SOUDAN.
GREAT LOSS OF LIFE: OFFICIAL DETAILS,
The following telegrams have been received at the War Office from the seat of operations in the Soudan, from the Sirdar of Egypt to the Secretary of State for War:

- SUARIM, SATURDAY, 8.25 A.M.—Smith, with a brigade of Egyptian troops, advanced from Teb at daylight on the 19th. Found Tokar strongly held by Osman Digna and 2,000 men. A fter severe fighting the dervish force completely defeated. Tokar occupied. All principal Emirs and 700 dervishes killed. Osman fled south, pur- sued by Smith with a few horsemen. Our loss sixty- eight killed and wounded. SUAKIN, SATURDAY, 9.50 A.M.-Smith, with three bat- talions and one squadron Cavalry Egyptian troops now occupies village of Afafite, four miles south of Tokar, Osman Digna's camp. Our casualties are :—Killed: Captain H. L. Barrow, South Lancashire Regiment and Egyptian Army, and twelve Egyptian soldiers. Wounded: Captain J. R. Beech, 28th Hussars, slightly, four Egyptian officers severely, and forty-two soldiers; all the wounded are doing well. Smith reports Egyptian troops behaved with grat steadiness and gallantry in severe hand to hand fighting. A "Daily News" correspondent says :—The Arabs of the surrounding districts bring in cattle and milk, and a market has been established. General tranquility now prevails throughout the district, which is wonderfully fertile, with quantities of cotton and dhurra everywhere. The troops are comfortably hutted, and the wounded are doing well. Great gratification has been caused by the receipt of congratulatory telegrams from her Ma- jesty the Queen and the Khedive. It is noted as a curious coincidence that Tokar was retaken and the Egyptian flag was again set flying over the ruined Government buildings on the anniversary of the fall of fokar seven years ago. FIGHTING WITH THE ITALIANS. ROME,TUESDAY.--A. despatch received here from Mas- sowah states that a force of six hundred men from the district of Agameh, having made a raid upon Endeca, a place on the frontier of the Italian territory, near the Burl Peninsula, Captain Pinelli, the officer in command ' of the garrison at Arafali, marched against the invadeis with a company of native infantry and a detachment of Inative irregulars. The enemy were surprised by Capt. Pinelli's force near Aquilat, and defeated in two succes- sive engagements, losing two hundred men, including Askeas, their leader, and two chiefs of lower rank. The enemy also lost heavily in wounded and prisoners. Of the Italian force, the native infantry had one man wounded and the native irregulars two killed and six wounded. Osman Digma, according to a telegram from Suakim , has "made good use of his time," being a hundred miles from Afafite, on the Kassala road.

div.head: "PASTRY
div.p: "PASTRY
THE LONDON STEVEDORES.

The London stevedores on Tuesday night withdrew the notice calling the men out on Thursday. At a private meeting of members of the Shipping Federation, on Tuesday evening, the Chairman expressed .the hope that the men would not strike. If they did, they would find- that the Shipping Federation was prepared to fight to the bitter end. Work was proceeding quietly at the London Docks,on Wednesday. The stevedores are working on all vessels except those of the Shipping Federation, who have been able to provide all the men they require. The threatened strike has quite collapsed.

div.head: EVICTIONS AT SILKSWORTH.
div.p: EVICTIONS AT SILKSWORTH.
SERIOUS RIOT.

The evictions atLordLondonderry'SSilkSWorthCothelY were resumed on Wednesday, and resulted in serious riot. Eight houses were cleared, and 38 persons were evicted. The evicting party on leaving the village were followed by an excited mob of several thousand persohs, who kept up a continuous howling and jostled the police who were protecting the emergency men. Stones were throvan,and Superintendent Oliver, who was in command, and several of his men were injured. Orders were then given to charge the mob. The policemen, using their truncheons right and left, put the crowd to flight. Most of the people succeeded in escaping unhurt from the con- stabulary, but the number of wounded was still large enough to prove the vigour of the onslaught. More than thirty persons who had participated in the distur- bance and the flight afterwards treated for broken heads or minor injuries at Sunderland Infirmary. Lord Londonderry has written a letter for publication, in which he gives a history of the dispute, and states that the principle which is being contended for by himself and the Coalowners' Association is that every man shall be allowed perfect liberty in deciding whether he shall join a trade union. On Thursday the eviction of miners was continued. and there was some renewal of the previous day's dis- turbances.
