MR. CHAMBERLAIN AT BIRMINGHAM

The Right Hon. Joseph Chamberlain, M.P. presided at the annual meeting of theßirntingham Liberal Union- ist Club on Saturday. In the course of his speech he said that he did not think that Mr. W. J. Davies would, under any circumstances, consent to oppose Mr. Jesse Collings, who was certainly a direct representative of labour. Dealing with the Irish question, Mr. Chamber- lain remarked that Mr. Gladstone had conceded every one of the points demanded by Mr. Parnell, and now the latter had raised his price. Now, he said, he must have control of the tariff, he must have power over the cus- toms, and be able to protect Irish industry against British manufacturers; and, above all, Mr. Parnell says he must have an understanding that there shall be no veto, and there shall be no attempt to set up any supremacy of the Imperial Parliament. Mr. Gladstone declined to go fur- ther, and the result was that if he were to bring in a Home Rule Bill to-morrow he would find himself opposed by the representatives of the majority of the Irish nation.

div.head: DESPERATE ATTEMPT AT MURDER.
div.p: DESPERATE ATTEMPT AT MURDER.
SUICIDE OF THE ASSAILANT.

_ A married man called Edward Luke Roberts, living apart from his wife, and who recently lived with a married woman named Jane Lindop, separated from her husband, at Bucknall New-rd., Hanley, on Sunday night entered Mrs. Lindop's house, from which he was turned out a fortnight ago, and after felling her with a hammer shot her with a revolver. He then shot himself dead. The woman was found alive, and lies at the hospital in a dangerous condition. The mystery surrounding the terrible tragedy which occurred at Hanley was in no way cleared up at the in- quest, held on Tuesday before Mr. West Jones, borough coroner. Mary Roberts. the wife of the deceased man. gave evidence of identification, and informed the jury that his name was Edward Luke Roberts. She was married to him four and a half years ago, but only lived with him a few days, on account of his violence. Two days after marriage he began to threaten her. He was of a very passionate disposition, and slept with a razor under his pillow. She had never known him to possess a pistol. She left him on account of his threats. The inquiry was adjourned for a fortnight, to see whether Mrs. Lindop might recover. Late on Tuesday evening it was stated at the infirmary that she was slightly better, and that a bullet. which was found deeply embedded in her skull, had been extracted.

div.head: TERRIBLE COLLIERY _EXPLOSION IN
div.p: TERRIBLE COLLIERY _EXPLOSION IN
CANADA. LOSS OF OVER 100 LIVES.

HALIFAX, RUNDAT.—An explosion occurred yesterday at Springhill Colliery. Details of the disaster are still somewhat meagre, but they serve to show that it is one of great magnitude, it being believed that the death-roll will not fall far short of 100. The Springhill mine is the most important in the Cumberland coalfield, giving employment to upwards of 1,000 men. There were nearly all work at the time, and about 150 men were em- ployed in the immediate vicinity of the scene of the ex- plosion. All the latter are among the killed, injured, and missing. Hundreds of miners escaped by the con- nections with other slopes, but it is feared that almost every man working in that part of the mine where the disaster occurred was killed, including Mr. Swift the manager. Seventy-five bodies have already been recovered, and twenty men have been brought to bank in a terribly in- jured condition. BRINGING UP THE DEAD.—HARROWING SCENES. - - -

HALIFAX. MONDAY.—ii;-;/;;;iling loss exceeds that of any previous disaster in the history of Canada. Accord- ing to the latut estimates there are 117 dead and fifteen injured. ' The searchers are still bring out the dead, and. up to midnight ninety bodies had been identifiet Several are, however, unrecognisable. The wounded were all insensible from the after-damp, and have been tempor- ariry restored with much difficulty. Not a person in town slept during the night of Saturday and Sunday, and there were signs of mourning on all sides. Women and children walked the streets in the rain weeping and mourning, while here and there -little groups of miners met to discuss their hairbreadth escapes. Many of the survivors only got out through sheer luck, or by their own exertions. The cause of the disaster is still a my- stery. Several conflicting theories have been advanced, but they are all pure conjecture, and the most expert miners are totally at a loss to account for the explosion. A shop in the town has been converted into a tempor- ary morgue, to which all the corpses have been taken. The building is constantly crowded with weeping rela- ting of the dead, who have come for the purpose of iden- tifying the bodies and taking away the remains.

div.head: lIVHITECHAPEL TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE lIVHITECHAPEL TRAGEDY.

The inquest on the body of Frances Coles was resumed at Whitechapel on Monday morning. Witnesses iden4- fled Sadler as visiting the coffee shop in Whitechapel at 6.30 a.m. on the 13thinst. Another witness proved that the deceased visited Mrs. Shuttleworth's shop at 1.30 a.m. Duncan Campbell, a sailor, who was staying at Well-st. Sailors' Home, said Sadler came there about 10.30 on the morning of the 13th. He said he had been robbed, and producing a pocket knife, asked witness to buy it. Witnessgave him a shilling. Witness afterwards heard of the murder, and went into the lavatory, where he washed the knife in clean water. It turned the water salmon colour. Thomas Robinson, marine store deale-, said he bought the knife from Campbell for sixpence. Witness sharpened the knife, for it was blunt, and ate his supper with it. Chief Inspector Swanson, of the Criminal Investigation Department, said when Sadler was taken to the station he asked," Am I arrested for it ?" Witness said, " Certainly ; but it is necessary to take a statement from you to help us to throw some light upon the matter." Sadler then made a statement which was taken down. Two medical witnesses were examined, one of whom said the knife sold to Campbell could not have produced the wounds on the deceased, if, as alleged, it was blunter than it was now, and that the deceased's throat was cut while she was on the ground. k drunken man could not have inflicted the wound. The inquest was again adjourned. SADLER AGAIN REMANDED. John Thomas Sadler was charged on remand at the Thames Police Court, on Tuesday afternoon, with the murder of Frances Coles, at Whitechapel, and was for- mally remanded until Tuesday next. FUNERAL OF THE VICTIM. - _

_ The burial of Frances Coles, who was murdered on the 13th inst, at Swallow-gardens, Whitechapel, took place on Wednesday afternoon at the East London Cemetery, Plaistow. A crowd of about two thousand persons had assembled in the roadway and on thk. pavement. The service was an inipressive one, and the relatives of the deceased were greatly affected when the coffin, laden with flowers, was lowered into the grave. During the service reference was made to the circumstances under which the deceased came by her death, and the fervent hope was . expressed that the aqqastsin would be brought to justice. SUDDEN DEATH OF A WITNESS. Charles Guiver, one of the leading witnesses regarding the presence together and conversation of Sadler and the murdered woman Coles, in the lodging-house, 8, White's-row, has died suddenly. He was night watch- man at the house. The Coroner has ordered a post mortem examination of the body.

div.head: MURDEROUS ASSAULT BY A
div.p: THE MURDEROUS ASSAULT BY A

NAVVY. On Thursday the prisoner James White, Ship Canal labourer, was again brought up at the War- rington Borough Police Court charged with com- mitting a murderous assault upon Thomas Kelly, Ship Canal labourer, on the night of the 7th inst. The complainant had now sufficiently recovered to be able to appear. The magistrates were Captain Ridgway (chairman), and Alderman Sutton. The evidence of the prosecutor and Joseph Starkey,Ship Canal labourer, of Frederick-st., Latchford, brought out the following circumstances. The two men had been havini a glass together at the Packet House, Bridge-St.. and, soon after ten o'clock, were on their way threugh the Old-road to the model lodging- house in that road, where the complainant lodged, when the prisoner met them. He had had no disagreement with either of them, but he was not sober. He struck Starkey in the mouth and knocked him down, and on his asking what that was for, said, with an oath, he would serve the complainant the same. He knocked Kelly into the gutter with the buckle end of his belt, and then kicked him about the ribs two or three times. James Lynch, Ship Canal labourer,deposed to seeing the prisoner and Kelly in the Norton Arms, Latchford, about half-past nine on the night in ques- tion, and to White going out about ten o'clock, some ten minutes after Kelly. Witness left soon after, and then saw Kelly lying in the Old-road, across the road, and the prisoner standing on the other side with his back against the wall. Witness tried to lift Kelly up. and White came across and kicked Kelly twice on the back of the head, , and was going to do so a third time, when witness told him it was a shame; and he replied that he would give Lynch the same. There was no quarrel in the Norton Arms between theprisoner and Kelly. Catherine Knock- ton a widow, living in Old-road, said she heard a noise, and came out, and saw White kick Kelly twice. He was bleeding from the right ear, the hack of the head, and the mouth. The prisoner ran into the lodging-house when he saw a crowd coming. She went out and informed Mr. Cobley, the landlord of the lodging-house. Eunice Ashurst, of Old-road, gave corroborative evidence. The complainant was brought into her house. William Cob- ley, the lodging-house keeper, said he was informed by Mrs. Knockton of what had happened, and the prisoner was apprehended as he was going to bed. Police-Ser- geant Taylor deposed to apprehending the prisoner about 5 minutes to 10, and to having 'Kelly carried into Mrs. Ashurst's house, and subsequently on the police ambulance to the Infirmary. At the police station whither the prisoner was conveyed by P.C. Ward, White said it was not he who committed the assault but a man just like him with a velvet coat on, who had come into the lodging house and told him that he had done for a man in the Old-road, and he (the prisoner) had placed him on a form, and was going to bed when he was arrested. Sergeant Taylor ascertained that there was no truth in this story. Dr. Smith, senior house sur- geon at the Infirmary, testified as to Kelly's injuries, and said he remained unconscious till the Tuesday, after he was brought in, and then became partly con- scious. The drum of the right ear had been ruptured, and that ear would be permanently deaf. He was fairly well now, but would have to be in the Infirmary a short time longer.—The prisoner, who said lie had nothing to say in answer to the charge, was committed for trial to the Liverpool Assizes.

Mr. John Dillon has been removed to the prison infirm- ary, owing to ill-health, by order of the prison surgeon. Both Mr. O'Brien and Mr. Dillon are now in the hospital, but in separate _wards. Mr. Dillon is much broken in
Mr. O'Brien, although 5 subject for hospital treat . ment. is 141b3. heavier than when he was last imprisoned in Galway Gaol. Both gentlemen, it is stated, are satis- fied with their treatment..

div.head: AN AMERICAN VESSEL ASHORE. 01P'LOSS OF 17 LIVES.
div.p: AN AMERICAN VESSEL ASHORE. 01P- 'LOSS OF 17 LIVES.

A Reuter's telegram, dated San Francisco, Sunday, says :—The American ship Elizabeth, from New York, went ashore on the North head on Saturday night. A lifeboat, which went to her as4istance, capsized, and the captain of the boat was' drowned. Three of the crew of the vessel, the captain's wife, and her two children were, however, afterwards rescued, but the captain and the rest of the crew, numbering 16, were drowned. The Elizabeth will be a total loss.

div.head: DEATH OF LORD ALBEMARLE.
div.p: DEATH OF LORD ALBEMARLE.

The Earl of Albemarle died on Saturday morning, at half-past eight o'clock, at his seat, Quiclenham Hall, Norfolk, in his ninety-second year. He fought at Water- loo. and, with the exception of General Whichcote, was the only officer now on the British Army List who was present at the famous battle. From 1832 to 1835 he re- presented East Norfolk, was an unsuccessful candidate for Lynn in 1837, and for Lymington in 1841.; but was returned in 1847 for the latter, and sat till April, 1850. On Wednesday a funeral service was held at West- minster Abbey on the remains of the late Earl. A wreath sent by the Queen bore the inscription :—" A ,mark of sincere respect to pne of the heroes of Waterloo. '

div.head: AN M.P.'S DIVORCE SUIT.
div.p: AN M.P.'S DIVORCE SUIT.

-- - Evidence was heard in the Edinburgh Court of Session on Wednesday, in the action for divorce instituted by Mr. Alexander L. Brown. M.P., on the ground of his wife's adultery with Wm. Henry Shiels, brewers' travel- ler, 59, Marchmont-road, Edinburgh. Evidence swas given that Mrs. Brown, who is the daughter of a retired clergyman had become much addicted to drink. In the autumn oflBB3 Mr. Brown and his wife met Shiels on board a yacht, on which occasion Mr. Brown remarked that he was not the sort of man to come to the house, to which Mrs Brown replied, " Oh, that will be all right." Evidence was also given as to Shiels and Mrs. Brown being frequently seen in company in Mr. Brown's - grounds, and one instance of misconduct was sworn to by a gamekeeper and a farmer's son. A medical certifi- cate having been put in to the effect that Mrs. Brown could not be examined in open court, evidence was al- lowed to be taken in caztera. The case was not con- cluded.

Churchill THE Tory party have not yet done and Toryism with Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL• It is true that the SALISBURY family party have succeeded, with the help of Lord HARTINGTON and Mr. GOSCHEN, in dispensing with his services during the present Parliament as a cabinet minister; but he is still to be reckoned with so far as the country is concerned. He sees better than any other Tory leader the tendency of public opinion, especially amongst the working classes, and he is ready to sink a ship-load of fossilized notions in order to have the working classes on his side. Like Lord BEACONSFIELD, be makes it his business to educate his party; but there is no small number of the Tories who dislike him as a schoolmaster, for they are quite content to let things alone. And that is Toryism. Why should they trouble about making changes in order to meet the wishes of the people? Because, as Lord RANDOLPH tells them, if they do not, if they wrap themselves in "one eternal negative," the constituencies will fall away from them, and they will be "condemned to useless and impotent opposition." • Precisely, and that is exactly what is happening. As things go, his lordship will have the sat isfaction of saying—" I told you so," when he sees that the constituencies have resented the present policy of" masterly inactivity" by returning Mr. GLAD- STONE to power. It is suggestive, by-the-by, of the change which has come over Lord CHURCHILL that, in his speech to his constituents, he should warn them of the task before them by saying of Mr. GLADSTONE :—" You have a most remarkable-- perhaps the most extraordinary man as your poli- tical opponent whom the century has produced-- a man who by his increasing age, accompanied by his increasing brightness, becomes day by day more and more the object of popular veneration and popular hope." The meeting didn't cheer this statement, for, though true, it was to them an unpleasant truth.
Lord R. CHURCHILL still stands where he did on the Irish Land Purchase Bill. He said:—

• The whole principle of the purchase of land in Ireland by die State for the benefit of the occupiers, as an adjunct to the establishment of popular local Government,l can support, and will freely sup- port; but land purchase by itself, without the slighest guarantee that popular local Government in Ireland will be established, without any connec- tion whatever with the principles of popular local Government in Ireland. I cannot. There was no applause at this announcement' but when he went on to add that, having male his protest and put it in writing, he should take no part in the Parliamentary op- position to the Bill, there was an immense sign of relief, and the cheering was loud and lqng• Be independent, if you mat, but spare, oh spar.P

the Government! With regard to other questions, it would seem that the member for South Padding- ton has been studying the Liberal programme; and that—to borrow an old simile—he would have the Tories steal the clothes of the Opposition whilst they are bathing. It is but fair to say that his lordship is not a new convert to Free Educa- tion, and that, ,as he pleads, he advocated it some years ago, when men who occupy a high position in the Tory party regarded the proposal as "rank heresy." He got the idea, of course, from advanced Liberals, who have advocated Free Education since the passing of the Education Act twenty years ago. With regard to another plank of the Liberal platform— " one man one vote " he regards it as "a very small offer," but hopes the Tories will be "sensible enough not to allow the Liberal party to manufacture capital out of the cry." This means that he would have the Tories to commit themselves to this re- form; but he is not sure that they will have the sense to do so. Curiously, whilst on this question, Lord CHURCHILL expresses himself as being deter- mined "never to part with the twelve months' residence qualification." He thinks that a twelve months' residence is a test of the "solidity and capacity of an elector." But it is to the citizen and not to the residence that the vote should attach ; and what we need is to get rid of the rem- nant rags of property and residence qualification. The present writer was debarred from voting in two Parliamentary elections because of a single change of residence from one town to another. Could anything be more absurd than the loss of rights of citizenship from such a cause? Looking ahead towards the next Election, which, Lord CHURCHILL remarks, must take place within the next fifteen months, he is disturbed at the at- titude of the Tory party to the labour movement. He is in favour himself of the Bill for giving miners an eight hours' day. As regards trade dis- putes, he says : I observe that a section of the Tory Press, repre- senting a section of the Tory party, thinks it neces- sary whenever a strike occurs to immediately denounce the leaders for resorting to extreme mea- sures, to egg on the employers to resort to extreme measures themselves against the men, and if the employers win - -if they defeat the men—to utter shouts Gf triumph over the victory of the employers, and to hurl torrents of ridicule on the futile efforts of the men. Gentlemen, if you ask me whether think that from the point of view of the Conserva- tive politicians such a course is wise, and such an idea is sensible, I tell you that it is nothing short of Scandalous.

Yes, scandalous is the right word, and working- /nen, Tory as well as Liberal, have to ask them- selves whether they can support a party which thus shows itself hostile to them in matters of the most vital importance. Lord CHURCHILL may take the right view; but what of that? This one Swallow cannot bring .sunamer to the toilers who are still in the winter of their discontent. _
liow can a Royal Commission on these matters help them? It simply means a bit of hood- _ .
Winking urtil the elections are over. Let them look at the past history of Toryism, _ _

_ 4nd remember its resistance •to every move- trient which meant placing power in the hands of the people. It is only a few sears since the present PRIME MINISTER brought the country Within measurable distance of a revolution by his
resistance to the Liberal demand that the fran- chise should be extended to labourers in counties

as it was in boroughs; and to-day we see him and his followers denying to Irishmen the rights and liberties which are the precious heritage of their brethren in England. The Tory party is the party of the classes, and they are not to be trusted in legislating for the masses. As for promises, they are =Lade to be broken. There was a promise to Ireland in 1886 of conciliation and of equal laws; and how shamefully that promise was broken is
seen in a hateful Coercion Act which is at this mement being hatefully administered.
MR. G. BARTLEY, member for Is- Income-tax. lington, made out a capital case in

the House of Commons, on Tues- day, for inquiry into the bases of levying the in- eorne-tax, its mode of collection, system of appeal, 46e. ; but he addressed himself to deaf ears so far as the Government were concerneel,for his motion, on a vote being taken, was rejected by a majority of 5:5. Mr. SMITH admitted that there was great dissatisfaction, but pleaded that the question was beset with difficulties, and stated that the Chan- tellor of the Exchequer was considering the matter l_tr°lll every point of view. He said he " hardly evi any class deserving more commiseration than those who derived asmall income from capi- ‘4l) 'without having any means of increasing it by their industry." But these people are sively in a haPPY condition compared with others who, through the loss of the bread-winner, are suddenly mePrived of even a small income. Mr. BARTLEY is °/1 the right track in urging that "industrial in- , !?lnes up to £5OO should be exempted from income- l'a3c "; for this would be a much-needed relief to the classes who most feel the pressure, and who having, as the phrase goes, to "keep up appear- , anees " find it impossible to make provision of even Small incomes" for their children. The person lao is receiving £2OO a year from investments is in a much better position to pay income-tax than the Bitlaried clerk, manager, or professional man whose illoome ceases when he is unable to follow his em- Aloyment. It is a fact of no small moment as hearing upon this question that out of 415,000,per- aons who pay income-tax under "Schedule D" no fewer than 215,000—that is more than one half of the whole—pay on less than £2OO a year. The total sum received from the tax upon incomes is °°or £13,000,000; and it is estimated that, if ex- enlPtion were granted to £5OO a year, the loss to tllle revenue would not be more than £1,000,000. virlic is not a large problem to grapple with, and if ,117•GrOSCHEN cares to set about the solution,he will mo difficulty in accomplishing the task. What Wanted is not ability, but willingness; and it to be feared that if a little extra burden is to be t'Llit upon the wealthy, the present Chancellor of to" Exchequer will not be the man to lend himself the proposal. It is a matter ever to be re- 17.retted that the country did not return Mr. GLAD- C 11.141 to power in 1874, when, with a large surplus 'l and, he was pledged to the abolition of the ,3nle-tax,. At that period such a thing was pO5- 10:.e, for the tax realised less than £6,000,000; but 1):eil the Tories went out of office, in 1880, it may Le laid to have been impossible, for the burden to lifted was one of over £9000,000. It thus 4faPPeos that the nation has been bled to the tune th°v" 150,000,000 since the greatest financier of t:o.age offered to abolish the tax. The oppor- ItY then thrown away is not likely ever to l'ettlrn dra. , but we may at least ease this enormous a 41 upon the nation by raising what the teh'ouseationists call "the standard of exemption." If tionan who have large incomes pay their propor- te share of taxes, there will be no need to ate those who have comparatively small in- c°lfles into the mysteries of "Schedule D."

div.head: " TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: " TOUCH AND GO."

Are we not having "something too much" of Ober-Ammergan ? The latest move is to raise a fund for a new organ, which is to be "an English offering to the Ober-Ammergau Parish Church." The offering will, of course, be accepted, for the people seem to have " taking " ways with them.

The Wesleyans of Cadishead have been perform- ing the oratorio entitled "The Captives of Baby- lon," which reminds one of the play known as "Modern Babylon." After the performance of the drama in a neighbouring town, a woman who was leaving the pit was heard to say:—" It's a regular swindle; aw've bin looking fur a Baby Lion o' neet, but aw've seen nooan." She attached a mean'ng of her own to "Babylon."

The disease amongst horses known as pink eye is still prevalent at Warrington, though the epi- demic is believed to be on the decline. Mr. Fer- guson, veterinary surgeon, has had to attend as many as 43 animals in one stable; and it is esti- mated that as many as 200 horses in the town have been affected. The malady is something like typhoid fever as seen in the human subject. It is very contagious and often rapidly fatal.

At a meeting, on Tuesday, of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, some discussion took place on the injurious effect upon Runcorn of the noxious vapours from Widnes. The matter was adjourned for a fortnight. It should be followed up. The opinion prevails that if proper precautions are taken the nuisance can be in a large degree abated. Runcorn is not called upon to die in order that the trade of Widnes may live.

A navvy named John Kelly seems to have emu- lated the ways of the bull in the china shop, for he is reported, whilst he was drunk on Saturday night, to have gone " clean through " the window 'of a Warrington pork butcher. It could scarcely be said that he was " elevated," for it was given in evidence that lie sat in the window. In this respect he had the advantage of" the Spanish Champion " who "in the dust sat down." Kelly's escapade should make him more careful, for it cost him well ' nigh k 2.

It is satisfactory to find that the General Pur- poses Committee of the Warrington Town Council have revised the proposed list of members of the new Water Committee in the direction suggested in our columns last week. The Committee, as it now stands, is strong in men of experience in Cor- poi ate affairs, whilst there is still a fair proportion of what may be called the younger members of the Corporation. It is to be hoped the new broom will sweep clean—that is to say, carefully guard the interests of ratepayers and manufacturers. 1

The English occupation of Egypt cOntinues to result in loss of life—a fact which is brought home by the news that Captain H. L. Barrow, formerly of Warrington, is amongst the list of those who were killed at the taking of Tokar last week. No- body seems to know why this fighting has become necessary, or how long the British occupation is to last. We have been in possession nine years ; and it is about time there was some statement as to how much longer we mean to:expend blood and' treasure without a definite object.

The Government majority against Mr.Pritchard Morgan's motion in favour of Welsh Disestablish- ment was 32 only. It is very much like an inti- mation of an early notice to quit ; and it is not at all surprising that it should have given the Minis- try a shock. It comes to this, that the case against the Church as an establishment in Wales is so strong, that .a considerable number of Conserva- tives even cannot be brought to vote on the mat- ter. They see how the wind is blowing, and they do not care to run the risk of shipwreck.

The Government of the Classes is taking good care of the railway interest in appointing no fewer than five railway directors to serve on the Select Committee to inquire intone hours and work of rail- way servants, it is simply scandalous to bias the Committee in this way. It is like setting the cat to watch the cream. To rest9re the balance, there should be five representatives of labour on the Committee; hut the Government have no concep- tion of fairness in such a matter.

If the Royal Commission on Labour is to be nobbled in a similar way, it will excite contempt rather than interest. Can it be that Lord Chur- chill has forced the hand of the Government in this matter? It looks like it—judging from his speech on Saturday. The Commission is an after- thought, for if it had been decided upon sooner there would have been no need of the Railway Committee. It is estimated that the General Election will be over long before the Royal Com- mission presents its final report. This will suit the Tories very well; but will it suit the labouring classes? Are they to be shelved in this easy fashion?

It is stated that Lord Cross has promised to re- ceive a deputation of representatives from the tex- tile factory workers, Chambers of Commerce, and influential employers who wish to urge the impor- tance of Indian factory legislation on the lines of the English Factory Acts. As Secretary for India, his lordship has a splendid opportunity of doing the right thing; but he has not, hitherto, shown himgelf equal to it. The cotton trade in this country is in a very bad condition, and manufac- turers complain bitterly of the way in which they are handicapped in the race with India.

The Lord Mayor of London has been delivering aa address to young men which is said to have proved "almost identical with a sermon preached by Mr. Spurgeon twenty-seven years ago." There is a cry of plagiarism, but Mr. Savory pleads that, so far as he is aware, he had never seen Mr. Spurgeon's sermon. The Rev.. W. Rogers states that Mr. Spurgeon about the time he preached his sermon employed a person to pick plums out of the Rump Sermons in Sion College Library; and he asks might not the Lord Mayor's amanuensis have poached upon the same manor ? " Perhaps, but hat would mean two preachers; and two blacks don't make one white.

Several cases of alleged breaches of the Coal Mines Regulation Act were heard at St. Helens, on Monday. They arose out of the death of James Twist, who was killed on the 19th October, through an explosion of gas in No. 11 pit of the St. Helens Colleries. Somebody was at fault, but the difficulty was to 'fix the blame; for, if it is hard to get at the truth as to what takes place above ground, it is harder still when the inquiry is as to doings underground. After a five-hours hearing, some of the cases were dismissed and others nith- drawn. It is a most unsatisfactory result ; nut the officials of the Treasury are to be commended for their perseverance in the matter.

It has been suggested that baccarat is not an illegal game, but the issue which is likely to be raised by a certain high-life case is whether cheat- ing is an offence. As to this, a London contem- porary settles the point by quoting the following from 8 and 9 Victoria

"Be it enacted; that every person who shall by any fraud or unlawful device or ill practice in play- ing at or with cards, dice, tables, or other game. . . . win from any other person to himself or any others any sum of money or valuable thing, shall be deemed guilty of obtaining such money or valuable thing from such other person by a false pretence with intent to cheat and defraud such person of the same, and being convicted thereof, shall be punished accordingly."
A destructive fire broke out on Tuesday morning in Archer-st., Notting-hill, London, nearly twenty occu- piers of shops and other premises being among the sufferers.

A woman named Ellen Hoyle walked into the canal at Shipley during the fog on Wednesday. She had given evidence the same day at the inquest on Frank Seed, a labourer, who was drowned under similar circum- stances. •

The trial commenced at Guildford Assizes on Thursday before Mr. Justice Stephen, of Louisa Brown, charged with killing her domestic servant, Ann Scott. His lordship ruled the evidence insufficient to justify the case being sent to thejury, but on minor counts the pri- soner was sentenced to six months' imprisonment.
If you value your wife's health see that she uses " SUNLIGHT SOAP. —Advt.

*** NEW STORY.—On Saturday next, March 7th, a new story will be commenced in the columns, of the " Examiner " entitled "Percival Gordon, or the Child of the Regiment." We commend it to our readers in the belief that it will be found to be as interesting as previous tales in this journal.

div.head: UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUNCORN
div.p: UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUNCORN

The fourth of the series of lectures on " The growth of the political systems of Europe" was delivered in Bethesda Schoolroom on Friday evening, by Mr. H. J. Mackinder, M.A. The subject for the evening was "The Franks."
UMBRELLAS 11E-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. & V. DUTTON'S Sankey-st.. Warrington.—.Adyt. BRITISH AND FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETY, WIDNES.

A 'fleeting of the Widnes auxiliary of the British and Foreign Bible Society was held in the Baths Assembly room on Thursday night. The audience was of only meagre proportions. Mr. J. Brock, J.P. presided, and addresses, in advocacy of the claims of the Society, were delivered by the Rev. T. Law, Rev. G. LI Garrett (vicar), and the Rev. Charles T. Moss, formerly of Madagascar, and deputation from the parent society. A collection was made at the close of the meeting. A'r HALEnANX.

At Widnes Police Court on Monday Edward Rogers was charged with assaulting Joseph Woodward on the 14th inst. The charge had been reduced from unlawful wound- ing to assault. The man lodged at 12, Johnson-st., Hale- bank, and on the night in question the men had some " words," ending in a scuffle, during which Woodward received a wound on the left side of the head, which bled profusely.—Mr. Knowles for the defence admitted that his client caused the quarrel but pleaded fora lenient sen- tence. A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed. BASSINETTES.—J .S. Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington.—Advt. A WIDNES PROPERTY OWNER AND THE PURITY CRUSADE.

Mrs. Ann Sutton, of Widnes, was charged at the City Police Court, Liverpool, before Mr. W. J. Steward, stip- endiary magistrate, with having been wilfully a party to the continued use of a house for immoral purposes at 11, Seagrave-st., Liverpool. Mr. Moss prosecuted, and Mr. Neale defended. The Bench considered that there were extenuating circumstances in the case, and Mr. Stewart contented himself with accepting the bail of the defendant's son-in-law, who was bound over on her behalf not to permit the house being carried on as a disorderly one.
RUNCORN BOWLING CLUB.

Mr. Cooper, of Wilson's Hotel, Bridge-st., has just had the bowling green attached to his house re-formed and re-laid with fresh sods, at considerable cost, and during the summer it is expected to be one of the finest greens in the neighbourhood. A club has also been formed under the title of Runcorn Bowling Club, with Mr. Isaac Stubbs, president; Mr. H. Coward, vice-president; Mr. Cooper, treasurer; and Mr. W. Garrett, secretary; and a committee of local gentlemen. Many persons have signified their intention to join the club, and a meeting was held on Thursday night to adopt rules and make necessary arrangements. LA.WN MOWERS.—Garland, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington, and at Earlestown.—Advt.

div.head: WIDNES GYMNASIUM.
div.p: WIDNES GYMNASIUM.

With the object of increasing the funds of this admir- able institution an assault at arms and gymnastic display took place in the Drill Hall, on Thursday night, before a large company. Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P., was annonnced to preside, but he had been suddenly called to the West Indies on business, and was unable to be pre- sent. He had forwarded a cheque for £3 as a subscrip- tion to the gymnasium. The chair was taken by Cap- tain Lewis. The display was given by a team composed of Widnes and Warrington Gymnasts under the respec- tive leaderships of Mr. E. W. Pettitt, of Liverpool, and Mr. A. Alexander, F.R.G.S. The various exercises was gone through in a highly creditable manner, and were viewed with much enjoyment. The foiling tournament was a feature of much interest. ASSAULT ON A RUNCORN POLICE SERGEANT. - • - -

A boatman named John Squires, was brought before the Runcorn magistrates on Wednesday, charged with having been drunk and disorderly and assaulted P.S. Gosling. On the previous night whilst opposite Mr. Crosby's shop in High-street, P.S. Gosling heard screams from the direction of Stone Croft, and crossing the canal in a boat, he found the prisoner viho was drunk kicking his wife in Vine-yard. The constable caused him to desist from his violence, but he refused to enterhis house and was about to be apprehended, when he ran away. The constable followed him home, where the prisoner struck him and kicked him, and in self-defence he drew his staff, and felled his assailant with a blow. The pri- soner was then locked up and the magistrates fined him ss. and costs for the drunkenness, and £l, or a month, for the assault. RUNCORN COFFEE AND COCOA HOUSE CO. LIMITED.

The thirteenth annual meeting of the shareholders of this Company was held in Westminster Cocoa Rooms on Mond# afternoon, under the presidency of Mr. Thos. Handley, the chairman of directors. The report stated that the receipts from refreshments amounted to £1,066 19s. 2d., being an increase on the previous year of £7O 7d. During the year the unoccupied portion of the premises had been let, whic h with the reduced cost of provisions and increased returns showed a profit on the twelve months' working of £ll5 Os. 3d. This, with the balance of £25 Us. 7d. from the previous year, made a total of £l4O us. 10d., which the directors proposed to distribute as follows: To 6 per cent. dividend on paid up capital, £lO5 ss. 9d. to write off furniture and fitting account £27 7s. 5d., and carry a balance forward of £7 18s. Bd. The reportand balance sheet were adopted. UMBRELLAS RE-COVED at the shortest notice.—J. & W. BUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. STEALING A BOYS BREAKFAST AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday a navvy named Walter Leggett, was charged with stealing three pieces of bread and butter belon.zing to John James Charlesworth, a boy. Charlesworth Is in the employ of Mr. Moores, carter, and his duty was to wait opposite the Police Station to a -.Alain horse, to help lurries up Bridge-st. On Tuesday morning he placed his breakfast can and bread and butter on a I,3dge at the Police Station and while he was away with his .horse, P.S. Gosling saw the prisoner who was accompanied by two other navvies, take up the bread and butter and after examining it place it in his pocket and walk away. When he had reached the fountain, his companions whispered some- thing to him and he returned and replaced the parcel be- sides the can. The Sergeant then apprehended him. His first excuse was that he had taken it for a lark and then that he was hungry. Mr. Brundrit said it was a cruel thing to rob a lad of his breakfast and imposed a fine of ss.

OH, YES!' Cough Mixture, Chirett,a Balsam. Relief in three minutes. Cures Brcruchitis. Hope. late Methuen, Deansgate, Manchester, and all Dealet7.—Advt. RUNCORN PROPERTY AND INVESTMENT COMPANY. The annual meeting of shareholders was held at Bank Chambers, on Monday, when the directors' report and balance sheet were adopted. The report stated that dur- ing the year, the directors had erected ten dwelling- houses in Ross-st., on lower Long Croft Estate 4 and six dwelling houses in York-st.,_ on Greenway-road Estate ; the latter had been disposed of in one lot and six of the former had been sold to separate purchasers. Although little profit had been made on the buildings the Company had received full value for the freehold of the land on which they stood. The directors had also sold three cot- tages with the freehold of the laud, in York-st., leaving only two cottages remaining in the possession of the Company out of fourteen originally built, and which the directors hope to dispose of shortly. The directors had now in course of erection, seven bay-window houses in Victoria-road on Greenway-road Estate and had made a provisional agreement for the sale of the houses with the freehold of the land as soon as they were completed and ready for tenants. The directors painted to the improved financial position of the Company, and stated that they intend to further develope the Company's lands, by the erection of a number of dwelling houses during the pre- sent year with a large cash balance now at the Com- pany's bankers.—Mr. John Simpson the retiring direc- tor was re-elected.
CHITCHLEY'STaiIoring meets the times.—Advt.

div.head: ER, SATLRDAY, FEBRUARY 28, 1891.
div.p: ER, SATLRDAY, FEBRUARY 28, 1891.
ST. JOHN'S BIBLB GLASS, RUNCORN.
At the weekly meeting of this class on Monday, Mr. W. G. Jackson read-an excellent essay on "The French Revolution: its causes and effects." PRESENTATION TO MISS HANNAH WILLIAMS.

At the—City-road Presbyterian Sunday School, Chester, an interesting presentation of a timepiece from tbe school, and a hymn book from the C. E. Society, was made to Miss Hannah Williams, a teacher and active member, on leaving for Runcorn. Miss Williams is a sister of the Rev. J. Polford Williams, pastor of St. John's Presbyterian Chapel, Runcorn. In addition to the above presentation, Miss Williams was the recipient of a present from her class. WESTON SONS OF TEMPERANCE.

The 11th annual tea and Public meeting of the" Nil- Desperandum " division of the Sons of Temperance was held at Weston, in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, on Wed- nesday evening. There was a large number of members and friends present. At the public meeting, which was well attended, Mr. D. Bisbrown, G. W. Patriarch of Che- shire, presided, and referred to the numerical and finan- cial condition of the order, and held that the moral was even more important than the financial aspect of the work. It was recognised that being a Son of Temper- ance tended to thrift, and was conducive to a higher moral tone. During the pastyear 20 new divisions and 21 cadet or juvenile sections had been opened, showing an increase in the adult order of 1,349, making a total membership in this country of 25,089. div.head: SCALDING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SCALDING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.

• Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner, on 4:3-n Monday, held an inquest at Runcorn Police Court, on the body of an infant 18 months old,named John Shallcross, son of a chemical labourer, who lives in Duke-st., on the Bth of January, Mrs. Shallcross was taking break- fast with the child on her knee, when another child four years of age upset a cup• of tea, some of the hot liquid falling upon the deceased. The burns were not very serious, but the child gradually sank in consequence of the shock to the system, and died on Sunday morning. A verdict of" Accidental death "was recorded. . div.head: EXTRAORDINARY FATALITY AT WESTON CHEMICAL WORKS.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY FATALITY AT WESTON CHEMICAL WORKS.

Mr. Tatlock, coroner, on Wednesday, held an in- qmest at Chester Infirmary on the body of Samuel Chatwood, 22 years of age, labourer, who died from injuries received at Weston Chemical Works, near Runcorn, on Monday. Deceased and another young man named John Littler were working a steam waggon hoist, Littler being at the top and deceased at the bottom. The signal for putting the hoist in motion was the sound of iron catches which deceased fastened to the waggon to be hoisted. Littler heard the catches, and set the hoist in motion; but seeing the cage without the waggon coming up, and deceased with his head down- wards, wedged between the cage and a cross beam, he lowered the cage, and deceased fell to the ground. Chat- wood was picked up conscious, but could not tell how the accident occurred, and he was removed to Chester Infir- mary, where his rig,ht leg I iad to be amputated. He died the same night. The medical evidence went to show that death resulted from shock and loss Of blood. The jury returned a verdict of *4 Accidental death," but thought the company ought to provide better signals.

div.head: POLICE CONSTABLES' SOIREE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: POLICE CONSTABLES' SOIREE AT RUNCORN.

A most pleasant and unique gathering so far as Runcorn is concerned, took place on Wednesday night, when the members of the police force of the Runcorn Petty Sessional Division were entertained to tea and a social evening. The idea of relieving by a little healthy relaxation the policemen's mon- otonous round of duty, originated with several tradesmen, viz. Messrs. S. Coventry, T. Cooke, T. Woods, and J. A. Smith, who formed themselbes in- to a committee, and solicited subseriptioas towards the object they had in view. The following gentle- men responded most willingly and generously : Sir Richard M. Brookes, Bart., Messrs. John Brund- rit, C. W. Hazlehurst, S. B. Chadwick,C. Reynolds, J. Reynolds, J. Handley, G. L. Wigg, A. Thomas G. L. Davies, Dr. Steel, P. Speakman C.C., John Mccleston, (Blackburn) and Dr. MacDougall. With ample funds at their dispozal, the Committee issued their invitations, anh on Wednesday a company of about fifty sat down to an excellent knife and fork' tea, the tables being pre- sided over by Mrs. Coventry, Mrs. T. Cook, Mrs. T. Woods, and Mrs. J. A. Smith. The company, which consisted of the sergeant and constables and their wives and 'Sweethearts, also included Mr. Superintendent Large and Mrs. Large ; and Mr. Superintendent Leah and Mrs. 'Leah of Crewe. The room had been gaily decorated with bunting, whilst the platform was draped with curtains and adorned by numerous plants, the appearance of the building being very bright and attractive. After tea a concert was given by a number of local amateurs, the chair being occupied by Superintendent Leah, in the absence of Mr. P.' Speakman, who had been called away on business. In opening the proceedings, The Chairman said it afforded him very great pleasure to have the honour cf being present with them on that ' auspicuous occasion. His experience of Runcorn, as most of them knew, was a very short one, coming to the town as he did in June 1884, and leaving in June 1886. Run- corn being his first place as Superintendent, lie looked upon those two years spent amongst them with no small amount of pride and pleasure. (Applause.) Since he hail left, the Police of the county and particularly of Runcorn had passed through a trying ordeal. Even the good name of the magistrates was assailed. They were charged with certain practices,but during his time in the town he never saw even the shadow of those shortcom- ings with which they were elarged. ( Applause.) He had found that the members of the Runcorn Bench gave their time and attention to their duties, and on all occasions administered even-handed justice in a straightforward and conscientious manner, with no other object in view, he was sure, than to maintain the peace and goodlorder of the town. (Applause.) As those present knew, they had come out of a furnace without being tainted, and he would leave the public to judge for themselves as to the charges imputed, but he thought they could not have a better proof than to look at that meeting. He was of opinion that the police must not plead guilty, at least to everything that was laid to their charge. (Hear, hear.) He thought they would agree with him that they had rules and regulations laid down for their guidance which had never been found wanting in any way during the trial, and if those rules and regulations were followed out and the police discharged than in a conscientious manner, they need not fear any inquiry. (Applause.) On the other hand he felt that they would not only receive the support of the .Standing Committee, under whose control the police now were. , but also of the citizens of Runcorn and or the people of Ithe country generally. (Applause.) The following programme was then gone through in excellent style, and afforded much pleasure to the guests. Instrumental overture, " Gay Cavaliers " ; song, " Little Heroes," Mr. Flollinshead ; song, "Killarney," Miss Rigby, St. Helens; comic song, "Oh, let it be soon," Mr. Evans, Widnes ; duet, "The Gipsey Countess," Miss Clara Eden and Mr. Wesley Cooke; clarionette duet, "Home to our Mountains," the Brothers Outhwaite ; comic trio, "Three nice young gentlemen," Messrs. T. Cooke, S. Coventry. and W. Cooke; recitations, (Lancashlre dialect), " Owd Boone's Goose," and "Bobby Grundy's Shop," Miss Wells, St. Helens; song, "Steering home," Mr. A. Cay Gill; comic duet, "The sailor's duet," Misses Evans and Rylands, (Brothers Johnson Widnes) •, violin solo, "Caliph of Bagdad," Miss Smith; duet, "No Sir," Miqs Joynson, Widnes. and Mr. W. Cook; song "When the robins come again," Miss Eden; instrumental trio' Messrs. Outhwaite and Sons; song" Tit for Tat," Miss F. Joyson(Widnes) ; comic song " Gilhooley's supper party,' Mr. Rylands ; song "Nancy Lee." Mr. Hollinshead ; song "Scenes that are brightest," Miss Rigby; glee" Till we meet again." En- cores were frequent and generally responded to. Mr. W. Cook was the accompanist.—Mr. Coventry proposed that the best thanks of those present be given to the donors for their generosity, and remarked that he hoped this was only the inauguration of an annual pleasant evening for the Runcorn police force. It seemed to him that the police as a class had been overlookqd. if not neglected, and hence they had been brought together in this social way to enjoy themselves.—Mr. J. A. Smith seconded the motion, and said the monotonous round of very unpleasant duties the police had to perform called for greater recognition trom the public than had been the case in the past. The great services the police rendered to the community seemed to be overlooked; it was not the amOunt of crime they detected and the number of crim- inals they. brought to justice, but it was the greater amount of crime which they prevented that was of the greatest value. Prevention was better than cure and very much cheaper. (Applause.)—The motion was carried unanimously.—Mr. T. Cooke moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman, Superintendent Large seconded, and it was carried.—Superintendent Large then moved that the best thanks of the meeting be accorded to the com- mittee who had organised mid carried out that social evening. He hoped it would hot be the last, not because of the good things provided, but because of the kind feeling which had prompted it, and as displaying the friendly spirit with which the police force was regarded. (Applause.)—Superintendent Leah seconded the motion, which was carried by acclamation. Votes of thanks were also accorded to Mr. W. Shaw and Mr. Whittler,for the loan of flags, Mr. Thomas. Halton-road, for plants, Messrs. Spearing and Son, for cooking the meats, and to all the ladies and gentlemen who had in any way assisted at the entertainment. The forms were now cleared, and various amusements indulged in until eleven o'clock when an excellent supper was served. In the course of the evening retreshments of various kinds were pro- vided, including cigars for the gentlemen. A most en- joyabfe evening was brought to a close by singing "Auld Lang Syne."
PRES6OT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians Was held on Thursday afternoon at the Workhouse Whiston. There were present Major Wareing (chair- man), the Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, Messrs. Wm. Tyrer, C. B. Johnson, J. Marsh, G. Davies, W. Middlehurst, J. Kenwright, J. Leatherbarrow, J. Mercer, J. Birchall, J. Ranson, Joseph Ellison, J. Buckley, W. Daine, E. Syder, P. Longton, and Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk.) WORKHOUSE INMATES.—MY. Hale (master of the Work- house) reported that there were 573 inmates in the Workhouse this week, 563 in the preceding week, and 597 in the corresponding period last year. There had been 93 vagrants relieved during thq week, against 57 in the corresponding week in 1890. • THE WATER SUPPLY.-At a meeting of the Visiting Committee it was reported that the water supply at the workhouse was inadequate and the matter was referred to the Building Committee. The Chairman said that the question at present was in abeyance, and it would not be judicious for the board to say anything. The subject then dropped. CONSUMPTION.-Mr. Middlehurst remarked that he noticed some of the inmates were suffering from con- sumption and he thought it might be necessary for the guardians to keep their eye on the effect that Dr. Koch's cure'had, in other institutions, where it was being tried, with the view of bringing it into use in their own Work- house. _

MEDICAL OFFICERS ASKED TO EXPLAIN.—The Clerk read a communication from the Local Government Board, drawing attention to the fact that the column headed "Present state on termination of the case" had not been filed up for the past half-year by certain medical officers, and the books as at present kept afforded no information to the Guardians or their relieving officers as to the con- dition of each patient at the termination of the week.— The Clerk said the medical officers must be asked for an explanation, and the subject dropped. No MORE EMIpIATIO?I.—A circular letter was read from an emigration society asking the Guardians if they cared to sena any of their girls to Canada in the spring about May.—The Clerk did not think the Guardians were prepared to consider that question now.—Mr. Tyrer was of the same opinion.—The Clerk continuing, said the Guardians were not favourable to emigration, as the reports they had received of these already sent were anything but satisfactory, and not one half the children had been traced.

OUTRELIEF.—The Clerk said the Local Government Board had asked for the usual return as to the number of in-door and out-door paupers within the Union. That report had been prepared, and showed that on the Ist January, 1891. there were relieved indoors. 814, and outdoors, 3,579, making a total of 4,393. This total, as compared with the preceding year was an increase of 360, and the outrelief generally was rapidly increasing. —A long discussion ensued and a motion was proposed that the subject be considered by a sub-committee. The iProposition was ultimately withdrawn it being under- stood that the relief committees would take the matter into consideration .—This was the principal business.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at the Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were present Mr. A. Thomas, J.P. (ex- officio), Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. E. Aaron, J. Baguley, Mclntyre, Brandreth, P. Hall, Parr, J. W. Eirkman, and H. G. Linaker (clerk).

div.head: FRODSHAM WATER SCHEME.
div.p: FRODSHAM WATER SCHEME.

The minutes of the Frodsham Parochial Committee stated that the Clerk had communicated with the agent of Mr. Higson and the representative of the late Mrs. Perrin, inquiring whether they would sell the Authority the land required for the purpose of constructing water- works for the township of Frodsham. He had received replies, stating the owners of the property would be consulted, and the result communicated as soon as pos- sible. The Committee recommended that application be made to the Local Government Board for permission to borrow money for carrying out the proposed water- works for Frodsham.—The Clerk said he should ask for a sufficient amount, and what was not spent could be re- turned to the loan. The estimate of Mr. Timmins was £3,000, and there would be a further amount for the purchase of land and way-leave.—The minutes were ap- proved.
TILE PaLIITION OF KECKWICK BROOK.
The Clerk reported thatin accordance with Mr. Aaron's

motion at the last meeting, he had written to Mr. Brun- ner and laid the case of the pollution of the Keckwick ; Brook before him; Mr. Brunner had not acknowledged the receipt of the letter, and he (the clerk) did not see that Mr. Brunner had asked the President of the Lecai Government Board any question upon it; so that the authority were no further than they were a fortnight ago.—Mr. Aaron: And the Local Government Board had taken no notice of it? The Clerk no.—Mr. Aaron: What is to be done now ?—The Chairman : Wait a little langer ; don't be so impatient.—Mr. Aaron: We have waited three years. and it is time something was done. Tho Clerk read the letter he had forwarded Mr. Brunner, and Mr. Aaron said it was a very good one, and he thought it was a shame that Mr. Brunner as the repre- sentative of that division had so neglccted his duty.— Mr. Brandreth : (jocularly) Do you move a vote of cen- sure upon him ? (Laughter.)—The Chairman: No, no. —Mr. Aaron: I think it a great shame.—The Chairman said perhaps Mr. Brunner had not been in the House of Commons.—Mr. Aaron said he knew he was there, but he was busy with the Subsidence Bill.—Mr. Mclntyre : I hopeyou will Eubside too. (Laughter).—Mr. Aaron : Put the letter and everything else in the paper and let Cheshire see what sort of a member they have.—Mr. Mclntyre said the Local Government Board had said they were investigating the matter and they would reply , when the investigation was concluded.—Mr. Aaron de- scribed the deadly nature of the pollution, and said the authority ought to protect the farmers in the matter.— Mr. A. Linaker (Law Clerk) said the Government was making a general inquiry into the pollution of streams, and perhaps that was keeping this matter back—The Clerk said if the Local Government Board sanctioned the Authority takinc proceedings, it would meal the spend- ing of a lot of money in an atteqlpt to close Mr. Earp's works, and the Local Governmerit Board would not give their sanction unless they considered there was a very good case.—lt was -decided to allow the matter to rest another fortnight.
WIDNES CHEMICALS AND THE FARMERS.

Mr. Parr said he and other farmers had to complain of the chemical vapours from Widnes. He must admit that the vapours had not been so bad during the past month as during the previous months, but still they des- troyed timber and hedges and also pasturage. If a farmer laid down clover to improve his land, he found in a year or two that it was nothing but a wild moor. It was high time something should be donein the matter.— The Chairman said he did not think this was within the province of the Authority.—Mr. Parr replied that surely if a small private nuisance came within the powers of the Authority, this great public nuisance did.—The Clerk : Is it injurious to health ?—Mr.Parr said the fumes 1 gave cattle " grape." They were an injury and a nuis- ance.—The Chairman: We should have to get permis- sion of the Local Government Board to take proceedings. (Laughter.) The Clerk: If it is injurious to health you can take proceedings.—Mr. Parr said the ratepayers ought to be protected from such a nuisance, and he sug- gested that a letter be written to the Inspector under the Alkali Acts.—Mr. Brandreth said the same , complaint came from people in the Widnes dis- trict. The nuisance was caused by some leakage in the Chance process, and Mr. Carey, the secretary to the Chemical Union had promised that every attempt should be made to prevent the fumes escaping.—Mr. Aaron agreed with Mr. Parr that the vapours were both in- jurious and a nuisance. He knew from his own know- ledge that if the plant for carrying out Chance's process were properly fixed there would not be any nuisance from it, and were the plant fixed in the Workhouse gar- den the inmates of the house would not smell anything. The subject was deferred for a fortnight in order that the opinion of the Medical Officer might be obtained, Mr. 1 Parr in the meantime to take observations.
NUISANCES. • Inspector Farrington reported a number of nuisances in various parts of the Union, and he was empowered to take the steps he thought advisable. A NEW RATE.
It was resolved to levy a rate of p. in the £ in the Sanitary district for the next half year.

div.head: RUNCORN, BALTON, AND WESTON WATERWORKS' COMPANY.
div.p: RUNCORN, BALTON, AND WESTON WATERWORKS' COMPANY.

The half-yearly meeting was held at the Public Hall on Monday afternoon. Mr. John Brundrit, J.P., chairman of directors, presided, and there were present Messrs. William Hayes, John Simpson, T. Bankes, W. Whittaker, Walter Timmins, T. D. Tim- mins, W. F. Salkeld (secretary), and W. Jones (assistant). The directors' report, which was taken as read stated that" the revenue account shows a balance of £842 14s. id. including £l7B 7s. id. brought from the previous half-year, out of which the directors recom- mend a dividend to be declared of four pounds ten shil- lings per centum per annum, free from income tax, payable on and after the first day of March ; this will absorb £675, leaving a balance of £167 14s. id. to be carried forward. The repairs to engines, boilers, &c., during the past year have been carried out to the satisfaction of the directors. The water in the well continues as previously, and of godd quality." i The Chairman, n moving the adoption of the report and balance sheet, and the declaration of the dividend pro- posed, said he might fairly congratulate the shareliblderit upon the improved state of affairs since the last half- yearly meeting. There was an increase in the receipts for water of £lOO, while on the other hand the expenses had decreased by about the same amount, which was a very satisfactory state of things. One reason for this less expenditure was that the directors had adopted the method of covering the boilers with asbestos, which had conduced to the maintenance of the heat, and so caused less fuel to be used; and the initial cost had been amply repaid by the results. The severity of the winter had been a matter of great anxiety to the Board, inasmuch as the unusually hard frost had caused many pipes to burst, and a. consequent great waste of water took place. It was a rather singular fact that even at the present time, although all the plumbers of the town, the Com- pany's men, and others were working overtime trying to put matters right, there yet remained a fortnight's or .three weeks' work, and a waste of water which they could not avoid was still going on. There had been 39 new houses erected during the half year, and as building was constantly going on, there was no doubt as each half year went by, they would have a corresponding increase in the number of 'houses to be supplied. In conclusion, the Chairman alluded to the loss the Board had sustained by the death ii>f Mr. Ebenezer Timmins, one of its most able members. His vast experience in engineering, and especially in pump ing machinery, had been of the utmost possible use to the Board, and his advice, when sought, was always given in a mild and unassuming manner, and yet with a force and dearness that carried conviction to all who had to do with him.—Mr. Hayes seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.—On the proposition of Mr. W. Timmins, seconded by Mr. T. Bankes, a vote of thants was accorded to the Chairman, and a similar compliment was paid to the Secretary (Mr. Salkeld) and his assistants, on the motion of Mr. Whittaker, seconded by the Chairman.—Mr. Salkeld, in reply, assured the meeting that he and those who worked with him, did their best for the company.
A MEMORIAL WINDOW AT FARN- WORTH PARISH CHURCH.

In memory of the Rev. Thomas Moss, who, for forty years, was Vicar of the parish of Farnworth, and of other members of the family, a beautiful stained glass window has been placed in the chan- cel of St. Luke's Church by Mr. Thomas Moss Hors- fall, a descendant, who has amassed great. wealth. The window is a large one, divided by four mullions, and surmounted by a number of small circular lights. In the upper part of the centre light there is a representation of the crucificion with the monogram "I H S." To the left are figures of Mary, the mother of Christ, and Thomas, and to the right of these are figures of John and Timothy. Besides these figures in the panels, are repre- sentations of Moses lifting up the brazen serpent, Abra- ham offering up Isaac as a sacrifice, Gideon and the fleece, Solomon offering the prayer at the dedication of the Temple and the Annunciation. At the base of the panels are the following figures emblematic of Christ's passion—" The crown of thorns, the three nails, Pilot's scourge, the spear, reed, and sponge and the seamless vesture." In the small circular light at the top of the window are representations of the four Evangelists. The colours are rich and mellow and the figures lifelike. The inscription is as follows :—" This window is erected in

div.head: THF BLOOD IS THE LIFE.
div.p: THF BLOOD IS THE LIFE.
Given pure Blood and the result is perfect health and strength. To secure perfect Blood all impurities must be removed from it. How? We will in a few words, attempt to explain. . .

All the blooa in the body passes through the kidneys, las it does through the heart, and while doing so, if the kidneys are in perfect health and worlang order, the impurities which are in a state of solution are eliminated I and carried out of the system. A moment's thought will convince how all important the kidneys are. If they are in any way deranged the poisonous matter is not extracted, but courses through and through the system, gathering its forces daily and deposit- ing its baneful acid crystals in different parts. div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
BY "AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT."
That good progress is being made with the con- struction of the viaduct across the Big Pool to con- nect the new Victoria-road with iill Brow.

That the waters of the pool and of the canal have been effectually dammed off, and the concrete foundations of the piers of the arches are now laid, and to judge from the busy aspect of the place, the superstructure will soon be raised.

That at the same spot the new offices of the Manchester Ship Canal repairing works are rapidly rising from the ground, and they will form a most handsome block when completed. That the foreman's lodge i already roofed over, and the carpenters are at work on the interior. That it is of a most picturesque design, and one quite unique in the neighbourhood. That the police soiree on Wednesday was a most pleasant and enjoyable gathering, and the trades- men concerned are to be congratulated on upon the happy idea, and the magistrates and other gentlemen for their generous donations. That according to the song a policeman's lot is not a happy one; their duties do not allow of many social evenings with their friends, and the period of reNxation on Wednesday was therefore all the more welcome.
That our worthy Superintendent Large had made arrangements for the protection of life and pro- perty while his men were enjoying themselves, and timid householders need have no fear.

_ That the Privy Council in answer to the petition of Widnes Local Board for a charter of incorpora- tion have granted & Local Goverment inquiry into the subject, and the General Purposes Committee have fixed Wednesday, the 25th March next as the date of the inquiry, which will be held at the Town

That the lion. T. IL W. Pelham, one of her Ma- jesty's inspectors, has been appointed to hold the inquiry, and take evidence. That there is felt to be only one outcome, and that is the granting of the charter asked for. That the size and importance of the town com- mercially demands incorporation; the population being 30,000, and the rateable value £135,000. _ _

Dia' t the Local BGard election will take Place as usual in April, when the retiring members are Messrs. F. Liddell, B. Brown, F. Hayes, J. Taylor, and D. Wright, and it is not probable they will be opposed, as a contested election at the present juncture would be a waste of public money. That according to the scheme accepted by the Local Board, the Council, when formed, will consist of 18 councillors and 6 aldermen.

div.head: RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB.
CONOERT AND SOIREE.

The second annual concert and soirée in connec- tion with Runcorn Liberal Club, was held in the Public Hall, on Monday night. A large company assembled, and the affair throughout was of a most successful character. The proceedings were opened by Mr. W. Occleston in a few well-chosen words, in which he advocated the claims of the club, and im- pressed upon those present the advantages to be gained thereby. The first item on the programme was the song "Come into the garden, Maud, which was sung by Mr. J. Morrison (Widnes) with his ac- customed taste and expression. Later he gave "Love's golden dream" with much effect, and the hearty plaudits of the audience were well deserved. Miss Dora Gray, R.A.M. (of Manchester), who has a voice of much sweetness and power, sang "Queen of the earth," in a paannr that highly delighted the audience, and in response to an encore, she sang "Sunshine and rain." In the second part of the entertainment she ren- dered the song "Last night," in chaining style. Miss Clara Taylor (Runcorn) contributed " Spinning " and "Never more," in which her rich and full soprano voice was heard to great advantage, and she was enthusias- tically encored, a compliment which she acknow- ledged. The duet "Oh, that we two were Alaying " by Miss Gray and Mr. Morrison, was a very enjoyable piece of vocalization. Mr. William Sweetman (Liverpool)made his first appearance before a Runcorn audience and scored a great success. He possesses a bass voice of bsautiful ton k 3 and wide range, and sang with much expression and power, "The Arab's bride," " The mighty deep," and" In cellar cool." For his last two efforts lie was vociferously encored and sang " The Village Blacksmith," and "Still as night." Mr. A. G. Davies (of Rainhill) undertook the humourous part of the entertainment and his endeavours to please and amuse were appreciated to the full and he was en- cored on each appearance. His items included the song "‘English as she is spoke" and the sketches "Soft Tommy "and "Scenes at a party." The duties of accom- panist were ably carried out by Mr. E. Wynne Hum- phreys and Mr. R. J. Ravenscroft. At the close a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to all who had taken part in the concert on the proposition of Mr. A. R. Norman. The room was then cleared for dancing, which was in- dulged in until an early hour next morning to the excel- lent music of Wood's Quadrille band. The catering was ably carried ,out by Messrs. Spearing and Son, of Church-st., and the liquors were supplied by Mr. Brookes of Halton Castle Hotel. Mr. W. Wright was an efficient M.C., his assistants being Mr. J. Bate and Mr. W.Carroll. The secretarial duties of the Committee were carried out by Mr. A. Riley.

div.head: SUBSIDENCE BILL.

A letter was read from Mr. Brunner in which be unreservedly took all responsibility for the provisions of the bill.

BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
THE MURDEROUS ASSAULT BY A NAVVY

At the Borough Police Court, on Monday, James White, Ship Canal labourer, remanded from the previous Mon- day—was again brought up charged with committing a brutal assault upon Thomas Kelly, Ship Canal labourer, on the 7th inst. As the prosecutor was still unable to appear, the prisoner was.again remanded to Walton jail.

div.head: NON-MAINTENANCE OF RELATIVES.
div.p: NON-MAINTENANCE OF RELATIVES.

At the Borough P‘alice Court, yesterday, John Finn was charged by Mr. Basil Shearer, on behalf of the War- rington , Board of Guardians, with leaving his child chargeable to the Union. This was his fifth appearance for a like offence, and he had been imprisoned several times. The cost incurred in this case had been £l3. He was committed for trial to the Quarter Sessions as an incorrigible rogue.—Enoch Jervis, tailor, charged by the same officer with leaving his wife chargeable to the Union, was ordered to pay the amount due, £3 18s., by instalments of 10s. a week. THEFTS HY BOYS.

At the Borough Police Court yesterday, John H. Gor- ton and Thomas Quinn, boys, were charged with steal- ing on Wednesdny night and on Thursday a quantity of sweets from the stall of James Naylor, the Market Place. It appeared that the prisoners in the prosecutor's ab- sence had forced the bolts of the stall and carried off a number of cheese cakes, confectionery, spanish juice, and other things. The lads on being apprehended admit- ted the theft. Gorton had been previously convicted in November. The magistrates sentenced them to be kept in the bridewell till to-night, and to be chastised this afternoon with twelve strokes of the birch rod each. THEFT AT A LODGING ROUSE.

. Thos. McDermott was charged at the Borough Police Court, yesterday, with stealing on the previous day, at the lodging house of Louisa Spencer, a man's shirt and a singlet the property of Joseph Herbert, farm labour- er, a native of Ireland. The prisoner took advantage of Herbert's absence on duty with a thrashing machine to obtain the shirt and singlet from the landlady, declarino. notwithstanding her remark that she thought they be- longed to Herbert, that they were his own. He went to live at another lodging-house, and the complainant re- porting the matter to the police on his return, was Appre- hended there. The prisoner was sentenced to a month's imprisonment with bard labour.

div.head: CHARGE AGAINST A REFRESHMENT HOUSH KEEEER
div.p: CHARGE AGAINST A REFRESHMENT HOUSH KEEEER

At the Borough Police Court, on Monday, Richard B. Wright. refreshment house keeper, Bewsey-st., was charged with havinc, his house open during prohibited hours, namely at 20 minutes past 11, on the night of the 13th inst.—A Constable stated that at the time mentioned there were two men on the premises, one eating tripe, and he went in and informed the defendant that he should report him.—Another Constable corroborated.— The defendant said about a minute to 11 on that night two gentlemen came into his place and had a cow heel. The constables never saw or knew about them. The two young men the police saw came in and had some peas he scraped out of a pan.and which he gave them for nothing, as it was after 11 o'clock.—The case was dis- missed.

div.head: MALTREATMENT OF A PONY
div.p: MALTREATMENT OF A PONY

Nathan Tay;o7,-..)-f-Croft, a man aged 68; was charged at the Borough Police Court yesterday, with cruelly treating apony by driving it while in an unfit state, on the 13th inst. Mr. Unsworth defended, Charles Wilson, agent for the society for the prevention of cruelty to animals, deposed to seeing the defendant driving the animal in Winwick-road, it being very lame through having a diseased fetlock joint, suffering great inflam- mation and pain, also very weak and utterly unfit foi work. He admitted that the pony was lame, and said he had bought it for £2, and it was lame when he bought it. Detective-Sergeant Monaghan corroborated, and Wm. W. Hill, M.R.C.V.S.' supported their tes- timony. Mr. Unsworth pleaded that his client was a poor man, and just used the pony to fetch groceries from Warrington, and drove itvery slowly. The pain suffered by the animal could not be much. The defendant him- self suffered more, being very rheumatic.—He was fined 2s. ed. and costs, £1 4.5. 6d. in all.

div.head: CHARGE AGAINST A MARINE STORE DEALER.
div.p: CHARGE AGAINST A MARINE STORE DEALER.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, John Barton, marine store dealer, was charged with neglecting, on the 11th inst., to enter in a proper book, the purchase of cow horns, together with the names of the persons from whom he purchased them. He was also charged with committing a similar offence as to scrap iron, on the 12th inst. A constable proved the case. The cow horns and iron, be said, were those which John Smith and Alfred Lee had recently teen convicted of stealing. The Mayor said it was a remarkable thing that whenever there was a slip like this it was always in the case of stolen goods. The magistrates knew pretty well that these slips were not always such accidents as peoplo would have them believe. These poor lads dould not be tempted to go and steal as they did if they did not know a place where the articles would be received. The de- fendant was fined ss. and costs in each case, in al £1 ss. 6d.

div.head: AN AUDACIOUS THEFT FROM A CHILD.
div.p: AN AUDACIOUS THEFT FROM A CHILD.

At the Borough Police Court on Tuesday, Florence Smith, wife of John Smith, labourer, 4, Back Akin-st., and a native of Plymouth, was charged with stealing, about 12 noon, on Saturday last, a purse containing 9s. 9d. cash, from the person of William Yates, a little boy, son of Thomas Yates, a labourer. It appeared from the evidence that Mrs. Yates sent the child with the purse containing half a sovereign to bring some milk for dinner. He bought the milk, receiving 9s. 9d. change, and came away, with the money in the purse in his hand. The prisoner crossed over to him in Mill-lane, and said, "Here take this and fetch me a small loaf from that shop, and I will hold thy purse while thou fetches me it." He handed her the purse he carried, and took hers, and went to the shop, that of Thos. Allen, baker, for the loaf. Then it was discovered by him that the purse the boy had contained only a halfpenny: Information was given to the police, and Sergeant Monaghan soon apprehended the prisoner. While they were crossing a piece of waste ground together, he noticed a little confusion on her part. They had no sooner got to the police station than a boy came in and handed up a purse which he said he had 'found on the waste ground. Mrs. Yates subsequent- ly identified this as the purse with which she had sent her son out. The prisoner admitted the theft. She now manifested the greatest emotion, sobbing violently throughout the proceedings. She said she committed the theft because her husband was out of employment. The magistrates decided that she must restore the stolen money, and pay a fine of 10s. and costs, or go to prison for 14 days.

With the assistance of the soldiers and P.C. Fisk witness took the defendant into custody.—P.C. The prisoner was sent to jail for four Months' hard labour.—David Hughes, of Liverpool, a militiaman, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-st.,- on Sunday night, and assaulting P.C's. GAMESTERS /N THE STREETS.—John Ward, Joseph Hughes, William Cana, William Henry Lee, Frank Lee, Thomas Bibby, William Whittaker, John Naylor, and George Higham, all boys, were charged with playing a game of chance for money in Winwick-road, on the 15th inst, Hughes, Cane, and Lee were fined 2s. 6d. each, and the other boys were dismissed.—Joseph Lee, David Wilcock, Benjamin Williams, and Geo.
