FIGHTING.—THROWING A MAN INTO THE RxvEn.,—Peter Ford, apprehended under a warrant, was charged with fighting near the Arpley Bridge on the 25th of October. A young man gave evidence, from which it appeared that on the date in question he found the prisoner and another man fighting near the bridge. One of the men said he would give in, and another man said " Pitch him over Peter" upcn which the prisoner threw the man into the river, and, as far as witness could see, left him there. The prisoner was bound ever in his own reco,g- nisances of £lO and two sureties of £5 each, to keep the peace for six months ; in default a month's imprisonment with hard labour.

DOGS UNMUZZLED.—THE POLICE AS WELL AS THE DOGS CHAFE AGAINST THE MUZZLES.—For having their dogs at ,CHAFE unmuzzled Edward Priddon was fined 3s. 6d. and and costs and Peter Tomlinson was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. Chief-Constable Hunt said this order as to muzzling dogs would have to be done away with. It was a most irk- some thing for the police to have to look after these dogs. CHIMNEYS ON FIRE.—Wm. Garrett and Wm. Jones for having their chimneys on fire were fined is. each. KEEPING LODGERS IN UNREGISTERED HOUSES.—Wm. Baines and Daniel Collard, of Nos. 5 and 7, Edward-st., respectively, were charged by Mr. Norman, inspector to the Rural Sanitary Authority,with keeping lodgers with- out having their houges registered as lodging-houses. M. Crosfield, and E. J. Guesc. NON-ATTENDANCE AT SCHOOL.-Mr. U. Thomas Wilkinson, painter, 72, Dallam-s., is. and order for attelidance ; Thomas Dunbobbin, Ship .Canal labourer, Latchford, 2s. ed.
IVEDNEspey.—Before Alderman Holmes. DRITNK. —Richard Rogerson, of Sefton View, Waver- tree, was fined ss. and costs for being drunk in Bridge- st., on the 24th inst.

FRlDAT.—Before Messrs. J. White, (chairman) and C. White, and Alderman Harrison. Dritmc AND INDEcENT.—James Wright, a native of Dumfriesshire, for being drunk and guilty of shamefully indecent conduct at Bank Park the previous afternoon, was fined £5 and costs; in default a month's imprison- ment.

ASSLULT CASES. Ann Mallen was charged with assaulting Julia Dooley, on the 21st inst.,.in Foundry- lane and Julia Dooley was charged with assaulting Ann Mallen, on the same occasion; Mallen was also charged with wilfully damaging the window of Catherine Moon. The quarrel was about club money. Mr. A. Browne iappeared for Mallen. The charge of damaging the window was dismissed, and each defendant was bound over in the sura of Rs to keep the peace for six months, and pay her own costs. —Sarah Ann Warburton was charged with assaulting Elizabeth Bond, in Chapel.st., on the 24th inst. The as- sault was committed because the complainant cut down la clothes line on which the defendant had hung clothes right in front of the complainant's door, refusing to re- move them. The defendant was bound over in the sum of £5 to;keep the peace for six months, and ordered to pay the costs, 9s.—James Taylor was charged with as- saulting Mary Taylor,his daughter-in-law, in the/Rodney public-house, Winwick-road, on the 21st inst. The de- fendant had called the complainant most approbrious names, upon which she had thrown some whisky in his face,and he had thereupon thrown a glass of beer at her, cutting her face and necessitating her going to the In- firmary. 'He was bound over to keep the peace and ordered to pay costs.

DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS. TIIESDAY.—Before Messrs. W. C. Jones (in the chair) and William Long. CAT AND LION, SrnErroN.—Mr. George F. F. White, Warrington, said he had an application to make to the Bench. Mr. Lyon, the owner of the Cat and Lin, Stretton, purposed to rebuild the inn on the same site. The new building would be a. trifle smaller, but Mr. Lyon thought it would be more courteous to the Bench to submit the plans.—The application was acceded to.— The license ?f .the Cat and Lion was subsequently trans- ferred to William Ostler, who had been recently selling under the temporary authority of the Bench. DRUNKENNESS.—.The following persons were fined for drunkenness ; Thomas Johnson, labourer, at Appleton, on the 7th February, is. and costs; George Spencer, labourer, at Appleton, on the 15th February, is. and costs ; Benjamin Roberts, labourer, Appleton, on the 14th February, is. and costs; John Bennett, at Moore, on the 7th February, is. and costs.

LOCOMOTIVES 017-THE HIGIINV-A-VT—James Vernon, des- cribed as an engine driver, was summoned for having on the 26th December, acted in contravention of the byelaws made by the County Council by using on the highway a steam locomotive between the hours of 5 p.m. and 1 a.m., namely, at 8 p.m. The case was before the magistrates at thP last sessioas, and was adjourned to enable the defendant to appear. The defendant now said he was unable to get to Stretton owing to the slippery state of the roads. The wheels would not bite. Mr.' Long said the defendant made a mistake in going beyond London Bridge that night.--A fine of 2s. 6d. and costs (7s. 6d,) was inflicted.
• ASLEEP.—Joseph raylor, labourer, for having been asleep on a lurry at Stretton, on the 19th February, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs.

HIGHWAY OBSTRUCTION. William Armstrong, la- bourer, Victoria-st., Warrington, was charged with wil- fully obstructing the highway at Grappenhall, on the 19th February, by allowing a cart to remain thereon for 22 hours. A fine of 2s. 6d. and costs was imposed. DOG CASES.—Gilbert McWhannel, agent, was charged with allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled and without a collar at Preston Brook, on the 18th February. A similar charge was preferred against Hannah Halliday, farmer, Moon', and George Kinsey, farmer, Dutton, and each of the three defendants was fined 3s. 6d., including costs.

Ax UNLICENSED Gux.—Richard Cowap, a youth living at Little Leigh, was charged with carrying a gun with- out a-license at Great Budworth, on the 27th December. The defendant was fined 2s. 6d. and costs.

ASSAULTS AT DARESBURY BOARD SCHOOL.—Margaret Heywood was summoned for having on the 27th Janu- ary, at Daresbury, assaulted and beaten Alfred Withen- shawe, six years of age. Margaret Ellen Withenshawe, the mother of the child, was charged with assaulting the defendant in the last case, who is a monitress at Dares- bury School. Mr. A.Browne,who appeared for the lad and Mrs. Withenshawe, said that on the 27th Januarythe lad returned home crying, and complained of a pain in his cheek. The mother noticed that it was red, and her son informed her that the monitress had struck him with her open hand because he had run away from the school. As a matter of fact, the child had never run away from sckool : he was away on the previous day, but it was be- cause he was unwell. He was unable to eat anything on that side of his face for ten days or a fortnight. The day after the assault Mrs. Withenshawe, believing that she had a maternal right to inflict a little punishment if necessary upon the monitress, went to the school and asked "What did you mean by hitting my little boy on the face ?" The mon- itress denied that she had struck him. Mrs. With- enshawe then struck the monitress with her open band acrass her face, and told her not to commit another assault on her child. After some evidence had been given Mr. Browne said he would make an offer to the Bench. If the School Board would withdraw their sum- mons, he was also willing to withdraw the summons against the monitress. Mrs. Withenshawe was asked to apologise to the monitress in the presence of the head- master and children; but this she strongly objected to do. She had, however, apologised to the court that morning. The Chairman said that although the sum- monses would be dismissed, the 13ench thought there were faults on each side. The monitress ought not to have struck the child with such severity. If he would not do what he was told she should have reported him to the head-master. Mrs. Withenshawe should not have taken the law into her own hands. The summonses would be dismissed. ,

RUGBY. ST. HELEN& RMS.. 3RD. V. WIDNES SANGERS.—PIayed at Widnes on Saturday. Final result :—Rs, 1-1-1; Rangers, 01-10-0.

_ RUNCORN A v. EARLESTOWN.—Thene teams met on Saturday, at Runcorn, and at the close of play Runcorn had registered two-goals, four tries ; Earlestown, nil, RUNCORN v. B:RUUMEITON.—Runcorn, without the ser- vices of Faulkner and two more of the usual forvtards, were at Broughton on Saturday, when a capital game was,witnessed. Broughton were also ehort of Flower and one or two others,. but still they played up very well indeed,, and in the first half did most of the pressing. Hampson scored, and Houghton safely placed the goal. In the second half Houghton exhibited splendid kicking powers for Runcorn,. who. were nearly scoring on several occasions, and once Crompton only missed dropping a goal by a matter of a few inches. Runcorn eventually won by a goal to nothing, and everybody admitted that the game had been a most interesting one. Calrow, Hassall, together with the old Broughtonfranger, W. Edge, played very well behind, whilst the wing three- quarters ram fast and well. Forward the- Broughton men were seem to much advantage, and Skidmore, Rome, and Glendinning were ever prominent. Houghton, the Runcorn full back, was very safe ; and Davies and Hughes ran and passed' well, but Crompton seemed a tittle off colour. Riley was about the most prominent of all the forwards.

WARRINGTON Ir. WIDNES, "A."—Notwithstanding the fact that some considerable local interest was.centred in this return fixture, only a meagre number of onlookers had assembled when Widnes kicked off against a biting wind. Some ponderous kicks opened the strumle, but when the game settled down Thoroley, Lloyd,ancl Moly- neaux went offrwith a rush,. and Lawless, getting pos- session, looked like scoring after a fine run. The tem- porary relief which followed,was neutralized by Vrebster's punt, and a grand bit of-pa.ssing by Randles, Mather, Jolley, and Daniels ended in the last-named being pulled down on the line. There were a tight few minutes here, but Widnes forced the leather from the dangerous prox- imity to their goal, only•to see Mather from •a line-out get a beautiful try. The Warringtonians were playing a fine game, and the grand, combination of theforvrards ended in Lawless and Mather passing, and running into their:opponents' territory.. The game continued fast and exciting, tbe visitors' backs again indulging in fine pas- sing, with the result that Daniels gpt a rattlinery, a good attempt by Webster. failing. Chiefly by the aid of a. strong rnsh by Webster and a long punt from Sampson, Widnes were beaten back, but only a minor accrued. The Widnesians were still powerless to clear their lines, Warrington playing with rare spirit, and Lawless slipped after getting clear. Immediately afterwards an irresistible rush by the whole of the visit- ing forwards ended in Teare passing beautifully to Mather, who got his second try near the posts, the Place failing. After the dropout, Taylor raised the hopes of his side by intercepting a. pass and. running to midfield; but Widnes touched dawn from, a long shot at goal. Attempts at passing by theAome-backs were easily frus- trated, and Daniels taking die, ran grandly to the line, when a minor was given, and another followed after a rush by Molvneux Thornley,. Barnes, and Isherwood. Directly after this"Thornley dribbled over and scored, but the place again failed, half-time arriving with. War- rington 0-4-4 to nil. Restarting. the visiting forwards attacked most vigorously, Lloyd,. Isherwood, Knowles, I and Randles being notable, and. the Chemicals being decidedly lucky in escaping with, only a minor. Directly after this the Widnesians dribbled capitally to neutral ground, but the advantage gained was as quickly lost, as Daniels, Knowles, Teare, anal Molyneux caused their opponents to beat a hasty retreat. Daniels then looked like scoring after dodging about, and Widnes still sus- tained a most determined attack by their opponents. Eventually Ridgway relieved to half-way, Sampson tackling finely.. Warrington,who all through, had dis- played very fine form, then monopolized the play for a lengthy period, until the oval was driven to Sampson, who replied grandly, and from some ensuing play Teare passed out wide to Mather, who scored easily,. Jolley kicking a good goal. •By the aid of the kick-off from centre, the homesters looked like scoring, but the visitors' custodian was too safe i and the sphere was soon in midfield, where Randles got off with a run to the posts. Here a pass from Lawless to Jolley enabled the latter to pass beautifully to. Webster„ who took the ball and chance, and although obstructed by a couple of op- ponents' romped over in grand style. Soon afterwards Craig got clear away, but a magnificent tackle by Samp- son ended his career, and the whistle blew with War- rington 15-5 to nil. WARRINGTON v. WIDNES.

The improved form of Widnes during the last few weeks no doubt accounted for the large attendance at Wilderspool on Saturdap,.when the return match betwee_n_ the above clubs was brought to an issuer Warrington were victorious in the frst match this season by a solitary try, but since that time Widnes have been steadily on the improve, and their successive victories over Wigan and Stockport did not give the match that one-syled character which one originally was inclined to expect. That both sides meanb business may be gathered from the fAct that they mustered their strongest fifbens, not a single absentee being noted from the teams originally selected.

1 A good-humoured crowd of 7,000 lined the arena when Smith kicked off towards the pavilion goal, and, James Bate being the recipient, play was contested at the half way flag. Smith and Holt led Holt led up the Widnes- ians to an attack on the home goal, and some cross passing by the visiting half backs was frustrated by Barnes and J. T. Bate. Frank Turner and Donohue be- came prominent with a fine dribble down the open, and Evans (Widnes) essayed to get clear, but found a barrier in Berry. Widnes would not be denied, and a strong rush of the Widnes. front rank, who were playing a strong game, was cleared by Barnes, and Widnes being penal- ized, the kick taken by Massey gained but little ground. 'Fair Turner, Ashton, and J. Jolley gained ground by short individual efforts, and although the Widnes goal was endangered, the home backs were at fault in their passing, and Barber and Evans, with judicious kicks, took play to more desirable quarters. Boscow was how- ever, safe, and although the visitors twice within a minute tested him, he was equal to the occasion, and did not allow his opponents to intrude on Warrington territory. A mark by Massey was poorly taken, but J. W. Evans, with a long kick, again placed Widnes on the defensive. This the visitors did not relish, and taking advantagepf faulty play by the Warrington forwards in screwing a pack, rushed he oval at headlong speed into the home quarters, a., daring save by James Bate staying their progress. Fair :Turner made an effort to break through, but the tackling was particularly accurate, and an effort to make the game more open was frequently spoiled by the too close attentions of the opposing half backs. Berry came through and partially got clear, but Peters tackled well. Some sharp passing by the visit- ing backs was intercepted. by Fair Turner and Evans, and although the latter pair had a chance, it was inglori- ously missed, and Peters with a fine kick got the oval to Boscow, who replied with his usual accuracy. Again, Warrington relieved. but Widnes were evidently deter- mined, and another fine rush of their smart forwards harassed the home defence. Barnes toiled Barber when , the latter had a fine opening, and relief was gained, Jolley, Frank Turner, Holmes, and Donohue supplement- ting this with a fine dribble, taking play on the verge of the visiting line. No sooner had a pack been formed than the Widnes men again demonstrated their useful- ness by a grand dribble to the home posts, Barnes saving in fine style. J. W. Evans intercepted a movement of the Widnes backs, and Holmes and Davies augmented this by a rush to the 25 flag. The home skipper was at fault a moment later. James Bate ran well and passed to Massey, but no use whatever was made of it. After Barnes had cleared, a spell of exchange kicking was wit- nessed, and Brennan putting in a huge punt, the oval was mulled, and Widnes rushing the ball over the line, Hartles scored near the.corner flag. No goal was kicked, and this being the last point of interest, half time was called with Widnes leading by a try. Frank Turner re- started, and Widnes were busily saving, a minor accruing from the kick off, James Bate got clear of a scrimmage and punted to Hartles, and a combined effort almost resulted in a score. J. T. Bate put in a tricky piece of play, and the hopes of Warrington reached a high pitch when the home half passed finely across to Barnes, who in his eagerness to snap up the oval, failed to gather and Widnes cleared. Boscow and Harties each in turn cleared their lines, but an effort by Boscow was neutralized by his forwards, who were a trifle too anxious. Barnes dodged finely. Davies essayed to run through, but to no purpose. Povey was repeatedly cheered for fine dribbling, and although Warrington continually pressed, no major point could be scored. The home enthusiasts 'wore a depressed look as the thought of the Warring- tonians receiving defeat became more apparent, and many were the calls for an extra effort. Evans put int, a tricky run along the touch, and Barnes taking the pass was pulled up near the .line. A combined rush of the forwards compelled a minor. The drop out still saw Warrington plodding on with the hope that victory would be theils, and at ' last their efforts were rewarded, for Bate putting in a fine run was pushed into touch a yard from the line, and Donohue being well up, received from the throw-out and scores were now equal. Fair Turner took the place without success. Warrington played with renewed vigour. and after Jolley had tried hard to force his way, Barnes hitd extremely hard lines, being knocked into to-iich a yard from the line. Frank Turner almost notched a point on the stroke of time, but only a minor resulted, and a tcugh game was finished with the score —Warrington, 0-1-3; Widnes, 0-1-0. . Teams :—Warrington: J. Boscow, back; J. T. Massey, T. Barnes, and J. W. Evans, three-quarters; James Bate and J. T. Bate, half-backs ; H. Ashton, Fair Turner, Frank Turner, J. Jolley, T. Davies, W. Berry, 'T. Donohue, J. Holmes, and W. Povey, forwards. Wid- nes: Hartles, back; Brennan, Peters, and Barber thrke- qearters ; Drummond and Evans, half tacks ; Smith, Whelan, Holt, Hewitt, Johnson, Gordon, Hamltnati, Lyons, and Kenyon,

div.head: SHIP CANAL
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL
SIrOCKING FATALITY ON THE WORKS Ar RUNCORN.

A shocking accident occurred on the Ship Canal Works at N) Man's Lane. Runclrn, on Wednesday morning. By means of a Scotch Crane, a number of men were en- gaged in placing a portable pumping engine on a pon- -toosi,-but not-being inth position intend 44, James Kidd, the derrick driver, was signalled to.lift up the jib and he did so. When he raised the engine about 1.8 inches, a link of the chain smashed,.the engine dropped suddenly to the pontoon, and the jib ots.the crane came crashing down upon the top of it, breaking up the machinery of the engine. In its descent the jib struck a youth named Charles Henry Coyle on. the back. of the head, and killed him almost instantly. Two fitters engaged in the work had marvellously narrow escapes,. the jib falling within six inches of one of the men. INQUEST. _

The inquest on the body was held at the Police Court, on Thursday afternoon,. by Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner. Mr. Arthur Hook,, an engineer,represented the Ship Canal contractors,- and Inspector Millington was present for the police.---. Tames lUdd, Sandy-lane,Weston Point, the driver of the derrick, gave evidence bearing out the above facts, and said the chain was not broken by a jerk.—Peter Coyle, pf the Railway Inn, Dunham- o'th-Hill, said he was foreman fitter on the Ship Canal works. The deceased was his son, and was 15 years of age. He was an assistant to the fitters. Witness had built the crane when it was new, and he had lifted a heavier weight with it than eight tons. He should not be afraid to lift from ten to twelve tons with the crane. The chain, in his opinion, was sufficient. He had been a contractor's man for 32 years; and 17 years a foreman fitter, and he thought the frost had affected the chain,, and caused it to crack.' The driver was a first-class man. —The Coroner : Why did net the link go in the severe frost P—Witness replied that he did not think the crane was used at that time. He had seen the broken link tested, • and it was good iron; he could not find any fault with it.—Mr. Walter Timmins,. en- gineer, said he had examined the crane and chain by the directions of the Coroner. The crane was by one of the best makers in the north of England, and he-consi- dered it "A L" It was strong enough for the work. He had had the broken lint put to a very severe test, and it was a first-class piece of iron, without flaw. He-should be perfectly satisfied to lift ten tons with that chain. He thought the link had been affected by the frost,, and he suggested that it was a good plan to run the chain of a crane up and down several times before using it. This made the iron more homogeneous. A warm chain would be strut-4er than a cold one. Even his warm hand upon that link would increase its strength.—Evidence was also given by WilParn Jones, a labourer, and Frederick Trol- lope, fitter, of 19, Stanley-st.—The Coroner then summed up, and the jury returned a verdict of "'Accidental Death."—The• Coroner said the jury would no- doubt ex- press, with him, their sympathy with Mr. Coyle in the sad loss he had sustained.

div.head: PROPOSED CORPORATE LOANS.
div.p: PROPOSED CORPORATE LOANS.

A public meeting of the ratepayers of Ardwick Ward, Manchester, called in compliance with a requisition pre- sented to the Alderman of the ward (Mr. ,Toseph Thomp- son), was held on Wednesday night, in Ardwick Town Hall, to consider" the question now before the public as to whether it is proper that the ratepayers of Manches- ter shall further subscribe towards thecost of the com- pletion of the Manchester Ship Canal.' There was a good attendance. Mr. Alderman Thompson presided, and there were on the platform repvesentatives of the ward in the City Council and other leading ratepayers. The Chairman said it was a meeting to consider the sub- ject of whether the Manchester Ship Canal should be finished or whether it should remain incomplete— whether this great effort, that had cost many million's of money, should be left as a dreary but grand ruin' or whether it should be carried to completion. Now the 'question "'light be naturally aske& why was it that the Directors of the Company did not appeal to the public to raise money sufficient to carry on this great work ? The reply' to that was that they lxid already made their appeal. Thiy had offered to issue certain preference shares bearing interest at 4 per cent. and the public had not responded as fully as could be desired, and it was manifest that if there was still rather a large amount of unused stock in the hands of the directors it was not very likely that the public would come forward and sub- scribe two millions more. The directors were therefore brought face to face with this question—was the canal to stop, was it to be left as a failure, or should we ask the Corporation of Manchester or other Corporations to do what was unusual but what was certainly legitimate —should the Corporation be asked to come to the res- cueand make a temporary loan of money to the amount that was required. The object of the meeting was to ask whether they were prepared to sanction such a pro- posal. Assuming that the Corporation of Manchester agreed to make a recommendation in favour of the pro- posal, the as:ent of the ratepayers would then have te be secured. A public meeting would be summoned, at which every ratepayer had a right to appear or to be represented, and, if necessary, a poll of the ratepayers would be taken. He thought it was desirable for the ratepayers to authorise the City Council to raise on the best terms they could the money that was required to carry out the great work. (Applause). A resolution in support of the object of the meeting was unanimously adopted. THE SHIP CANAL BRIDGE AT LATCHFORD LOCKS. A fresh start has now been made with the making of the great bridge that is to span the canal at Latchford locks, and considerable progress is being made towards the completion of the bridge. The masonry is practically finished, and preparations are being made for the girders to be placed in position. The framework has been erected, and Mos.t of the ironwork' has arrived,

"A REPLY TO CANON WOOD."

Sir,—ln your issue of Saturday last, there appears, under the above heading, a summary of a sermon preached by me in the Greenway Road Primitive Metho- dist chapel, on the 15th inst. As I do not wish to be misunderstood, kindly permit me to say that the address referred to was not delivered as "a reply to Canon Wood." It sought to deal with the spirit of religious intolerance generally rather than with any particular exhibition of it. I should have preached, ere long, on the same subject had Canon Wood's sermon never been delivered. His discourse simply furnished a local illus- tration of the spirit I was combating, and induced me to lay additional emphasis on a few points. I deem it necessary to make this explanation as a guard against misapprenhension. Much that I said, however germane to the general question, would, if viewed as "a reply to Canon Mood,' be justly chargeable with unfairness and irrelevance. Yours, etc., Frodsham, February 23rd.
HENRY DAVENPORT.

div.head: MORE LIGHT WANTED IK RUNCORN.
div.p: MORE LIGHT WANTED IK RUNCORN.

Sir,—Owing to the fog which presumed to settle over our benighted town, the streets of Runcorn, on Wednes- day night, were literally as dark as a bag. It appears that according to Cocker, or some other equally infallible authority, the moon should have put in an appearance some time during Wednesday night; but the fog upset all calculations, and never a moon showed up, the conse- quence being that,owing to the cheese-paring and short- sighted economy of our local rulers, which turn off the gas on moonlight nights, locomotion if any kind was rendered, to say the least, exceedingly inconvenient. The lamps give forth but a " dim, religious light" at the best of times, but still they are better than none, and I think it is little short of a scandal that the streets of a town the size of Runcorn should, so far as the public lamps are concerned, 'have been in total darkness on such a night as that of Wednesday.—l am, Sir, yours respectfully,
J. A. CHADWICK 13, Bridgewater-st., Runcorn, February 19th, 1891.
"GAS" VERSUS COMMON SENSE.

Sir,—The Rev. Hugh Price Hughes is reportedto have said at.a meeting in Manchester, the othsr day, that " A Christian who voted for a brewer at an election was a Christian humbug !" I would say to him as The Monu- ment said to The Bridge: "Now don't go off half cock : folks never gains By usin' pepper-sarse instid o' brains." I would also like some of our wealthier brewers to say how many times they have been pestered by these Piety- mongers for subscriptions when their coffers have been getting low. They haven't been above pleading for some of these (according to them) ill-gotten gains, and have been glad to get them. But, Sir, the brewers are thankful that Providence has given us this fulminating parson, whose words have done more damage to any cause he advocates than aught else that has been brought against them. He, and that other genius of the same kidney, W. H. Stead (General Booth's biggest cats-paw), raised a moral smell around •ParnM, and what is the re- sult ? Parnell is, to-day, the strongest man in the whole Irish Party. If those two had held their tongues and their pens, and had smothered their incorrigible vanity, Parnell would now be, politically, a thin.' of the past. We don't want self-constituted morality readers ; and we would remind them of what a greater than either of them said about the one Who was without guilt cast- ing the first stone. When they have pulled the beam .out of their own eyes, they may set about taking the mote out of other people's. "My heart ferments not with the bigot's leaven; All creeds I view with toleration thorough, And have a horror of regarding heaven As anybody's rotten borough '- February 20th, 1891.
PLUTO.
MR. C. M. PERCY AND THE EIGHT HOURS
MOVEMENT.

Sir,—lt is not likely that Mr. C. M. Percy will be any more successful than some others have been in their opposition to an eight-hours day for miners. Indeed, the reasons advancea by Mr. Percy for opposing this great reform are unusually weak and inconclusive. In the first place, he says "as a life-long Liberal I oppose such a proposal as an unwarrantable interference with the liberty of the workman and emplver." Why, I should like to know, is such interference unwarrantable ? Does Mr. Percy .argue that all interference with the liberty of workpeople 'and employer is unwarrantable ? If so, he is entirely belated—he has come upon the scene at least half a century too late. He must be aware that for a longtime past the legislature of this cOuntry has inter- fered with the liberty of employers and employed, and that there are classes of workpeople who can point to such interference as the charter which emancipated them from a degrading slavery, and raised them to a higher and more human plane of existence. If Mr. Percy does not object to all interference, then he merely objects to it:in an industry in which he is specially interested, and that is a different thing altogether. He next opposes the eight-hours' day "as a miner's friend, and as a citizen, because it will neither improve the health, nor lessen the danger of the miner." Here, I consider, Mr. Percy falls into a transparent absurdity. A miner is liable to the dangers of his employment all the time he is at work. If he work ten hours a day he is liable to those dangers for ten hours, but if you reduce, his hours of laistour by one-fifth—that is to eight a day— you of necessity lessen his liability to injury or death by one-fifth also. And so with regard. to health. If you shorten by one-fifth the period during which a man is placed under unwholesome conditions, you must at the same time proportionately increase his chances of re- maining in a healthy state of body. There are other veiy cogent reasons for believing, -that a shortening of hours would both improve the health and lessen the -dangers of the miner, hut I think I have said sufficient under this , head to show how ridiculous are some of the arguments with which it is thought fit to oppose an eight-hours day.

Mr. Percy further says:—" I oppose it because it will reduce the production of coal, and increase the cost, and reduce wages." Now, in this sentence Mr. Percy calmly takes for granted something in support of which he brings forward not a tittle of proof. It so happens that in different parts of England at the present ti me both the long-hours and the short-hours systems are in operation, and the experience gathered from this seems to run en- tirely contrary to what Mr. Percy asserts. The miners of Northumberland and Durham work six and seven hours a day, yet it is said that they produce as much, man for man, as do those miners in other parts of the country who work longerhours. The shorter hours can- not have materially increased the cost, else the coal of •those two counties would have been driven out of the market long ere this ;and as for reducing wages I fancy Mr. Percy will not say that the miners of Durham and Northumberland are paid less than are miners in other parts of the country. Mr. Percy falls into a complete fallacy when he asserts that long hours mean high wages and short hours low wages. Speaking theoretically. ;wages are not,re,gulated by the number of hours worked but by entirely different causes, " and almost every work- ing-man can testify from his own experience pr observa- tion that short hours are very often accompanied by high wages, and long hours by low wages. Mr. Percy speaks of manufacturers being crippled by the increasing price of coal. 'Does he mean that all this increase of price has gone into the pockets of the miners in better wages? It would be interesting if he would let us know how small is the proportion of the increase in price actually received by the miners.—Yours. &c., Warrington, Feb. 24th, 1891

IN DARKEST IGNORANCE, WITH 3.IbSES ; AND
THE WAY OUT.

"Professor Huxley, is over fond of giving the go-by to a difficulty by altering the text of his authority. FO as to make it conform to the view he has sd)pted.w--/lfr. Gladstone the Nineteenth Century."
Sir,—The happy juxta-position of the very different letters of "Master of Arts" and " Veritas," affords parallel readings which relieves me of the necessity of

wasting my time and your space Upon the latter. The man who rushes into print, and wants the anthropomor- phism of the Old Testament" defined and proved "to him, has certainly to look up to his subject. An idea of his fitness for the task he has assumed maybe gathered from the fact that he instances "Newton, Herschell, and other eminent interpreters of nature" as being unin- fluenced by the disturbing influence of geology and biology upon old beliefs. This luminous idea might pass current if " Verdes " was " localizing " and exhorting the uncritical menthers of his "class," but displays a sad want of that" adequate preparation "insisted upon by one of our critics. I should have thought it to have been within the mental scope even of a " Veritas " to have grasped the idea that even Newton and Herschell might very well remain uninfluenced by the undis- covered.

Again I must express the great pleasure I have experi- enced in reading the letter of "Master of Arts." He is one with whom it would indeed be a pleasure to travel in search of that evasive quarry—the truth. But, 'even in such good company and with so good a purpose, I must decline to go one step further than I can find solid ground. I make no assumptions myself, and decline to admit any from others. Once open the gate of assumption, and error and illu- sion will bealmost sure to creep in. That gate shut and locked,and one source of error and illusion is elireinated. In most investigations it is best to begin at the begin- ning. Now the writer of Genesis 1. begins by describ- ing things and narrating actions which were distinctly beyond human knowledge and experience, as having happened before his own appearance on earth ; I cannot but regard this as a distinct claim to the possession of Divine Inspiration or Revelation on the part of the writer. After the somewhat anomalous announcement of the creation of vegetation before there was a sun to warm it, he affirms the creation of the world and its in- habitants in six days. And this is done in such a definite and special manner as to leave no doubt in any sane mind as to what the writer 'meant. The evening and the morning being the first day, and the Creator having been said to have "rested on the seventh day," is surely conclusive as to that. And this view did obtain until the disturbing influence I have spoken of arose with the modern sciences of Geology and Biology. Here, how- ever, Mr. Gladstone and other reconcilers step in and "alter the text of their authority, so as to make it con- form to the view they have adopted." And with what effect ? In helping poor Moses over the hedge of scien- tific inaccuracy, they deposit him in the mire of literary incapacity. Their explanation is tantamount to saying one of three things—either the writer of Genesis 1. did not know what he was saying—did not mean what he did say—or was wilfully perverting the truth. A queer way of rehabilitating an author is to destroy the impres- sion that he was something of a humbug by showing him to have been an imbecile or an impostor! Can fatuity go further? However, "any schoolboy" will be able to discomfit "Moses "by reference to his text book of geology, So again with the statement as to the specific creation of plants and animals. The logical deduction from well ascertained facts is clearly diametrically opposed to the dictum of this claimant to inspiration. Now I think we may fairly ask what kind of inspiration it can be that , enables a writer to cram so many physical inaccuracies in such a small space? One thing, however, is clear— the findings of science and the assertions of this writer are utterly opposed and incompatible; the acceptance of the one necessitates the rejection of the other. Long thinking on this subject has convinced me that this propisition is almost axiomatic—that wherever the Bible makes assertions outside the results of human ex- perience and those assertions can be brought face to face with the facts involved, the facts are established and the assertions discredited.

And here may 1 suggest to my friend Mr. Alfred J. Jolley who speaks in the tone of one having authority, that I vas"- preparing "for this great subject when he was in long clothes, and that there will be ample scope for the use of even his colossal intellect if he will set it to the task of rehabilitating his friend Moses without making himself and his subject ridiculous. In the meantime perhaps a littleness of that assumption of sup- erior knowledge and information so little backed by facts would be more becoming. In this as in most other subjects we are all of us merely learners ; and finality of knowledge can no more be ascribed to a Jolley than it can to a Moses.—Yours, ace.,

div.head: JOHN PEERS. The Haws, Penketh, Feb. 2, 1891. ---- HOURS OF LABOUR AND COST OF PRODUCTION.
div.p: JOHN PEERS. The Haws, Penketh, Feb. 2, 1891. ---- HOURS OF LABOUR AND COST OF PRODUCTION.

Sir,—ln your issue of 21st instant you invite the readers of your paper to say what they think of Mr. C. M. Percy's letter on the eight hours movement. In my humble opinion, and from having had upwards of 20 years' experience in connection with collieries I quite agree with Mr. Percy, and so believe that any interfer- ence by law with the liberty of miners and their masters as to the number of hours they shall work, will bring on greater evil in this country than the American Tariff Bill has already done to some of the iron manufacturers and men also in this country. Some of the iron-workers in this country have had a very hard time of it on account of stoppageof works, not 50 miles from Warrington, from the effects of the Tariff Bill in America which without doubt has prevented a certain class of goods made in this country being sent now at a profit, and in consequence closed the works entirely. This to the writer's knowledge has caused many aching hearts of mothers with large families. Besides this, the workman was driven on to the highway and into the woods. Somebwere "on the road" breaking stones; others in the woods cutting down trees at very low wages, and in the very depth of winter. But will that great change be any lesson to those that suffered so much for a short time? I trust it will, and I hope that every man, be he an iron-worker or collier, that may have read Mr. F. Monks's speech, will take the , good advice given, and put his house in order while there is yet time. Facts are stubborn things, and with such facts before us from such experienced gentlemen as F. Monks and C. M. Percy about the production in America and the present progress that theyare now making there, unless our houses are put in order, and very soon too, the outlook for the future is not so bright as we would like to see it.

Mr. Percy tells us that we in Warrington know some- thing of the iron trade. I fancy we do, but we have seen it worse and very much better, than at the pre- sent time. Mr. Percy asks the question, is it flourishing at present ? As to that question, I ask those who May by chance read Mr. Percy's letter to judge for themselves, especially those immediately connected with the making of iron, as the wxiter is not an iron-worker and, if the iron trade cannot flourish now, is it possible to do so if further burdens are placed upon it, which Mr. Percy de- clares will be the case if the eight-hours movement is made compulsory by law? Mr. Percy tells us also that our American competitors are at present exceeding us in the make of pig iron, their yearly make being 10,000,000 while in England we make something over 8,000.000, and that Americans are putting good coal into railway wagons and selling it at 3s. per ton. With these facts before us, what position shall we be in soon, especially if our manufacturers are further burdened with 6d. or ls. per ton added to the Present high price of coal, which is sure to follow if the eight hours movement is carried into law ? Unless a considerable reduction is made by the owners of the mines in the present rentcharges, which is much needed even at the present time, without any further expense being added to the cost of production by an eight hours day Bill, it must he injurious in its effects. Can anyone doubt what Mr. Percy says about iron and coal being sent into England from America ? I am in- clined to think not, and to further substantiate the re- marks of Mr. Percy, and if there are any who doubt his remarks I refer them to Mr. F. Monkes address, entitled "A visit to America," delivered in the Museum Lecture Room, at Warrington, on the 17th inst. Mr. F. Monks has been an eye-witness of the great resburces at hand in America, and was highly pleased in giving the audience the result Of his visit, which must be very in- teresting to all that heard it or those that have seen it in print, :for it is full of good advice; especially so to iron- workers and iron producers. Mr. Monks,without question, is one among the few far-seeing manufacturers of iron. He knows the need for good management to avoid waste, for he tells his audience in plain English that the amount of waste in some works in America would ruin an Eng- lish firm if they did likewise; and he tells us also that in America they are not yet abreast of our English mills in finished bar iron. So much for old England in wire- drawing. Mr. Monks says their equipment is n) better , than in England, but that their system of working is different, and gives a larger output than our English mills do. Surely this a hard nut for our Warrington wire-drawers to crack, :and • will require new nut crackers to be used, if they wish to get the best nut.

My advice is to wire-drawers—" Do not be contented with the prosent system, but find one that will excel the American system, and one that will reduce the labour and cast Of production." If this is' done what have Englishmen to fear? Mr. Monks tells us very plainly that we have nothing at all to fear either in production or position in life. At the same tittle we must keep before our eyes the advantages set forth by Mr. Monks in reference to the American immense deposits of coal and ore that can be worked very cheaply. This is also stated to be the case by Mr. Percy, and clearly proves what the consequences will be if any extra burden is placed upon iron and wire manufacturers. The question, then,.in my humble opinion, will be among some of our iron manufacturers whether it will not pay them better to go to America and erect works there where they know, with good management, what can be done, rather than remain here to be ruined, as Mr. Percy says they will be, if an Eight Hours Bill be- comes law. Therefore, I trust nothing will occur as to the restriction of labour, which will press upon manu- facturars so hard as to make it impossible to compete with Americans, and so compel them to close further work 4 here, and drive them over to America to erect works there.—Yours truly,-
CONSIDERATION. Warrington, February 23rd, 1891.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 28, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 28, 1891.
THE GOSPELS AND THEIR AUTHORSHIP.

Sir,—After the extraordinary effusion of Saturday last, Mr. Gandy should scarcely expect me to bestow much attention on anything he may have to say upon the above subject. His labyrinthine logic displayed in the matter Of Professor Beet would of itself discourage me from any prolonged argument with him. But when I come to his attempt to deal with the facts and evidence of early Christian literature—and find that he accepts the very enlightened view—to say nothing of its charity —that " the Christians of the first three centuries—were of all men the most unprincipled liars and forgers," I am simply in despair of ever reaching him. My friend is evidently not acquainted with the best current litera- ture upon this subject and the present state of the argu- ment as maintained by the highest critics and scholars of our day, with reference to the gospels and their author- ship, as founded upon the evidence supplied by the earliest Christian writings. It may suit him to quote general and indefinite remarks from Mosheim, or from some obscure and little known modern writer; but he must not expect me to accept such sweeping statements against the particular and individual cases I have in- stanced, namely Papias, as cited by Eusebius, and Iretkeus, whose testimony I quoted. I beg to remind my friend that he has not touched my argument. The point under discussion is, who are the ;authors of the four gospels? I gave the passage from a ' lost work of Papias preserved for us in Eusebius, in which ?vies says that Matthew and Mark wrote certain gospels. I also stated that this Papias received his information from two personal followers of Christ ; that he lived from the year A.D. 70 to the year 165, very far on into the 2nd century. I also referred to lrenceus who wrote only a few years after him, A.D. 177,and who tells explicitly that the four gospels were written by Matthew, Mark, Luke and Jahn and had ever been received as such in all the churches. I pointed out that this testi- mony takes us back to the very days of the apostle John —since Irenteus was a disciple of Polycarp who was a disciple of John. His evidence, therefore, is virtually the evidence of the last of the apostles, for he would get his information from John through Polycarp. Mr. Gandy's statement, therefore—taking into account the passage of Papias—is absolutely not true—when he either tells us that we have no mention of the gospels before the time of Irengeus, or that "they were presented to the world upon no other authority than his." If one will exercise a little common sense, it may be easily seen how impos- sible it was that the whole of the then Christian world could have been imposed upon for the first time by Irenmus. If this irreproachable Christian Father had been the " unprincpled liar" some modern slanderers would have us to believe the early Christians were—it is hardly likely that some of the wits of Antioch--the edu- cated scholarly men of Alexandria, Rome, and Athens, many of whom were then flourishing in the churches there, would not have called Irenceus to account and demanded to know upon what authority " othei than his" own he presented his gospel to the world. The very absurdity of the statement is its own refuta- tion. •

But my friend having appealed to Mosheim—to Mos- heim he shall go. On page 64, Ist vol. he may read— "Before the middle of the , second century (A.D. 150) most of the books composing the New Testament were in every Christian church throughout the known world, and were regarded as a divine rule of faith ; hence it may be concluded that it was while some of the Apostles were still living, or certainly while their disciples and immediate successors were everywhere to be met with, that these books were carefully distinguished from other writings written by man. That those four of them which are called Gospels were combined during the life of St. John, and that the first three were approved by this holy personage we learn from the testimony of Eusebius (Hist. Eccles. 111. 24)." Further on Mosheim refers to the fraudulent writings falsely ascribed to Apostles, and to the necessity there was that the rulers of the churches should take care "to separate without delay the books which came from Apostolic hands from the mass (it trash, and to form them into a volume by them- selves" (page 66). But nowhere am I able to find in Mosheim that the fathers of the Ist or 2nd century- " coonted it pious to lie and cheat." The vicious mode of disputing called economical introduced by a class of heretics in an after agehad no application in that earlier time either to the men or to their special work. My friend may dismiss as a mere fancy what he calls the "aerial" regions of ecclesiastical history. I find some very solid walks there; and if he would tread the same paths with a more discerning spirit, he would not retail the old wives' fable about 'books "leaping on a communion table." He would know that this story is a mere fistion—and has no historical foundation whatever. He would also not blunder over the first Council of Nice having anything to do with decisions upon the Scrip- tures themselves. This Councit--never- de.lt withr-the question at all (see Dr. Westeott's Canon of the New Testament page 426.) I also deny point blank that any other Council made that to be Holy Scripture—which I was not Holy Scripture before—and which had not been already received at such a part from any conciliar deci- sions. "The Councils introduced no innovations—but merely proposed to preserve the tradition which had been handed down—that is they were merely declara- tive of what had been received as sacred scriptures in the churches." (Westcott, page 421). That in the second and third centuries the churches of Christ were infested with heretics, false philosophers, and fraudulent writers is true enough, and among such, many may fairly be described as "forgers and liars," but that the churches and the great body of Christians generally did not or could not distinguish between their false writings and the true Gospels is as foolish a state- ment as that our own age has not distinguished between the Scriptures and the Mormon imposture of Joe Smith. Let me also tell Mr. Gandy that I reject his very positive statement that the disciples of Christ were so ignorant "they could not write." He should have told us where he got that information from. We do know that Matthew the Apostle had been a tax-gatherer under the Roman Government, and it argues strange intel- ligence to say that such an officer " could not write." I may close now with making some very positive state- ments which my friend may verify if he will take the trouble to do so :—The truth of the authorship of the four Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles—which is the question under dispute—has been established upon un- answerable historical evidence. Dr. Lightfoot, the late Bishop of Durham, and Dr. Westcott, the present Bishop —two of the ablest scholars England has ever produced —have done this effectually in their respective works "Reply to the Author of Supernatural Religion," and "History of the Canon of the' New Testament." In Germany, Professor Tischendorf has answered the question "When were our Gospels written ?" a trans- lation of which may be got tor a shilling from the London Tract Society. In the same country, Dr. Bern- hard Weiss in his "Life of Jesus," has shown how positively the contentions of hostile criticism against the ancient testimonies to the authorship of the Gospel of John especially,have been refuted. Whilst Ernest Renan,' the ablest of French sceptics—in his "Life of Jesus " sums up his inquiriet by the words—",l admit the four Canonical Gospels as serious documents. All go back to the age which followed the death of Jesus ; "and speak- ing of the third Gospel and the Acts, he says—" The au- thor of this Gospel is certainly the same as the author of the Acts of the Apostles. Now, the author of the Acts.is a companion of Paul, a title which perfectly applies to Luke" (Life of Jesus quoted by Dr. Wace on the Four Gospels pp. 14, 31, and 43). Now,let me ask any thought- ful man who cares to know the truth in this matter— can he imagine that a sceptic of Ernest Renan's type, who has spent almost his life in the examination and sifting of ancient documents, could have come to such a conclusion if the testimony of Papias and Irenieus (with other witnesses of the second century whom I have not cited) is to be classed, as Mr. Gandy pretends, amongst that of "liars, cheats, and forgers"? • I advise my friend to read and think more upon this subject before he writes agaiii upon it. If he will spend the next twelve months in the close study of the English authorities I have referred him to in this and my former letter, he will perhaps rise to the conviction -that the whole canon of the sacred Scriptures is an "impregnable rock," and can be no more shaken by the shafts of modern scepticism than the everlasting hills can be by means of a pop-gun.—Yours, Sze.,
JOHN DIGNUM. Penketh, 19th February, 1891.

div.head: FIGHTING IN CHILI.
div.p: FIGHTING IN CHILI.
OVER 200 KILLED.

Telegrams from Buenos Ayres report heavy fight- ing on the 15th between the Chilian revolutionaries and the Government forces. The insurgents bom- barded and captured Iquique, six of the principal squares being reduced to ruins, and it is declared that 200 women and children perished in the wrecked houses. On the night of the 16th a mob of incendiaries attempted to fire the city, but were over- powered by the fleet and an armed fbrce of foreign residents, 175 of the mob being killed or wounded in the struggle. The presence of Admiral Hothant, in command of the English warships Espiegle,War- spite, and Pheasant, prevented much loss of life and damage to property. At the date of the des- patch a decisive battle was believed to be imminent north of Pisagua.

A Dalziel's telegram from Athens, Georgia, says that John L. Sullivan nearly, killed a brakesman on the rail- way train near theret, on Wednesday, while drunk. The Prince of Wales visited the. Shire Horse Show at the Agricultural Hall on Wednesday, and distributed the prizes to successful exhibitors. During the day the Council of the Shire Horse Society held their annual meeting. GENERAL YON CAPRIVI.
General George Von Caprivi de Caprera de Monte- cu, 'from an illustrious Italian stock.

He was born at Berlin on the 24th of February, 1831, his father being a high legal func- tionary in the Prussian ser- vice. In 1849 he entered Of army, in which his promotio] was rapid. He served wit] distinction in the campaign.
of 1864 and 1866, acted n

chief of the staff of the 10t Corps in 1870, and gained additional credit in all the battles of the Loire. In 1883 he was promoted to the command of the 39th division at Metz. The following year saw him transferring his services from the army to the navy, in which he succeeded Herr Von Stosch as the head of the admiralty. On William II coming to the throne, General Caprivi undertook the re-organisation of the navy, and in this gave such satisfaction to his Imperial master that he was rewarded by being appointed to the command of the 10th or Hanoverian Army Corps. On March 19th, 1890, the fotmal appointment of General Caprivi was notified as successor to Prince Bismarck, who ten da3s later quitted Berlin. The new German Chancellor is reported to possess great force of character and will, and personally beats a remark- able resemblance to Prince Bismarck, though, physically, even a bigger man than he.
SAD DEATH OF THE REV. H. C. STUBBS.

On Saturday the Rev. Henry Cuttill Stubbs, vicar of Ashton Hayes, Cheshire, hurried to the station to catch the tiain to Chester. He felt unwell when entering the train, but at Chester medical attend- ance had to be obtained. The rev, gentleman had to be removed to Ashton Heyes Vicarage, where he died on Thursday. The deceased was formerly classical tutor at St. Mark's Training College, Ful- ham, and afterwards for several years principal of the Clergy Daughters' School and Training College, Warrington.

div.head: CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
div.p: CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

A meeting of the Sub-Committee of the Cheshire County Council was held at Crewe on Thursday afternoon, to deal with applications made for grants in aid under the Technical Instruction Act. The meeting lasted several hours, and important resolotions were come to. It was decided, first, to extend the time in which applications should be received for grants to June nevt ; secondly, that no applications should be considered except from authorities who were disposed to levy a local rate; thirdly, that the divisions should be made propor- tionally between urban and rural districts, accord- ing to rateable value.

div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.

TUESDAY.—Before Mr. Brundrit and Major Hazlehurst. CATHERINE'S 40TH APPEARANCE.--Catherine McConn made her 40th appearance and was committed to prison for a month for being drunk and disorderly on the pre- vious day. _ _

WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Brundrit and Major Hazlehurst. DRUNKENNESS.—Susanah Beans, a well-known face at the court, went to gaol for a month in default of paying a fine of 40s. and costs for being drunk and disorderly. —John McCaffery was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for being drunk.
ALLEGED THEFT.—John Duggan, a navvy, was re- manded for a week on a charge of stealing a pair of boots value Bs. 6d., .the property of Thomas Whinyates, of Church-st.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. A. Thomas and Mr. James Handley.

TEMPORARY AUTHORITY.—George Turley was granted temporary authority to sell at the Norton Arms Hotel, Halton, under the license of the late Edward Badley. CHIMNEY ON FIRE.—Jas. Wood was ordered to pay 45. 6d. costs, for allowing the chimney of his dwelling- house to be on fire.

DAMAO. TO A H AYSTACK . —Alfred Thomas, Thos. Dean, and Samuel Jackson, boys, were summoned for unlaw- fully committing damage to a stack of hay, belonging to Matthew John Sweetma,n, coal dealer, Mill Brow. It was proved the boys had pulled the thatch off, and each defendant was ordered to pay 6s. Bd. damage and 3s. 6d. costs.

UNPROVOKED ASSAULT.—Wm. Hatthett, Ship Canal worker, pleaded guilty to assaulting Mary Collingwood, by striking her on the, face with his fist. He was fined 10s. and:costs, £l. Mr. Burton appeared for the com- plainant.

- DRUM( AND DISORDERLY.—For this offence Frederick Williams and Wm. Jones-were each fined ss. and costs, and Mary Smith and Mary Connolley-, were each sen- tenced to 14 days hard labour for disorderly conduct. ROBBERY.—WID. Hughes pleaded guilty to stealing a pair of boots and a vest belonging to Robert Foulkes, of 42, Norfolk-st. On Friday night the prisoner obtained the articles from Mrs. Foalkes on the plea that her son had sent for them, a statement which proved to be false, and he was apprehended an the Schooner Teaser. As this 'vas his first offence he was fined 10S. or 14 days.
WIDNES POLICE COURT.
WOXDAY.—Before Mr, H. Gaskell. jun. (chairman), and
Lieutenant-Colonel Easkll.

DRUNKENNESS.—Bridget Carlon, Pear-st., Ann Moor, Wellington-st., Emma Jones, no settled residence, John McMahon, Victoria-st., and John Tobin, 33, Katherine- st., were each tined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly. BEGGING.—John Ryan, no fixed residence, was charged in custody with begging in Victoria-road, Widnes, on Sunday afternoon, and he was committed to gaol for 14 days with hard labour. • ALLEGED THEFT FROM THE PERSON.—Mary Tracy, 13, Nelson-st., was brought up on remand charged with stealing 325. in money from the person of Roger Powell, on the 12th inst. Superintendent Noblett stated that the nrisoner, in company with another woman named Mary Jane-Riley-, who had been committed for trial, was seen on the night in question to take from the pockets of the prosecutor, who is a sea captain, and resides at Dun- garvan, Ireland, a purse containing 325., the prosecutor at the time being under the influence of drink. Since the case was heard against Riley the prosecutor had gone away with his ship,and had not since been heard of. The only thing he could do under the circumstances was to apply for a remand for another week. The prisoner was again remanded for a week. THEFT Yam! A PUBLIC-HOUSE. John McMahon, a young man residing in Victoria-st., was charged in'cus- tody with stealinga silk handkerchief, valued at 6s. 6d., from the Ship Inn, Widnes' on, the 21st inst. the pro- perty of Wm. Jones. On Saturday night, about eight o'clock,the prisoner came to the Inn the worse for drink, and was put out. A few minutes later he entered the house. again and broke a window. Prosecutor again put him out, and shortly afterwards missed the handkerchief. Mary Coffey, with whom the prisoner lodged, spoke to the prisoner wearing the handkerchief when he came home on Saturday night. The prisoner, who pleaded guilty, was fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days. . _ .
TiunsDAY.--Before Mr. Brock and Lieutenant-Col Gaskell.
DRUNICENKESS.—MichaeI Murray, Halewood; William Beresford,lrwell-st.,and Edward Roberts,no fixed abode, abodewere each fined ss. and costs for drunkenness.

BREACH OF THE PEACE.—john and Mary Moores, hus- band and wife, were each bound over to keep the:peace for three months, for fighting together in Wblmsley-st. -CHIMNEY ON FlRE.—George Whitfield, Wareing-st., was fined is. and 'costs for this offence.

PEOGY.—A fine of Is. and costs was imposed upon two youths named James Byron and Peter Carrigan for play- ing" peggy" in Warrington-road. &How. BOARD CASES.—A number of parents were a im- moned for neglecting to send their children regularly to school, and the usual fine of ss. was imposed in each case. A boy named Connor was sent to St. George's Industrial School until he is 16 years of age. UNLICENSED DOGS.—A fine of 7s. 6d. and costs was im- posed upon each of the following for keeping unlicensed dogs :—James R. Kendrick, Lacey-st. ; Samuel Reid, Widnes-rd.; Samuel Tonkies, Mersey- rd.; Sebastian Kendrick, Major Cross-st. ; George Illesketh, James-st. ; William Palin Ann-st. West; C. H. Chrimes, Viaduct-st.; and James McDonald, Mersey-rd. THEFT FROM WORKS.—Ann lane Wood. and Eliza- beth Ann Mitchell, girls, residing in Sankey-st., were charged .with stealing timber valued at 2d. from the works of Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon; and Co. Mitchell was fined 2s. 6d. and costs, and Woods, who has been twice previously convicted, was fined 7s. 6d. and costs. CRUELTY To A DONKEY.—James Marsh, Warrington- rd., was charged with cruelly ill-treating a donkey by working it whilst in an unfit state.—P.C. Cummings proved that on the 13th inst. the donkey was being worked in a cart, while it was suffering great pain from a large raw wound on the shoulder. In consequence of the poverty of the defendant, a fine of only 29. 6d. and costs 15s. 6d. was imposed.

A DESPERATE PRIZEFIGHT. A PUGILIST KILLED. COLUMBUS, Omo, THUR.SDAY.—A desperate prize-fight took place yesterday in this`State betw3en David Saville, Columtus, and Mink Tracey, Toledo. Eighteen rounds were fought; when Tracey was knockad out, and died from the injuries received a few hours later.

Mr. Charles Fox, secretary of the Borough Land and Building Society, Burnley, gave himself up to the police on Tuesday night, and confessed that he had defrauded the society. He is detained in custody. An old woman was on Tuesday found dead in a Gates- head lodging-house with her skull fractured. An old pensioner named Walters has been arrested on sus-
SUICIDE., 030 A PHILANTH'ROPIST.
Mr. Henry Hope Morley; known in connection with philanthropic work, committed suicide by cutting his throat at an hotel at Launceston, yesterday morn- ing.
DR. WESTCOTT.

The subject of this notice is now Bishop of Dur- 'ln March last succeeded his late comrade in studies, Bishop Lightfoot. The Right Rev. Brooke Foss Westcott, D.D., was born near Birmingham in January, 1825. He was edu- ;ated at Trinity College, Cam- bridge, at which he was Juccessively Scholar and Fe!- ow. He took his B.A. degree

in January, 1848, as twenty- , thin] _ Jr in mathematical honours, was brac- keted first (with Dr, Scott, of Westminster) in the first class of the Classical Tripos, and was second Chancellor's Medallist. His University career wasl more than ordinarily distinguished, as he obtained the Battie University scholarship in 1846, and again in the following year, and obtained the Bachelor's prize for Latin essay in 1847, and again in ' 1849. In 1852 he became an assistant master at Harrow, and remained there till 1869, in which year he was made Canon of Peterborough. The ability and scholarship, shown in his writings, not- ably in his "Introduction to the Study of the Gos- pels," led to his appointment to the Regius-Profes- sorship of Divinity at Cambridge. In 1884 he was appointed to a Canonry at Westminster, and on the death of Dr. Lightfoot, he was chosen as his succes- sor in the See of Durham—a selection most cordially received by Churchmen cf Very different schools of thought. Bishop Westcott co-operated with Dr. Hort in the production of a well-known edition of the Greek New Testament,and was one of the mem- bers of the New Testament Company for the revi- sion of the authorised version of the Bible. He is next to, or perhaps side by side with,Dr. Lightfoot, the most conspicuous and successful controversialist whom the German critics of the Tubingen school have had to confront in their attacks on what Canon Liddon has called the " title,-deeds" of Chris- tianity. By virtue of his rank, coming, with the Bishops of London and Winchester, immediately after the two archbishops, the new Bishop of Dur- ham became at once entitled to a seat in the House of Peers. Dr. Westcott is the 84:th Bishop of Dur- ' ham,the See of Durham having been founded in the year 635.
THE WESLE YAN CENTENARY. PRESENTATION CHAIR'.

Messrs. R. Garnett and Sons, ot Warrington, are exhibiting in their showroom, a Apecially designed chair, which is their contribution to the Wesleyan Methodist Connexion, and is intended to be used next week by the President of the Conference (the Rev. Dr. Moulton)—who is principal of the. Ley& College, Cambridge,—in the City-road Chapel, Lou- don, in connection with the Centenary services.. The chair is of classic design, made in fine figured Spanish mahogany, the panels being framed and richly carved. In the back are carved the letters —" The Wesley Centenary, 18917 and above this inscription, cleverly arranged in ebony, are seen the eastern and western hemispheres and the text in gold letters "The world is my parish." The back of the chair and the seat are finished in rich dark blue morocco, and the chair altogether is a work of most artistic construction.

div.p: MARKETS.

MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY.—There is no,appreciable. improvement in either the quantity or quality of workable business on the market. Spinners are not making much progress, and larger sales of cotton do not stimulate aaybody to go in for yarns at quotations. Cloth is not apprEelably improved. There continues to be some Eastern business workable, but prices are very poor. Printers and finishing cloths are not any better, and the home houses are only- keeping up assortments.

div.head: SHIPPING CRISIS IN THE NORTH
div.p: SHIPPING CRISIS IN THE NORTH

The shipping crisis-- is serious at Aberdeen,where all the dock labourers hays come out on strike to support the Union seamen and stevedores. Dock work it prac- tically stopped. THE LABOM COMMISSION. We understand that the Cabinet will decide to-day upon the terms of reference to the Royal Commission upon Labour, and that it is, espected the Commission will commence its sittings before Easter.

THE IRISH illigEL CASE. The hearing of the action for libel brought by Mr.. Timothy Harrington, M.P., one- of the joint secretaries' of the Irish National League,, against J. J. Lalor, pub- lisher of the "Insuppressible "'newspaper, was resumed this morning before Mr. Justice-Harrison and a special! jury. The action was brought to. recover £l,OOO dam-- ages. The jury found a verdict for Mr. Harrington fort £5 damages.
THE DIVORCE ACTION OF /MR. A. L. BROWN, M.P. _ _

The hearing of the divorce action by Mr. A. L. Brown, M.P., was continued at Edinburgh yesterday. Mrs. Brown had been examined in calvera, and denied any impropriety. The co-respondent Shiels was examined, and said he walked out with Mrs. Brown in Edinburgh, and visited Berwick by appointment, but no impro- priety took place. He visited Oakiea, but denien the charge of impropriety in the tool house or in the grounds. He kissed her when sitting, on Langlee Hill.

div.head: BACCARAT SCANDAL.
div.p: THE BACCARAT SCANDAL.

Yesterday, the correspondence between. the solicitors of the two parties in the baccarat case is published Messrs. Lewis wrote on the 24th inst. to. Messrs. Wont- ner and Sons, declaring they were prepared, on behalf of the defendants, to kefer the matter cA issue to the de- cision of three independent men of known position and honour; such trial to take place in open conrt. Messrs. Wontner replied on the same day, on behalf of Sir Wm. Gordon Cumming, declaring their cliontbad no intention of submitting hiscase to anybody but.o.4;/ury, and would not adopt the course suggested. THE WHITECHAPEL TRAGEDY.

The inquest on the body of Frances Coles., the victim of the latest Whitechapel mtirder, was resumed yesterday. Detective-Sergeant Butcher produced a plan of the locality, and said there were eight modes of getting away from the archway where the bodyufi the murdered woman was found. Ellen Caelanan said that at about L3O on Friday morning she and the deceased met a man in Commercial-st. It was not Sadler, buba shorter man, Coles went in • the direction of the Minories with him, although witness advised her not to. She had not before said that this occurred at three o'clock. Wm. Friday, a carman, deposed to seeing deceased speaking with a man in the Royal Mint-st., at ten minutes to two on the morning of the 13th. After some furthers evidence, the jury returned a verdict of "Wilful murder" against some person or persons unknown.
GERMANY AND FRANCE

BERLIN, YTIDAY ArrEnNoox.—Some onsation has been caused by an announcement in an Imperial Office Gazette that tiler Imperial Chancellor has instructed the Governorof Alsace and Lorraine to make no, further con- cessions in regard te the passport and other regulations on the French frontier.

THE EMPRESS FREDERICK'S VISIT. PARra, FRIDAY. - The Empress Frederick and her daughter, the Princess Margaret of Prussia.. left here by the tidal train at ten minutes past ten this•morning, their way to England. There was no demonstration, hostile.Or otherwise.
The Empress Frederick arrived at Dover at five o'clock yesterday afternoon, and proceeded by special train to Windsor.
YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF IiORDS. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on th& woolsack at a quarter past four.

lialscrotzAztaors.—The Local Government Provisional Order (Poor-Law) Bill passed through Committee and the Fishery Board Scotland Bill was read a second time. The House adjourned at ten minutes to fitfe. HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. OVERHEAD WIRES.—The House considered the London Overhead Wires Bill in regard to which after a second reading an instruction was moved to the Committee to so amend the measure as to bring its provisiwas in accord- ance with those of the Public Health Amendment Act. After considerable discussion the House diVided,when the instruction was carried by 99 to 83. XlVfratiemirr FUNERAL.—Mr. MATTHEWS,, vestioned as to the alleged disorderly proceedings at Litchfield, on the occasion of a midnight funeral Of the late Colonel Dyott, informed the House that the newspaper reports of the affair were exaggerated. Only one public-house was granted extension of time and that was situated opposite the church at which the funeral took place, He did not think the justices haa acted indiscreetly in giving an extra hour to this house. All was quietethere and no serious complaint made.

THE EIGHT HOURS BILL.—Mr. SMITH said the Govern- ment could not advance the consideration of the mines Eight Hours Bill until after Easter, and he therefore could not say when a day could be given for the debate. BANK NOTES.—Mr. GOSCHEN, asked to state whether it was his intention to propose any change. as to existing issues of bank notes, said he was unwilling to commit himself upon the matter of the future action of the Goviernmertt in any way. Tim LAND ,IND THE TAXIS.—On the motion to go into Committee of Supply, Mr. PROVAND called attention to the taxation on land, and moved that in the opinion of the house the proportion of taxation which fell upon and was payable by land and its rentals was insufficient and ought to be increased. He stated that, out of the 135 millions of taxation levied annually in this country, not more than five millions from all sources were taken j from the land, while, exclusive of the spirit and tobaccol taxes, 80 millions were levied upon the industries of the country. MT. J. STUART seconded the resolution.—Mr. H. CHAPLAIN maintained that the whole of the;burden of the rates eventually fell upon the •owner of the land. The Government were quite prepared, to divide the rates between the owner and occupier. After some discussion, the House divided, and Mr. PROVAND'S resolution was rejected by- 128 to 77. . . _
-The Balsa was counted out at half-past eight.

In the London Bankruptcy Court on Tuesday, a proposal on b'ehalf of Mr, G. M. Byrne, M.P., to pay a dividend of a shilling in the pound, with all costs, and vest certain equities of redemption in a trustee for the benefit of the creditors, was accepted.
WARRINGTON PERMANENT BENEFIT BUILDING SOCIETY.

The annual meeting of the members of this Society-was held last evening in Cairo-st. school- room. Nr. J. Kenworthy presided, and others on the platform were Rev. S. Kenworthy, Messrs. R. Davies, Kirkconnel, C. Twiss, j.. Dewhurst, G. Legge, Ji Critchley, T Ctitchley,. W. Dick, G. W. Gaskell,,X. Kay, J. Mather, P. C. Price, and R. Proud (secretary). There wasn fair attendance of mem- bers.

The Managers submitt3& their twenty-fourth annual report to the meeting. it)stated that "The total receipts are £5,663 7s. 2d. The advances made to borrowers, amount to £1,014 125.,-against £.2,.603 Ns. 2d. repaid leaving the balance of the mortgage accounts £47,028 10s. 10d. The amount subscribed by investors is £B4B 4s. 3d. against £2,826 10s. Od. withdrawn, leaving the balance of that account £444710104, 9d. The entrance fee is now 4s. per share. The profits,, after deducting working expenses, are £w.4..021 19s. W., out of which the managers declare a dividend at the na.te of £4 ss. per cont. which absorbs £1,684112e. 11'd., leaving a balance of £2O 3s. 7d., which is ca,rried to the contingent fund. There are 502 members upon the book,. whom 437 are investors, and 65 borrowers.

The CHAIRMAN, who movedthe-adoptian of the report,. said that building operations had not been very exten- sively carried on in Warrington of late years. What was the cause of it he was not prepared to say. One reason was, perhaps that there had, been sufficient houses for the accommodation of the people, but perhaps the pre- sent high rates had something to do with the non-build- ing of houses.' He saw a,statement not long ago, he thought it was made by Mr. Chamberlain, that where a borough's rates were- more than. 55. in the £ they were not fitf to. have local government. (Laughter.) If • that statement were true it would apply with strong force to Warrington.. (Hear, hear). As far as the Society was concerned he. thought it was in a thoroughly sound condition, All their advances dur- ing the year had been made on good security, and the securities for what they had:previously advanced were now in a very good position. (Applause).—Mr. R. DAVIES said the Society had now gone. on for 24 years, and the report they hadlnews- beforethem was, to the best of his belief,*, as good and sound as any before presented to the Society. (Rear, hear). He was not one of those who considered the rates of Warrington very high. If he had hi- way they would be nearly one half as much again. (Laughter.), Be should widen Bridge-st, and make the towar, more fit for loccmotion. He wanted to know- what they were to do with the 100,000 people they expected to have in Warrington ill a few years. He somedsimes, came into the town on a, Saturday night and he could hardly move along the streets, and what they were to do with the addi- tional 50,000 he did not know. He also held that they should try to make Warrington a sanitary town,' something like what he could recollect it to be, • when salmon was caught iwthe river. He could remem- ber when Mr. Taylor, of the. Feathers Inn, Bridge-st., who had the fishery, .caught eleven salmon in one day. He, however, scarcely hopedto see this great improve- ment made in his day.—The Rey. A- KEN-WORTHY having also given a short address, the report was adopted.
