An extraordinary scene was witnessed at Carrick-on- Shannon on Sunday. Mr. T. Healey, M.P., and other members of the high Parliamentary party, had arranged to address a meeting there. A band of fifty Parnellites marched into the square, armed with sticks, and a dis- turbance followed. The Parnellites charged the platform and hooted and groaned so continuously that the meeting had to be adjourned to the chapel yard. During the attack, which was continued by the Parnellites for a long time, many persons were injured. One of the ringleaders was arrested. • THREE MEN KILLED IN WALES. Three men were killed snd eight others seriously in- jured on Saturday afternoon, through the collapse of the foundations of a house in course of erection on the beach at Pwllheli. The three men killed were working in the cellaring,and were dug out dead. The remaining eight were engaged in the upper part of the building. One of the deceased was named Morgan, and lived at Pwllheli, and the other two were named Jones. The house faces the promenade, which was opened by the Postmaster-General last Whit-Monday. ... • EATEN BY WOLVES IN HUNGARY. Two clergymen of the Greek Church in Temesvar, Hungary, drove out in a small sledge with a coachman and two horses the other day. On their return they were pursued by a large pack of howling wolves, and, though the coachman drove the terrified horses at a mad pace, the wolves succeeded in mounting the sledge from behind, and in dragging off and killing the priests. The coachman and horses escaped. Next day two night- watchmen who were on duty on the outskirts of the city met with the same fate. A third watchman saved his life by climbing a tree. --40.---4-- A BRITISH VESSEL SUNK AND SEVEN LIVES LOST. A collision occurred at five o'clock on Saturday morn- ing near the British lightship Galloper, in the North Sea, between the steamer Ipswich, plying between Antwerp and Harwich, and the British barque Queen, bound from Rotterdam to Cardiff. The Ipswich struck the Queen at right angles, almosputting her in two and causing her to sink immediately. The captain and six of the crew who were on the bridge at the time jumped into the life- boat, but owing to the general excitement she capsized, and the occupants were drowned. The cook and three sailors, who had taken refuge in the rigging, were saved by a boat from the Ipswich.

At the Liverpool Police Court. on Wednesday, Alfred D. Golding, land,estate, and insurance agent, Central-buildings, north John-st., was fined £lO and costs for having wilfully been a party to the continued use of the houses,B and 10,Seagrave-st.,as disorderly houses. The defence was that Mr. Gold- ing was simply the secretary to a building society, who were the mortgagees of the property, and had foreclosed. The prosecution was the first of the kind under the "purity crusade," only the actual keepers having hitherto been proceeded against. Mrs. Ann Sutton, of Widnes, was proceeded against under similar ciroumstances in respect of the house 11, Seagrave-st., but as the Bench considered there were extenuating circumstances, bail was accepted on defendant's behalf for the future respectability of the house. • FIGHTING IN BURMAIL BURNING OF WUNTHO. RANGOON, WEDNESDAY.—The Shwebo colhmn has had a sharp action with the followers of the Tswabwa of Wuntho at Okpho. The enemy were routed with a loss of fifty killed. A number of guns and a quantity of ammunition also fell into the hands of the British. The casualities of the British were three European soldiers killed and ten wounded. Wuntho is held by six hundred of the Tswabwa's men, and will be attacked to- morrow. RANGOON, WEDNESDAY.—Wuntho has been occupied by Major Smyth's mounted infantry without opposition. Major Smyth reports that when the troops arrived there the Tswabw's Palace was being strongly stockaded. It has since been set on fire and destroyed. The villagers are now returning in large numbers, and laying down their arms. The Tswabwa is believed to have fled to Pinlebu, whither the column is now proceeding. Captain Hutchinson, advancing to 'Wynn from Yeu, found him- self confronted by a strong stockade held by the rebels near Okham. An assault was ordered, and the position was captured after five hours' fighting. The enemy lost , 27 killed. Captain Hutchinson was severely wounded in the thigh. Dacoits have attacked a village six miles south of Bhamo, inflicting considerable damage, and carrying off four women. A "Times" telegram from Rangoon, on Thursday, says Tswabwa's palace at Wuntho has been burned, in order to convince the people that his rule is terminated. Tsawabwa has retreated to Pinlaing, and the column is proceeding thither.

WARRINGTON UNlON.—Persons willing to CONTRACT for the supply of any of the undermentioned articles from Lady Day to Michaelmas next, to be delivered free of expense at the Warrington Union Workhouse, or at the Indus- trial Schools, Padgate, at such times and in such quantities as the Board of Guardians shall direct, are requested to send in TENDERS, properly sealed, endorsed, and free of expense, addressed to the Clerk to the Guardians, before four o'clock p.m. on Tuesday, the 10th day of March. The following are the articles for which tenders are required : Groceries and Provisions Shoes and Clogs Beef and Mutton Glazing „ Joints for Officers Brushes Milk Coffins Flour and Meal Best Oakum Rope for picking Loaves of Bread Best Penmaenmawr Stone Beer and Porter for breaking purposes Straw and Potatoes Leather Drapery, &c. Wood for cutting into Fire- Cord and Twill wood Coal and Slack Earthenware Samples of any of the above may be seen on application to the Master of the Workhouse. The Coal and Slack supplied must be to the satisfaction of the House and Schools Commit- tees. The Pit and quality of Coal must be named in the Tender. Forms of tender and full particulars as to the prob- able quantities of each article required may be obtained at the Clerk's Office. Each tender must be made upon the prescribed form, and properly enclosed and endorsed with the name of the• article tendered for. Each article tendered for must be of the size, material, or quality shown at the Workhouse or Schools. No Tenders for other Articles will be accepted. THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 29 H9l. NOTES ON GAMES AND . ATHLETICS. As Scotland managed on Saturday to, beat Ireland with rather more ease than did Englandothey will doubt- Ices look with confdence tothe great bat* at Richmond neat month. Four-goals and two triesisee wide margin and this, coupled with the big success of the English- men. goes to show tlie poor carsbre of the. Irish fifteen thia-year. The claims of Valentine to a place in the team that'is to do duty against Scotland'are being urged, and Crompton, the Runccrn three-quarter, is another player wiles& abilities deseree recognitions -- Seektg that Wigan cvereame Leedsa weekraero, Swin- ton did not bargain for a reverse a the Yorkshire town. As a Act, bowever, the .visitors were • sadly overplayed and had to accept defeat by a goal and three tries to a try, Bfiwiby being the onlySwintocian,who could score. The crowd were much annoyed at being kept waiting until 417.13 before a start was made,. the Lancashire players having been delayed en roan.; lip to the very last, althost, Salford lookd like winning their -fixture at ,Burton-cm-Trent, as they led by three tries to none. Then, however, F. Evemhed ran in and 4. goal follewed, the resulreeing a draw. The strength of the back play of the4limcorn men was manifested, at Broughton. where the- Cheshire crack; were victorious by a goal, placed by Houghton from a try by Hanrpson. This was the only point registered' ex- cept minorsa and Broughten• may be said 'to have done well againsesuch sturdy opponents. Houghton's display at full backvavas much admired. The West- Lancashire League competition on Saturday furnished a fluine surprise n the downfall of the pre- sent champions at home. NO one looked for the defeat of Wigan, and yet this was accomplished' by Warden, whoipeat them fairly and squarely. The scoring-powers of the Wigan men have fallen away of late. In the same tournament Leigh were vanquished by Avail, this being entirely due to a couple of dropped goals-by Anderton well on in the second half. The 12,000 -Spectators who paid a visit to Pike'a Lane on Saturday were peatly astonished at the terrible drubbing inflioted on Everton. When the draw forth& second round of the Lancashire ties was published this was regarded as the best of the whole series. Mark: the sequel, however. The Wanderers played as if for dear life for the whole hour and a half, and aehippEd their famous rivals by six goals to none. The game was quite as one-sided as the score indicates; the Evertonians being hardly ever even dangerous. It was a case ofalmost per- petual bombardment of the visitors' fortress, which often escaped owing to the poor shooting of the Wanderers'. forwards. The turf was very heavy and holding and in this respect favoured the home side without a doubt.. Everton were unfortunately, without Hannah, Doyle,. Latta, and Brady, whose absence of course made a differ- ence, especially that of the two backs. The defence of the Wanderers was marvellously safe, . and the speedy Everton forwards could make no impression on it what- ever. No club had previously scored more than three ghats against the Liverpool clubthisseason: The only League game that was down for decision on Saturday was looked upon as highly important. It was the first of the two between North-End and Sunderland, and as it was fixed for Deepdale, the champions of the past two seasons were sanguine as to the result. They were disappointed, however, and had to accept a draw, no goals being scored. Whilst the, forward play of the Wearsiders was in advance of that of the Prestonians, the backs of the latter were better, and Sunderland could not get through., The • cbampionship is still a matter of uncertainty, the Blackburn Rovers having now a fairly good chance of, carrying off the muoh4coveted prize. - I There was a general rejoicing when it became• known that Blackburn Rovers and Sunderland had escaped each other in the draw for the semi-finals for the FiX. Cup. Recent form points to these two great clubs meeting in the final tie, and whilst Sunderland are held in high esteem by many, other think experience will jiist about pull the Rovers safely home once more. They hay.ealready won the cup on four occasions, and if they hresuccess- ful fora fifth time it will indeed be a splendid victory. Of course, they have the Albion to account for-next Sat- urday, but this seems to be taken for granted. Notts area fine set of players, but they are not considered to be equal to the task of removing Sunderland from the competition.

FRODSHAM POLICE % COURT. On Monday at oakmer3 Petty Sessions the following Frodshatn cases were dealt with. AN ASSAULT AT NEWTON.—George Spruhe, Kingsley, was summoned by Frederick Bickerstaffe for assault on the 29th January at Newton,—Complainant deposed to haying attended a sale on the date named and to defendant coming to him and threatening to dash his brains out. Be struck him, in the face with his fists, blackening his eye.—Fined ss. and costs. WEAK Rtmr.—Jane Kerfoot, Queen's Head, Frodshatn, was summoned by Inspector. Robert Watts for selling adulterated- rum on the 13th: Jlanuary.—The Inspector stated that on the date named he called at the Queen's Head Hotel and purchased a pint of rum. He then told her it was to be analysed by the public analyst, and he divided it into three parts, leaving one sample with her. The following day he took one of the samples to Dr. Carter Bell, who analysed it, and certified that the rum was adulterated with 30. per cent, of water, or five per cent, more than allowed by Act of Parliament.—Defend- ant said she only pub the quantity of water to the spirit which she was told by the merchant.—The Chairman expressed the opinion that the spirit lost strength by keeping in the keg. The case was evidently one where there was no intentional adulteration. He believed the statement of the defendant. She would be let off by pay- ing the cost of the case, £1 Bs. 9d. THEFT OF it CARD:MAN JACKET.—Ellen Ellis, of no , known residence, was charged with stealing a jacket, I value 13s. 6d., the property of Messrs. Kay and Sons, clothiers, Frodsham, on the 2nd February; and Mary Hollins, also without residence, with receiving the jacket knowing it to be stolen.—Superintendent Walker, ex- plained that on the date named the jacket was seen at the shop of Messrs. Kay and Sons. Subsequently de- fendants went to a shop at Warrington and offered to pledge the jacket. The defendants were accordingly apprehended. The police did not believe the names which they had given to be correct, and there were yery great doubts as to one of them being a returned convict. He had had them remanded for the purpose of their being photographed, and they had distorted their features as much as possible, in order to avoid identifi- cation. They were committed to prison for three months with hard labour. DRUNKENNESS.—John Mercer, Thomas Hancock, Eliza- beth Hancock, John Connolley, and Mary Skelton and William Stanley, all of Frodsham, were charged with being drunk and disorderly. Fined ss. each.—George Jackson, of Frodsham, was summoned for being drunk and refusing to quit the licensed premises of the Weaver Tavern, on the 14th February. Fined 10s.
